title.rendered: Dubai launches Future Week bringing 10,000 global leaders, investors and innovators to emirate

content.rendered:
Dubai Future Week will bring leaders, investors and innovators together from November 18–21 to explore AI, business, health and technology.

Experts will examine how artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies will reshape business and everyday life.

Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence of the UAE, and Chairman of the Board of Trustees of Dubai Future Foundation (DFF), has directed Dubai Future Week to be held across Emirates Towers and the Museum of the Future.

Dubai Future Week 2026

Organised by Dubai Future Foundation, Dubai Future Week will bring several of the organisation’s established global events and initiatives together as part of a broader platform.

It will feature keynote addresses, debates, fireside conversations, workshops, international challenges and competitions, idea pitches, exhibitions, immersive experiences, specialist sessions and public activations.

Closed-door discussions will also form part of the programme.

Sheikh Hamdan: A global hub for ambitious ideas

Dubai Future Week represents the next stage in the development of Dubai Future Foundation’s global events and initiatives, bringing their communities and areas of expertise together.

Sheikh Hamdan said: “Dubai continues to strengthen its position as a global hub for the world’s most ambitious ideas and future-focused visions – a platform where impactful partnerships and initiatives take shape, and a destination for leading minds, experts and future shapers from around the world.”

The initiative continues Dubai’s efforts to design and shape the future under the vision of His Highness Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Vice President and Prime Minister of the UAE and Ruler of Dubai.

Sheikh Hamdan said the focus should be on using technological development to improve people’s lives.

He added: “Dubai calls on the world to embark on a new era of international collaboration that accelerates the use of technology in the service of people and societies. This requires directing investment and strategies towards technologies and innovations that advance human wellbeing, enhance quality of life, and help secure a better future for generations to come.”

Dubai AI Week and Future Forum brought together

Dubai Future Week will build on established events hosted by Dubai Future Foundation, including the Dubai Future Forum and Dubai AI Week.

Their communities, ideas and expertise will be brought together within the new platform.

Other major initiatives incorporated into the week will include AI Grandmaster, the Dubai Foresight Awards and the Dubai Future Solutions – Prototypes for Humanity exhibition.

The programme will also feature TED Talks.

Held under the tagline “For the Human of the Future”, the event is intended to examine technological, scientific, economic and social developments through their impact on people rather than treating individual technologies and industries in isolation.

AI, robotics, quantum computing and space

Technology will form a significant part of Dubai Future Week.

Its “How We’ll Think” track will examine intelligence, learning and knowledge in the age of AI, including the future of education, human cognition and decision-making.

Topics will include the skills future generations will require, the impact of artificial intelligence on how people access and interpret information, critical thinking, media literacy and cognitive enhancement.

A separate “How We’ll Innovate” track will look at robotics, automation and intelligent machines.

It will also consider developments in quantum computing, synthetic biology, materials science and space technologies, alongside questions over who controls technology, who benefits from it and how innovation should be governed.

Future of cities, homes and mobility

Dubai Future Week will be structured around five human-centred tracks:

  • How We’ll Live
  • How We’ll Think
  • How We’ll Innovate
  • How We’ll Feel
  • How We’ll Do Business

“How We’ll Live” will examine the future of homes, cities, mobility and longevity.

It will also cover climate resilience, net-zero infrastructure, nature-based urban solutions, rewilding, ocean health and ecosystem regeneration.

Security and defence, culture, identity and the changing meaning of belonging will also be considered.

Future of healthcare, food and longevity

Healthcare and wellbeing will form another major strand of the event.

“How We’ll Feel” will examine developments in healthcare, diagnostics, longevity science, mental health and biotechnology, alongside the future of sport, human performance and the wellness economy.

Food and agriculture will also be considered, including vertical farming, lab-grown proteins and AI-enhanced supply chains.

The programme is designed to examine how these developments could affect health, quality of life and the everyday experience of future generations.

Investors and entrepreneurs to examine future of business

Future Week will also examine how technology and changing economic models could reshape companies, investment and employment.

“How We’ll Do Business” will bring together entrepreneurs, investors and business leaders to discuss forces transforming business, finance and capital.

Topics will include decentralised economies, responsible applications of artificial intelligence in business, start-up ecosystems, evolving policy and regulatory frameworks and changes in the relationship between risk and return.

Participants will consider how companies can remain competitive and resilient as technologies, markets and models of value creation evolve.

The discussions will also examine what those changes could mean for people as employees, entrepreneurs and consumers.

Future Week will take place from November 18 to 21, 2026, across Emirates Towers and the Museum of the Future.

title.rendered: Saudi Arabia announces $2.5bn tech investment push as $1.2bn AI data centre expansion leads LEAP 2026

content.rendered:
Saudi Arabia announced around $2.5bn of technology investments and launches on the second day of LEAP 2026, led by major spending on data centres as the Kingdom expands infrastructure to support growing demand for artificial intelligence and computing.

The announcements span data centres, cloud services, technology localisation and research and development, including a $1.2bn expansion by Al Moammar Information Systems (MIS) and an $880m data centre development by NHC Innovation activity.

Al Moammar Information Systems (MIS) made the largest investment announcement of the day, committing $1.2bn to expand data centres in Saudi Arabia.

The investment will increase the company’s operational capacity to a total of 192 megawatts, supporting growing demand for computing and artificial intelligence services.

NHC Innovation activity announced an $880m investment to develop data centres in the Khuzam Digital Valley.

LEAP 2026 in Saudi Arabia

The project will provide integrated digital infrastructure with scalable capacity, targeting 65 megawatts by 2033.

Together, the two announcements represent more than $2bn of investment in data centre infrastructure.

Cloud infrastructure also featured prominently among the announcements. Mobily and BytePlus announced a joint investment of more than $150m to launch BytePlus cloud services in Saudi Arabia.

The investment is intended to expand access to advanced cloud solutions for companies and enterprises in the Kingdom. The announcements come as Saudi Arabia seeks to strengthen its position as a global hub for digital infrastructure and advanced technologies.

HPE and Intel launch Saudi Innovation Centre

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) announced an expansion of its “Saudi Made” programme, extending it from the localisation of hardware to integrated technology solutions.

HPE also announced the launch of the Saudi Innovation Centre in collaboration with Intel. The centre is intended to support startups and national talent working in artificial intelligence.

Nokia, meanwhile, announced the opening of its first research and development centre in Saudi Arabia.

The facility will focus on accelerating the development of AI-powered network automation technologies, strengthening research and innovation capabilities and developing advanced telecommunications solutions from Saudi Arabia.

Saudi investment targets digital infrastructure in Africa

Saudi investment in digital infrastructure is also extending into international markets.

Vision Invest and Africa Finance Corporation (AFC) announced a strategic investment in WIOCC to support the expansion of digital infrastructure in Africa and enhance connectivity and digital services across markets on the continent.

The investment forms part of a broader expansion of technology investment beyond the Kingdom while its domestic ecosystem grows across data centres, cloud services, research and development and technology localisation.

LEAP 2026 continues in Riyadh

LEAP 2026 continues through September 3 at the Riyadh Exhibition and Convention Centre in Malham.

The event brings together technology leaders, investors, innovators and startups from around the world, with its programme covering the future of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, digital infrastructure and advanced technologies.

The second-day investment announcements highlight the scale of capital being directed towards the infrastructure required to support the Kingdom’s expanding technology and artificial intelligence ecosystem.

title.rendered: UAE developer Arada enters Syria with $7bn New Damascus city including 11,000 homes

content.rendered:
UAE developer Arada has entered Syria with plans for a $7bn (AED25.7bn) fully integrated city west of Damascus, marking one of the most significant foreign real estate projects in the country since the beginning of its new chapter of national reconstruction and development.

The four million square metre New Damascus development will include 11,000 homes, 500 hotel rooms, 1,000 serviced apartments, a 300-bed hospital and education facilities for 5,000 students. Arada will develop the project through a joint venture with the state-owned Syrian Sovereign Fund.

Arada and the Syrian Sovereign Fund will act as partners on the development, with the master plan to be prepared in close partnership with the relevant Syrian government authorities.

The project will be fully aligned with Syria’s national reconstruction priorities and development goals.

Both organisations are also working together to identify further sites for development across Syria.

Arada plans $7bn New Damascus city in Syria

The agreement was signed at the Syrian Sovereign Fund’s headquarters in Damascus by Arada Group CEO Ahmed Alkhoshaibi and Mohammed Al Khayyat, Board Member and CEO of the Real Estate Development Sector at the Syrian Sovereign Fund.

President Ahmed al-Sharaa also received Arada Group CEO Ahmed Alkhoshaibi at the People’s Palace.

Arada’s entry makes it one of the first UAE developers to expand into Syria.

The New Damascus development has an estimated Gross Development Value (GDV) of $7bn (AED25.7bn).

It will be located near the Mezzeh district on a plateau approximately 10 minutes from Damascus city centre and 25 minutes from Damascus International Airport.

The site covers four million square metres and will include a dedicated 700,000 square metre public park. Plans for the mixed-use community include 11,000 homes spanning residential apartments, villas and townhouses, as well as branded residences.

The development will also feature 500 hotel rooms, 1,000 serviced apartments, education facilities for 5,000 students and a 300-bed hospital.

Office and commercial space, retail, extensive parks and recreational areas, government service buildings and other facilities designed to serve the community’s day-to-day requirements are also planned. The development model draws on the combined strengths of Arada’s Aljada and Masaar communities in the UAE.

Arada targets further development opportunities in Syria

Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed bin Talal, Executive Vice Chairman of Arada, said: “Syria is at a pivotal moment in its history, and the scale of the opportunity to rebuild and invest in its future is significant. Arada has spent nearly a decade delivering high-quality communities at scale, across multiple markets and in complex environments.

“Working with the Syrian Sovereign Fund, our organisation is uniquely well-placed to bring that experience to bear here, creating jobs, developing local skills, supporting Syrian businesses and contributing to the local economy. Arada’s success has been shaped by our willingness to make long term investments where others might hesitate with partners who share our vision to create genuine communities.”

The developer now has a project pipeline valued at $42bn across four markets and a portfolio of more than 66,000 homes.

Its operations span the UAE, the United Kingdom, Australia and, following the latest announcement, Syria.

The Syria expansion is the latest step in Arada’s international growth, with the developer and the Syrian Sovereign Fund already assessing further potential development sites in the country.

Syrian Sovereign Fund targets international investment

Mohammed Al Khayyat, Board Member and CEO of the Real Estate Development Sector at the Syrian Sovereign Fund, said: “Syria welcomes businesses and companies from around the world, and this strategic partnership with Arada is a powerful demonstration of what that means in practice. The Syrian Sovereign Fund’s mandate is to attract world-class investment that creates lasting value for the Syrian people, and we believe that this project represents exactly that.

“We’re grateful to Arada for their partnership and we look forward to working together to deliver projects that reflect the ambition and resilience of the Syrian people.”

The joint venture’s New Damascus development will be its first project, while the two partners continue to explore additional opportunities across Syria.

title.rendered: US launches new strikes on Iran as oil prices jump and Tehran threatens Gulf exports

content.rendered:
The US launched new air strikes on Iranian targets on Tuesday, quashing hopes that an exchange of fire last weekend might not lead to a wider renewal of hostilities.

Oil prices had already risen after that first exchange of direct attacks since July and after reports of two tankers being hit on Monday leaving the Strait, the global oil supply waterway that Iran has effectively closed to shipping. Brent crude futures, already up 2 per cent on the day, jumped almost 2 per cent more on the reports.

Tehran remained defiant, warning that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf, despite a threat by US President Donald Trump to hit Iran “hard” in response to the renewed Iranian strikes, and a warning from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that Washington was about to impose new sanctions.

“Today at 12 p.m. ET (1600 GMT), US forces began striking Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran,” US Central Command posted on X. “The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region.”

Iran’s state broadcaster said there had been reports of explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island, on the northern side of the strait.

US strikes Iran

The state-linked news agency Nour News said there had been reports of explosions in the port city of Bandar Abbas and in Chabahar, a port on the southern coast. The state news agency IRNA also reported the sound of explosions in Jask and Sirik.

US President Donald Trump posted on his social media channel that if Iran retaliated for the attack, “they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level”.

The Fars news agency cited an IRGC spokesperson as saying the US “will regret its new attacks”.

The US Embassy in Qatar urged Americans currently in the Middle East to exercise “heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions”.

The six-month-old conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before the weekend strikes, in which US forces attacked Iran’s Larak Island on Sunday and Iran responded by launching missiles at two US air bases in Jordan.

Tensions escalate

Although he warned of a US response to the Iranian strikes, Trump also told reporters on Monday that they did not signal a return to full-scale war, and a senior Iranian source told Reuters they were a “limited and contained confrontation”.

But pledges by both sides to respond to further attacks have highlighted how quickly a conflict that has increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure could spill back into military action.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had said early on Tuesday at a regional summit in Kyrgyzstan that Tehran would reciprocate immediately if Washington honoured its commitments under a June Memorandum of Understanding that was intended to halt the conflict.

The MOU declared an end to fighting that has now killed thousands in Iran and Lebanon since US and Israeli strikes began on February 28. But it also deferred many of the most difficult issues and paved the way for a broader 60-day negotiation period, which passed without further agreement.

Officials in the country have shown no public sign since then of bowing to pressure.

New sanctions incoming

“If the enemy wants us not to export oil from the Gulf, no one will be able to export oil,” Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf was quoted as saying by Iranian media.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told a press conference in Tehran that Washington was “addicted to making excessive demands and has mistaken negotiations for dictating terms”.

“As long as they act in this manner, they will certainly get no result other than what they have achieved so far,” he added, warning that Tehran would “use all our capabilities, whether on the battlefield or through our diplomatic apparatus”.

Before the latest attacks, Bessent had said Washington was likely to announce bank sanctions against Iran this week and next, stepping up an attempt to “economically asphyxiate” Iran’s leadership after six months of conflict.

At a G20 finance leaders’ meeting in Asheville, ​North Carolina, he said the US was also looking at targeting airline leasing companies and other entities that did business with the IRGC.

Missiles exchanged

“We have zero tolerance. We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime,” he said.

Iran’s leaders have defied decades of US sanctions, many of which have been aimed at curtailing Tehran’s oil revenues and acquisition of weapons components.

Bessent has also warned that countries doing business could face US sanctions.

The heightened tensions have renewed fears of oil supply disruptions from the world’s key crude-producing region.

“The tit-for-tat missile exchanges between the US and Iran bring validation to those who believe that even if not a ‘forever war’, this conflict will run and run,” said PVM analyst John Evans.

Highlighting such concerns, two supertankers carrying Saudi oil were struck by unknown projectiles within minutes of each other while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz late on Monday, according to data from shipping intelligence and tracking firms Marisks and Kpler.

title.rendered: Saudi Arabia to give 27 million people free access to Adobe AI tools in $4bn push

content.rendered:
More than 27 million Saudi citizens and residents are set to receive free access to Adobe’s AI tools under an initiative valued by the technology company at more than $4 billion (AED14.7 billion).

The programme, announced at LEAP 2026 in Riyadh, will give eligible people aged 13 and over 12 months of access to Adobe Firefly Standard and premium features within Adobe Express.

Adobe said it plans to make the subscriptions available by the end of 2026 through an expanded partnership with Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and HUMAIN, the AI company owned by the Public Investment Fund (PIF).

The $4 billion figure represents Adobe’s valuation of the free access being offered rather than a cash investment by the company or the Saudi government.

Adobe Firefly allows users to generate and edit images, video, audio and other creative assets using artificial intelligence. Adobe Express provides templates and editing tools for producing social-media posts, presentations, posters and other digital content.

The partnership will also create an image-generation model designed specifically for Saudi users and businesses.

Developed by Adobe and HUMAIN using Adobe Firefly Foundry, the model will respond to Arabic-language prompts and produce images informed by Saudi culture, visual references and creative requirements.

Tareq Amin, chief executive of HUMAIN, said effective artificial intelligence needed to understand the context in which it operated.

“Our partnership with Adobe combines Adobe’s creative technology with HUMAIN’s regional intelligence to bring greater cultural relevance to image generation,” Amin said.

“We are building it locally but designing it to compete and scale globally.”

Designed for Saudi culture

Adobe has also introduced Modern Standard Arabic support across the desktop, web and iOS versions of Adobe Express. The update includes right-to-left typography, Arabic text editing, adapted user-interface controls and templates designed around Saudi culture.

The companies said the initiative was intended to move the country’s AI strategy beyond investment in computing infrastructure and towards widespread adoption among consumers, students, entrepreneurs and businesses.

Eligible start-ups and early-stage companies participating in the ministry’s Center of Digital Entrepreneurship and The Garage will receive one year of free access to selected Adobe products from early 2027.

Adobe will also provide training and expertise, while courses delivered through the Adobe Digital Academy will be used to develop creative, marketing and AI skills.

Saudi Minister of Communications and Information Technology Abdullah Alswaha said the partnership would help translate the kingdom’s AI spending into opportunities for individuals and businesses.

Shantanu Narayen, Adobe’s chairman and chief executive, said combining the company’s technology with local expertise would help Saudi users turn ideas into commercial opportunities.

The initiative builds on a strategic agreement signed by Adobe and HUMAIN at the US-Saudi Investment Forum in November 2025.

It also adds a new dimension to the regional AI contest. While the UAE and Saudi Arabia have committed billions of dollars to chips, data centres and AI companies, the next phase may increasingly be measured by how widely the technology is used and whether that adoption creates new businesses, jobs and locally relevant digital content.

excerpt.rendered: Adobe and PIF-owned HUMAIN will also develop an Arabic-language image generator designed to produce culturally relevant Saudi content

title.rendered: The business case for Arabic IP

content.rendered:
As demand for Arabic content grows across publishing, streaming, gaming and digital platforms, the region is confronting an increasingly important commercial question: how should Arabic intellectual property be valued, financed and developed into businesses capable of competing internationally? The Congress of Arabic & Creative Industries in Abu Dhabi is putting that challenge at the centre of its 2026 programme.

Across the Arab world, writers, filmmakers, producers, game developers, entrepreneurs and digital creators are developing intellectual property with the potential to reach audiences well beyond its original format or market.

For these businesses to grow, the commercial infrastructure around them needs to develop at the same pace. Intellectual property needs to be protected and appropriately valued. Investors need frameworks that allow them to assess creative businesses and their assets. Entrepreneurs need access to forms of capital suited to the way creative companies operate. Creators also need clearer routes to develop an idea across books, film, television, gaming, audio and digital platforms.

These questions will be central to the fifth edition of the Congress of Arabic & Creative Industries, organised by the Abu Dhabi Arabic Language Centre.

This year’s programme examines how Arabic can provide a foundation for new creative economies, AI innovation, intellectual property development and public policy. The focus is increasingly practical: identifying the systems and tools that can enable Arabic creativity to grow commercially and reach audiences at global scale.

H.E. Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, Chairman of the Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi, said: “Abu Dhabi has made sustained investments in the institutions and platforms that enable creativity to thrive. Our next phase is to strengthen the systems that translate creativity into lasting cultural and economic value, creating the conditions for ideas and intellectual property developed in the region to be valued, financed, owned and shared with global audiences. The Congress of Arabic & Creative Industries brings creators, investors, innovators and industry leaders together to connect expertise with opportunity. Arabic is integral to our identity and central to the creative economy Abu Dhabi is building.”

Putting a value on Arabic ideas

One of the practical challenges facing the sector is determining what Arabic intellectual property is worth.

The issue extends well beyond publishing rights. A successful story may become a film or television series. Characters and narratives can develop into gaming properties. Books can move into audio, animation and other digital formats, while translation, adaptation and licensing can take locally developed ideas into new markets.

Unlocking that potential requires more consistent approaches to valuing the underlying rights.

The Congress session “Arabic Content Value & IP” will bring together IP professionals, publishers, platform buyers and investors to examine the issue, with the ambition of developing an industry-standard framework for valuing Arabic intellectual property.

The proposed Valuation Toolkit will address questions encountered across the industry, including how to assess Arabic book rights, value transmedia IP franchises, price game localisation and structure licensing agreements across different formats.

The discussion will bring together perspectives from different parts of the content industry. Participants include Natasha Matos-Hemingway, Chief Commercial and Marketing Officer (VOD) at MBC Group; Kinda Ibrahim, Regional General Manager of Operations for TikTok across Europe, the Middle East and Africa; and Rana Idriss, CEO and General Manager of Dar Al Adab. The session will be moderated by Dana Alhanbali, Founder and CEO of Bark & Berg.

Greater consistency around valuation could give creators and rights holders a stronger basis for commercial negotiations while making Arabic IP easier for potential partners and investors to assess. It could also support the development of more intellectual property across formats, rather than allowing its commercial potential to end with the success of a single book, programme or platform.

Finding the right capital for creative businesses

Alongside valuation is the question of how creative businesses access capital.

The economics of a creative company can look very different from those of a conventional technology startup. Its most valuable assets might be a catalogue of rights, a successful character, an established audience or a pipeline of creative work. Timelines for investment and return can also vary considerably between film, publishing, music, gaming and other parts of the sector.

These differences can make established financing models difficult to apply.

The Congress will examine the issue through “Financing Arabic Creative Industries,” a session focused on the financial gaps currently facing the MENA creative economy and the investment models, partnerships and policy frameworks that could support its continued growth.

The panel brings together entrepreneurs and investors with experience across some of the region’s most dynamic creative sectors: Mohamed Hefzy, screenwriter, producer and Founder and CEO of Film Clinic; Eddy Maroun, Co-Founder of Anghami; and Noor Sweid, entrepreneur and venture capitalist. The discussion will be moderated by Karim Sarkis, Partner at Strategy& in the Middle East and EMEA Media Leader.

The session will look beyond conventional venture capital to consider how financing might better reflect the realities of creative businesses. Co-investment structures, strategic partnerships, rights financing and creative-sector-specific investment instruments all have the potential to play a role.

For entrepreneurs, the implications extend beyond access to funding. The availability of capital affects the ability to retain intellectual property, invest in production, enter new markets and build businesses with sufficient scale to compete internationally.

Developing the infrastructure around Arabic creativity

Both discussions reflect a wider shift in how the Congress is approaching Arabic content this year. The emphasis is not only on producing more Arabic creative work, but on strengthening the economic and institutional structures around it.

H.E. Dr Ali bin Tamim, Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Arabic Language Centre, said: “Arabic is a foundation for knowledge, creativity and economic opportunity. Our responsibility is to ensure that creators have the tools, systems and opportunities they need to develop Arabic ideas and take them to new audiences. The Congress creates a platform where the different parts of that ecosystem can work together to turn ambition into practical progress.”

Demand for Arabic stories and creative content is already visible across publishing, streaming, gaming and digital platforms. The next stage is to strengthen the commercial structures that allow creators and businesses in the region to capture more of the value generated by that demand.

This is where Abu Dhabi’s approach is particularly relevant. Its investment in culture increasingly sits alongside investment in technology, education and the creative economy, providing an opportunity to connect creators with the expertise, capital and infrastructure needed to develop their ideas commercially.

The discussions at this year’s Congress reflect that shift in emphasis. Establishing more consistent approaches to IP valuation and identifying financing models that work for creative businesses are practical challenges. Addressing them could help create the conditions for more Arabic intellectual property to be developed, owned and scaled from within the region.

title.rendered: One in three UK employers cut entry-level jobs as AI use rises

content.rendered:
The UK has launched a number of progressive initiatives designed to tackle the growing problem of youth unemployment.

However, the landscape has become increasingly more complex due to the mass introduction of AI across a whole host of industry verticals.

Entry-level jobs have declined dramatically over the last number of years, and that has made the job market across the UK even more competitive than what it was.

New analysis of a Survation survey of 1,001 UK senior business leaders, commissioned by the Work Foundation at Lancaster University, finds more than one in three employers 36 per cent reduced entry-level jobs for young people over the past 12 months.

Almost half of medium-sized 48 per cent and large employers 46 per cent reported cuts, compared with 24 per cent of small employers.

Three in five employers 60 per cent agree that young people aged 16-24 are generally ready for the world of work, compared to 17 per cent who disagree.

Many employers are also taking action with 59 per cent offering placements, apprenticeships, internships or work experience, and the same share providing feedback to unsuccessful young applicants.

However, entry-level recruitment practices can also present significant hurdles.

Ben Harrison, Director of the Work Foundation at Lancaster University, said, Young people are entering one of the toughest labour markets in years, facing intense competition for a shrinking number of entry-level jobs and fewer opportunities to get a secure foothold in work.

“Our research suggests the challenge is not simply how to provide young people with more employment support. Opportunities for young people are declining, and for those living in weaker local labour markets, the options they face are constrained.

“But that doesn’t mean Government should step back from its drive to improve job security and pay – both of which will be key in reducing youth unemployment over the long term. The focus must remain on boosting the quality and quantity of roles available to young people. And that means doing more to directly create good jobs, while also providing additional support to employers to do likewise,” said Harrison.

title.rendered: A Dubai broker just closed the agency he named after his daughter. Here’s why

content.rendered:
Alois Kugendran founded a Dubai property brokerage named after his newborn daughter, hoping to build a profitable company while gaining greater control over his time.

Less than two years later, he has closed it.

Kugendran said the end of Amaya & Co Real Estate was not caused by a collapse in Dubai’s property market. Instead, it reflects the difficulties facing smaller brokerages as competition, operating expenses and customer-acquisition costs increase.

The former Betterhomes agent had previously helped scale a brokerage inside a proptech company. He believed there was space for a smaller, service-led agency where experienced brokers had more autonomy and clients received personal attention.

The model initially worked. Amaya & Co remained lean, developed a loyal client base and performed strongly in the communities it targeted. It also gave Kugendran more time with his young family.

But Dubai’s brokerage industry, and his own ambitions, changed.

“The market has become incredibly competitive,” Kugendran told Arabian Business. “We didn’t have proprietary technology or a platform that gave us a significant competitive advantage.”

The company did not experience a dramatic overnight fall in transactions. The bigger problem was consistency.

Ups and downs

A strong month could be followed by a much weaker one, while salaries, property portals, office space, visas, technology, marketing, compliance and licensing remained largely fixed.

Regional geopolitical uncertainty also made some international buyers more cautious. Kugendran said this did not create the underlying problems but exposed them more clearly.

Dubai’s property market remains strong after around six years of rapid growth. That success, however, has attracted hundreds of new agencies and thousands of agents competing for the same buyers, sellers and listings.

Property Finder and Bayut remain important sources of enquiries for secondary-market agencies. Off-plan brokers also spend heavily on social media and digital advertising to reach international investors.

Those channels generate business, but Kugendran said the combined cost of portals, paid leads and maintaining visibility can consume a significant share of an independent agency’s margins.

Some competitors also discount commissions or offer incentives to win transactions. Kugendran said he resisted entering a race to the bottom and preferred to compete through service, expertise and relationships.

Agent advice

His experience has changed the advice he gives successful agents considering opening their own firms.

“Being a successful real estate agent and running a successful brokerage are two completely different things,” he said.

Agents may question why their employer retains a large share of their commission. But that calculation can overlook the brand, leads, marketing, technology, management, training and compliance support that a brokerage provides.

Once an agent becomes an owner, Kugendran said, the job shifts from selling property to recruiting and developing other people while managing cash flow and operations.

His advice is to decide whether the goal is genuinely to build a company or simply to keep more commission.

Kugendran considered finding an investor or partner but decided that cash alone would not solve the problem. He wanted strategic backing that could also provide technology, infrastructure, distribution and access to customers.

What’s next?

He has now joined property technology company PRYPCO as general manager of real estate, where he will lead and scale its brokerage operation. PRYPCO already has businesses spanning mortgages, fractional ownership and property management.

Kugendran plans to connect those services while using technology and automation to improve agent productivity and make transactions easier for customers.

He does not regard Amaya & Co as a failure. The company gave him valuable time with his family and taught him what business ownership demands.

“Sometimes the right decision isn’t to keep growing something simply because you can,” he said. “It’s recognising when it has served its purpose.”

excerpt.rendered: Amaya & Co founder Alois Kugendran says intense competition and unpredictable revenue are making it harder for independent brokerages to scale

title.rendered: Abu Dhabi orders schools to overhaul long-standing rule in massive update for UAE parents

content.rendered:
Abu Dhabi private schools must let parents pay annual tuition through at least three equal instalments under school fee rules enforced by the Abu Dhabi Department of Education and Knowledge. Schools can structure payment schedules reaching 10 instalments during an academic year.

Full compliance applies from the 2025/26 fall term. ADEK also requires schools to publish approved fees and payment schedules online, creating a standardised payment process across Abu Dhabi’s private education sector.

Updated rules for schools from ADEK

  1. Tuition must be payable in at least three equal instalments during the academic year.
  2. Schools can offer more flexible schedules, including four, 10 or other instalment structures.
  3. First tuition payments can be collected up to one month before classes begin.
  4. Registration fees are capped at 5 per cent of annual tuition.
  5. Registration fees can be collected up to four months before the new academic year.
  6. Registration fees must be deducted from the final tuition balance.
  7. Schools must publish approved fees and payment schedules online.
  8. School websites must display the ADEK-approved stamped fee schedule.
  9. Parents using approved second-hand or donated items can avoid eligible textbook, uniform and device charges.
  10. Used materials must meet current school requirements.
  11. School charges must be separated into approved fee categories.
  12. Exam-related charges must be clearly disclosed.
  13. Schools must record who paid each fee.
  14. Schools seeking fee increases must meet ADEK licensing and financial reporting requirements.
  15. Exceptional fee increase applications require qualifying operating losses and at least 80 per cent occupancy.
  16. Schools must issue three payment warnings before suspending a student for unpaid fees.
  17. Each warning must be at least one week apart.
  18. Any suspension for nonpayment is limited to three days and can happen only once per term.
  19. Schools cannot tell students that unpaid tuition caused a suspension.
  20. Students cannot be prevented from sitting examinations because of unpaid fees.
  21. Schools can withhold report cards, transfer certificates or re-enrolment while fees remain outstanding.
  22. Parents must receive written notice at least three months before year-end if unpaid fees could affect re-enrolment.
  23. ADEK can impose penalties on schools that breach the fee policy.

Parents can spread tuition across more payments

ADEK requires every private school to operate three or more equal tuition fee instalments during each academic year. Payment structures can include three, four or 10 instalments.

Schools can collect the first tuition instalment up to one month before classes begin. Each operator must publish its detailed payment schedule on its website and can enter payment agreements with parents.

Registration charges follow separate controls. Schools can charge up to 5 per cent of annual tuition as a registration fee for enrolled students. Operators can collect that amount up to four months before the academic year begins.

Any registration charge must reduce the student’s final tuition balance. ADEK does not permit schools to treat registration fees as an additional charge on top of approved annual tuition.

Used books and uniforms can reduce family costs

Parents using qualifying used learning materials can also avoid specific school charges.

ADEK requires schools to waive relevant fees for devices, textbooks, uniforms and similar items when students use suitable resold or donated alternatives. Materials must meet each school’s current requirements, including valid textbook editions and current uniform specifications.

School operators must divide their approved charges across six categories. These cover tuition, educational resources, uniforms, transport, extracurricular activities and other fees.

Board examination charges can sit outside those categories. Schools can also levy administration fees linked to examinations where costs cover document processing, invigilation, mailing or related services.

Operators must identify examination charges, applicable grade levels and related administration costs on their websites. Fee schedules must remain within levels approved by ADEK.

Abu Dhabi schools face tighter fee disclosure rules

Private schools must publish their fees, payment procedures and schedules online. Websites must also carry the stamped fee schedule approved by ADEK.

Schools collecting tuition must record who funded each payment. ADEK requires operators to capture whether money came from parents, relatives, companies, charities, scholarships or other sources.

Fee increase applications face additional financial controls. Eligible schools must hold a valid licence, operate for at least three years and submit audited financial statements covering two academic years.

Exceptional increase applications require further conditions. Schools seeking such approval need two consecutive years of adjusted operating losses and an occupancy rate of at least 80 per cent. ADEK can reject applications that fail its requirements.

Late payments carry defined protections for students

ADEK also regulates how schools handle overdue tuition.

Schools must issue three consecutive warning notices to parents before suspending a student for nonpayment. Each notice must arrive at least one week apart. Any suspension can last no more than three days and can occur only once during a school term.

Operators cannot tell students about unpaid fees, including when explaining a suspension. Schools also cannot prevent students from sitting examinations because parents have outstanding balances.

Schools can withhold report cards, transfer certificates or reenrolment until overdue fees are settled. Parents must receive written notice at least three months before an academic year ends when unpaid fees place future enrolment at risk.

ADEK retains authority to intervene when schools breach their obligations. Noncompliance can trigger legal accountability and penalties under applicable regulations.

title.rendered: Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz are rising despite the ongoing war

content.rendered:
Despite the ongoing tug-of-war between Washington and Tehran over the Strait of Hormuz, oil flows are continuing to recover.

Analysts from Goldman Sachs have said that the volume of oil coming through the key energy waterway has returned to two-thirds of what it was before the conflict started on February 28.

The assessment from Goldman Sachs is almost contrary to daily reports about how the chokehold on the Hormuz was having huge economic ramifications for the energy sector.

Total exports of crude and oil products passing through the waterway have risen to 15 million to 16 million barrels a day.

In an interview with Bloomberg, Goldman analysts including Daan Struyven and Yulia Zhestkova Grigsby said that this number is still around 7 to 8 million barrels below pre-conflict levels, but well above a trough of 5 million to 6 million barrels a day in March.

“The rise in dark crossings by specialized shippers, and in ship-to-ship transfers shows that producers and shippers are adapting to the Mideast conflict,” Goldman said. Higher dark flows could “moderate the upside to crude oil prices even if Mideast disruptions last longer,” their note read.

How much oil is passing through Hormuz can be very difficult to gauge and fully determine, as many tankers often turn off their satellite transponders, a practice known as going dark, to avoid detection.

About 6 million to 8 million barrels a day of crude is transiting the strait, traders told Bloomberg this week.

The exports are helping keep global oil prices in check, they have dropped to around $89 a barrel from more than $120 in April.

However, many believe that any further deterioration of between Tehran and Washington could send oil prices and energy costs into a tailspin.

While a lot of oil is getting out of the Persian Gulf, flows of liquefied natural gas and refined fuels are lower.

“We continue to see greater price upside to European natural gas prices and deferred oil product prices in persistent disruption scenarios than for crude,” Goldman said.

excerpt.rendered: Before the US-Iran war an average of 100 tankers transited the Strait of Hormuz – that has declined to below 10.

title.rendered: FDA approves new pancreatic cancer drug months ahead of schedule

content.rendered:
A new drug designed to tackle pancreatic cancer has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) months ahead of schedule.

The new medicine hitting the pharmaceutical market in the US is Rasonque (daraxonrasib), which is a RAS inhibitor for the most common form of pancreatic cancer.

This groundbreaking drug will deliver a new treatment option to patients with advanced pancreatic cancer.

Rasonque, is a tablet that is taken once daily, and targets multiple forms of a protein called RAS.

RAS is the key driver of tumor growth in most patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma, which arises from cells lining the ducts of the pancreas.  

It is not known when the drug will be commercially available to international markets, such as the UAE.

Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, said today’s approval provides a critical new option for patients facing an extraordinarily difficult and historically hard-to-treat cancer.

“It is our fundamental duty to deliver more cures and meaningful treatments to patients as quickly as possible. I am immensely proud of the dedicated FDA scientists whose fast, thorough review and relentless commitment made this groundbreaking milestone a reality,” said Diamantas.

Some of the numbers released by the FDA show just how needed this new drug for pancreatic cancer is.

Approximately 90 per cent to 95 per cent of the 67,000 new cases of pancreatic cancer diagnosed in the United States each year are pancreatic adenocarcinoma, according to the National Cancer Institute.

However, despite representing roughly 3.2% of all cancer diagnoses, pancreatic adenocarcinoma accounts for a disproportionately high share of cancer deaths, owing to its typically late detection, aggressive disease course, and historically limited treatment options.

Angelo de Claro, M.D, Director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence, said the new drug showed unprecedented results in an area of high unmet need.

“The approval was granted 6.5 months before the user fee deadline, demonstrating the FDA’s commitment to accelerating the approval of new cancer treatments for patients with serious and life-threatening conditions,” said de Claro.

In May, the FDA issued a “safe to proceed” letter allowing the sponsor to initiate an expanded access treatment protocol for Rasonque, enabling patient access to the investigational drug prior to approval under applicable FDA regulations.

The most common side effects of the drug are rash, diarrhea, stomatitis (inflammation of the mouth’s mucus membranes), nausea, fatigue, vomiting, abdominal pain, edema, decreased appetite, and hemorrhage.

excerpt.rendered: The new drug was approved after a robust clinical trial involving 500 patients.

title.rendered: UAE schools 2026-27: What’s changing for students, teachers and parents

content.rendered:
UAE schools will reopen on August 31 2026, with new rules covering homework, assessments, digital tools and teacher development. More than 1.277 million students will return to over 1,180 public and private schools across the country.

Ministry of Education preparations include 11 new schools and educational complexes, 5,810 school buses and eight million textbooks. Public schools have registered another 26,700 students for the new academic year.

Below are the rules for students, teachers and parents respectively

Pupils

  1. Kindergarten to Grade 2 pupils will not receive traditional homework.
  2. Younger pupils will be encouraged to complete daily reading at home.
  3. Grade 1 pupils will face expanded Arabic language assessments across selected public and private schools.
  4. Grade 6 pupils in public schools will follow tighter controls on digital device use during lessons.
  5. Cycle 3 students will have Group A subjects assessed on a 50 per cent school assessment and 50 per cent central assessment basis.
  6. Grade 7 pupils will complete Project-Based Learning and Assessment across Arabic, English, mathematics and science.
  7. Students will undergo diagnostic assessments to identify learning gaps earlier.
  8. Schools will integrate National Education Charter principles into classroom activity, extracurricular programmes and student conduct.

Teachers

  1. Teachers must use diagnostic assessments to identify individual learning gaps.
  2. Teaching teams will use assessment results to adjust lesson planning and targeted academic intervention.
  3. Educators will receive training covering artificial intelligence, assessment, inclusive education, school safety and academic guidance.
  4. School leaders will receive dedicated training in AI-assisted decision-making and school performance management.
  5. Teachers will deliver integrated project-based assignments across several subjects, particularly for Grade 7.
  6. Educators will implement National Education Charter requirements within teaching, student activities and conduct policies.
  7. Schools will face national performance evaluations against approved education standards.

Families

  1. Parents of Kindergarten to Grade 2 pupils will be expected to support daily reading at home instead of traditional homework.
  2. Families will have a defined role in supporting National Education Charter objectives.
  3. Dubai private school tuition fees will remain frozen for the 2026 to 2027 academic year.
  4. Parents in Dubai will gain a formal consultation channel through the Dubai Parents Council.
  5. Families will need to follow the revised academic calendar, with classes starting on August 31 2026 for Ministry curriculum schools.
  6. Parents will receive more structured information from schools where diagnostic assessments identify learning gaps requiring additional support.

Homework changes for younger pupils

Kindergarten pupils through Grade 2 will no longer receive traditional homework under the Ministry’s revised policy. Schools will instead encourage daily home reading to strengthen early literacy, language development and cognitive skills.

Grade 1 pupils will also face wider Arabic language assessment during the 2026 to 2027 academic year. Ministry testing will cover 19,000 Grade 1 pupils across 162 public schools. Another 11,000 pupils across 130 private schools will participate.

Ministry officials expanded the programme after testing the assessment across 100 public and private schools during the previous academic year.

National Education Charter principles will also enter daily classroom routines. Schools will connect Charter objectives with educational outcomes, extracurricular activities and student conduct requirements. Families will receive a defined role in supporting implementation.

Digital use and student assessments change

Grade 6 pupils in public schools will enter an expanded programme regulating digital tools during lessons. Ministry research during the previous academic year covered 2,500 students at nine public schools.

Preliminary results recorded stronger academic performance in non-digital classrooms across mathematics, science and Arabic. Researchers also recorded better behaviour and greater classroom concentration.

Cycle 3 students face a separate assessment change covering Group A subjects. School assessments will carry 50 per cent of the weighting. Central assessments will account for the remaining 50 per cent.

Teachers will also conduct diagnostic assessments to identify learning gaps earlier. Schools can use those results for lesson planning, targeted interventions and individual reading support.

Ministry policy keeps digital technology inside classrooms while tightening how schools deploy devices during instruction.

Project learning expands across UAE schools

Project-Based Learning and Assessment will expand to more than 129,000 students across 366 schools during the academic year. Grade 7 students will complete an integrated project combining Arabic, English, mathematics and science.

Schools will use integrated assignments to assess practical application across several subjects within one project.

Public schools and private schools licensed by the Ministry will also enter a new evaluation programme. Reviews will cover all eligible schools across two academic years, beginning during the first semester of 2026 to 2027.

Assessments will measure institutional and educational performance against approved national standards. School leadership teams will receive findings identifying performance strengths, improvement priorities and required support.

Students begin classes on August 31 2026. Ministry curriculum schools finish the academic year on July 2 2027. Winter break begins December 14 2026, while spring break starts April 5 2027.

Teachers receive wider training programmes

More than 24,000 teachers, school leaders and education specialists entered specialised training before pupils return. Ministry programmes run across more than 80 courses and workshops, with dedicated development covering over 1,700 school leaders.

Training covers artificial intelligence, academic guidance, inclusive education, student assessment, school safety and educational leadership. Ministry programmes also address data-led assessment and support systems for pupils requiring additional intervention.

School leaders receive separate instruction covering artificial intelligence in decision-making and school performance management. Ministry data shows the leadership programme includes 500 School Principals and 1,200 Deputy Principals and Unit Heads.

Dubai families also enter the academic year with private school tuition fees frozen for 2026 to 2027. KHDA confirmed that private schools cannot raise fees during the academic year.

KHDA will also launch the Dubai Parents Council and Dubai Educators Council at the start of the academic year. Both groups will participate in discussions around education policies and programmes across Dubai’s private education sector.

title.rendered: Tetr business college launches global founder programme across Shanghai, London and Dubai

content.rendered:
Tetr College of Business has launched a year-long graduate programme that will take aspiring entrepreneurs through Shanghai, London and Dubai while they build and develop their own companies.

The Graduate Program in Entrepreneurial Leadership will begin in March 2027 and is designed for prospective founders, creators, early-career professionals and the next generation of family-business leaders.

Rather than studying entrepreneurship entirely within a classroom, participants will be expected to take a venture from its initial concept through product development, market testing, branding and fundraising.

The programme begins with four months in Shanghai, where students will explore artificial intelligence, product development, manufacturing and supply-chain execution.

Tetr said the aim is for founders to leave China with a functioning product, supplier relationships and evidence of customer demand.

Participants will then move to London for two months. This stage will focus on building a brand, understanding finance, developing a capital strategy and preparing a company for international expansion.

The final four months will take place in Dubai, where students will be introduced to investors, family offices, venture-capital companies and businesses operating across the Middle East, Africa and South Asia.

Dubai will also host The Pitch Floor, the programme’s concluding investor showcase. Participating teams will present the companies they have built to investors, entrepreneurs and industry specialists, with the aim of beginning funding discussions and preparing their ventures for further growth.

Fudan and Imperial partnerships

Tetr said the programme’s academic components will be supported through partnerships with Fudan School of Management in Shanghai and Imperial College Business School in London.

Participants completing the course will receive a certificate co-signed by the two institutions, alongside a portfolio documenting the business they have developed across the three markets.

“The world does not need more people who understand entrepreneurship in theory; it needs more people who can build, adapt and execute in rapidly changing environments,” said Tarun Gangwar, co-founder of Tetr College of Business.

“The ability to navigate uncertainty, respond to changing market realities and build across different contexts is increasingly what defines successful founders—and these are the capabilities we hope to develop through this programme.”

The curriculum will also include industry immersions, cultural experiences and applied projects intended to expose participants to the different commercial conditions within each city.

A dedicated Founder Reboot component will focus on resilience, decision-making and personal development, while Perspective Projects will require students to work with local industries and communities on practical business challenges.

The programme builds on Tetr’s existing approach of asking students to create businesses during their studies. Ventures established through its undergraduate courses include AI influencer-marketing platform Fluma, software company BluSpru, pickleball-equipment brand ServeClub and several consumer-food and hardware businesses.

Tetr said student-founded companies have collectively generated more than $1 million in revenue and secured more than $500,000 from investors.

Participants in the new graduate programme will also have potential access to Tetr Launchpad, a $10 million fund created to invest in student ventures.

Applications are open to candidates who have completed an undergraduate degree or diploma by February 2027. The inaugural cohort is scheduled to begin its first term in Shanghai the following month.

title.rendered: Qatar PM visits Iran in bid to revive diplomacy as Trump says US-Iran talks are not happening

content.rendered:
Qatar’s prime minister visited Tehran on Thursday in an effort to revive stalled diplomacy six months into the war, as US President Donald Trump said Washington was not currently talking to Iran.

“We don’t want to speak to them. We’re not looking to meet or anything,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office after the White House said a US economic campaign against Tehran would continue until Iran decides to negotiate meaningfully.

Major combat operations have been paused for weeks but there has been little progress toward a wider peace agreement or reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route. Six months after US and Israeli forces attacked Iran, killing its supreme leader and maiming his son and successor, the Iranian government is under economic siege, but it still holds power and has shown little urgency to negotiate.

Trump, facing political pressure at home over higher energy prices ahead of November congressional elections, has opted to focus on economic sanctions, but aggressively enforcing them would require taking measures against Iranian trade partners such as China and India.

In Tehran, Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani urged a return to diplomacy during talks with Iran’s top negotiator Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf on Thursday, Qatar’s foreign ministry said.

Qatar diplomacy in Iran

Iran in turn called on regional neighbours to prevent the US from using their territory to carry out military or economic attacks on Iran, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on his Telegram account.

Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told the Qatari prime minister that Tehran would strike US military and economic interests if Washington engaged in “mischief” against Iran, Iranian media reported.

Rezaei said the United States must take steps to meet Iran’s conditions before Tehran moved to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Those conditions include an end to the US blockade on Iranian ports, compensation and removal of sanctions.

“We do not trust the United States; it has repeatedly betrayed diplomacy and negotiations,” Rezaei said.

A June memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran collapsed in part over the future of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which about a fifth of global energy supplies passed before the war.

Strait of Hormuz control

Iran has sought to exert control over the strait and charge fees to ships it authorizes, while Washington insists it should remain an open international waterway.

Al Thani said on X that he stressed the importance of freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. He and the Iranian foreign minister also discussed a proposal to establish a temporary joint Iranian-Omani shipping corridor through the strait and a joint project to clear mines, Qatar’s foreign ministry said.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday that Iran and Oman had agreed in principle on administering traffic in the strait and sharing revenues, but a senior Iranian source later said the two countries were still working on the details of an agreement.

Iran is preparing a list of conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz after mediators asked Tehran to set them out, Rezaei said. Ships would use a designated central channel if the US met Iran’s conditions, he said through an interpreter in an Al Manar TV interview.

‘No negotiations happening’

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said on Thursday that Trump “continues to retain all options on the table” with regard to Iran.

“We’ve had Operation Epic Fury to destroy their military. Now we have Operation Economic Outcast to destroy their economy,” Leavitt said in an interview with Fox News.

“No negotiations are happening right now, and this will continue until the president feels that maybe they come to the table in a meaningful way,” she said. “We have not seen that yet.”

Tehran has lived under various forms of US sanctions since the Islamic revolution in 1979.

Despite suffering heavy military losses, Iran retains enough missile and drone capability to strike Gulf states that host US forces and disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The International Maritime Organisation has reported 70 incidents in the strait since February 28 that have killed 19 seafarers.

Thousands of others have died, mostly in Iran and Lebanon, since the US and Israel attacked Iran with the stated goals of denying Iran a nuclear weapon, helping Iranians topple their government, and destroying Tehran’s missile program.

excerpt.rendered: Qatar’s Prime Minister visited Tehran to push for renewed diplomacy as Donald Trump said the US was not holding talks with Iran six months into the war

title.rendered: AD Ports board backs $8.6 billion buyout offer from L’imad

content.rendered:
The board of AD Ports Group has strongly recommended its shareholders accept a $1.70 (AED6.25) per share offer from L’imad to take full control of the Abu Dhabi-based ports and logistics giant.

The board reached that conclusion following what is described as a fairness opinion from its independent financial adviser HSBC.

L’imad is Abu Dhabi’s sovereign investment arm, and ADQ is a wholly owned subsidiary of L’imad.

It launched a voluntary tender offer on August 18 to buy the remaining shares available in AD Ports.

ADQ is already the majority shareholder in AD Ports, with a 75.42 per cent stake in the company.

Launched a voluntary tender offer on August 18 to acquire the remaining shares in AD Ports. ADQ already owns 75.42 per cent of the company.

Under the offer that has been tabled, shareholders will receive AED6.25 ($1.70) in cash for each share they tender.

The price represents a 23 per cent premium to AD Ports’ closing price before the bid was announced and is about 95 per cent above the AED3.20-a-share price at which the company listed on the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange in 2022.

The offer values AD Ports at about $8.6 billion (AED31.8 billion).

AD Ports operates about 40 terminals in the UAE and has a presence in about 50 markets globally.

The offer is on the table under September 15, so shareholders have time before deciding whether or not to take the deal.

The deadline could also be extended by L’imad, but considering the recommendation from HSBC, it’s appears likely that AD Ports will take the deal on offer.

HSBC Middle East was appointed to run the rule over L’imad’s offer on August 21.

L’imad has stated that the offer gives shareholders a very attractive opportunity to realise certain and immediate value.

They believe the offer would also enable AD Ports to pursue its long-term growth, including acquisitions, without the constraints that come with me being a publicly listed entity.

The move by L’imad is just the latest in a series of deal it has brokered in an attempt to consolidate its strategic assets as it looks to build a huge portfolio.

L’imad was established in 2025, and has aggressively expanded its portfolio since its inception.

In July, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, approved the fund’s investment and operational framework for strategic sectors.

L’imad also owns a significant stake in Abu Dhabi real estate developer Modon Holding.

title.rendered: Dubai Airports CEO vows DXB ‘won’t lose its crown’ despite tough year

content.rendered:
The CEO of Dubai Airports has declared that it won’t be knocked off its top spot despite the ongoing regional uncertainty impacting the aviation sector across the Middle East.

Paul Griffiths believes that even though many networks were badly hit due to the US-Iran war, DXB will retain its status as the world’s busiest airport.

“We’ve been 12 years as No. 1 and I’m not going to lose that crown to anyone else,” said Griffiths.

He made the claim at a press conference on Wednesday, in which he disclosed $14.8 billion in contracts had been tendered for the Al Maktoum International Airport, Griffiths was in an upbeat mood.

DXB targets 70 million passengers

Passenger volumes are down 42 per cent in Q2, but DXB is still projecting to have processed 70 million by the end of 2026.

In 2025, they had 95.2 million file through the gates of the airport, but all things considered the operational efficiency of Dubai International Airport is impressive.

Griffiths said that DXB will remain a hugely important force in the global aviation game.

“You can’t take the first six months as an indicator of long-term strength. Our network, our position in the globe and our importance in global air traffic means that, no doubt, we’ll close this year still as number one,” said Griffiths.

Many international airlines remain absent from DXB, and other regional airports, but Griffiths struck an optimistic tone in terms of the numbers they are forecasting for Q3 and Q4.

Dubai’s flagship carrier Emirates is expected to have 90 per cent of its capacity restored.

“The airport has bounced back to about 86 per cent of its capacity. Every week, the gap between this year and last year gets smaller and smaller.

“I’m pretty confident by the end of Q3 we’ll have a full schedule, have all the airlines back and I’m hopeful we’ll get to that magic number we’ve been chasing for a few years of 100 million, within maybe 18 months,” said Griffiths.

Griffiths also disclosed that he is in engaged in a number of talks with a whole host of major international airlines.

He wants them to commence services to DXB and Al Maktoum International Airport (DWC), particularly as the Airbus A321 XLR narrow-body aircraft with longer range makes it more economical for airlines to serve cities that were previously not viable with wide-bodies.

India, Saudi Arabia and the UK have all remained the major source markets for DXB.

Earlier this summer, the introduction of Riyadh Air to the skies was a huge boost for DXB, and the entire aviation sector regionally.

“We are going to be on a fairly steady upwards trajectory for the next few months, and I hope that next year the traffic numbers will be similarly audacious as they have been in previous years,” said Griffiths.

title.rendered: Beyond empowerment: Emirati women redefine leadership

content.rendered:
Emirati women no longer need to be invited into the rooms where important decisions are made. Increasingly, they are building those rooms, leading the organisations inside them and opening the doors for the generation following behind.

That is the message from prominent Emirati leaders marking Emirati Women’s Day. This year’s theme, “Together, We Rise Stronger and Better”, reflects a national ambition to turn decades of progress into further action. For the first time, the celebration has also been extended into a month-long programme running until September 28.

The date marks the anniversary of the establishment of the General Women’s Union in 1975. In the five decades since, Emirati women have moved into senior positions across government, diplomacy, business, science, law and technology.

But entrepreneur and television personality Sara Al Madani believes even the language used to describe that progress must change.

“I just hate this word because I feel like empowerment means, ‘Give me power’, and I feel like women are powerful,” she said. “Have you heard of empowering men? It’s rare.”

Al Madani believes the emphasis should instead be placed on inspiration, showing women what is possible without suggesting that power must first be handed to them by somebody else.

“Inspire women. Show them they can,” she said. “Nobody needs anyone to hand them power.”

It is a characteristically direct assessment from an entrepreneur who entered business at 15, motivated by a desire to earn her own money and avoid placing limits on what she could achieve.

“I was telling myself, ‘I don’t want to ask anyone for money. I want to make my own money. I don’t want limitations,’” she said.

From visibility to influence

Muneera Al Taher, vice president of HR operations and Emiratisation at Jumeirah, said one of the most significant changes has been the greater visibility of Emirati women in senior positions.

“When I started my career, Emirati women in senior roles were the exception,” she said. “Today, you see them across government, business and industries where they historically had less representation.”

That visibility matters beyond the individuals securing those positions because it changes what younger women believe they can accomplish.

However, Al Taher said further progress is needed in the private sector, particularly in accelerating the movement of Emirati women into its most senior leadership roles.

“The ambition and the preparation are there,” she said. “Companies just need to be more deliberate about making sure the opportunities match.”

Jouslin Khairallah, senior Emirati lawyer, founder and managing director of KH Legal and a founding member of the Legaline platform, has observed a similar transition from participation to influence.

“Today, Emirati women are judges, ministers, diplomats, entrepreneurs, scientists and business leaders,” she said. “They are no longer entering spaces traditionally dominated by men; they are leading and transforming them.”

The next challenge, Khairallah added, is ensuring that progress remains sustainable across every sector and organisational level.

Balancing act

That means creating transparent routes into senior leadership, improving access to mentors and ensuring women do not feel forced to choose between professional advancement and family life.

“Leadership is not defined by a title,” she said. “It is reflected in the courage to make difficult decisions, the humility to continue learning and the determination to create a positive impact.”

Amna Al Zaabi, Contribution Management Division Director at the Authority of Social Contribution – Ma’an, said Emirati women had progressed from being offered opportunities to actively shaping them.

Women are not simply present at the leadership table, she added. They are influencing decisions, creating solutions and determining the direction taken by their organisations.

Al Zaabi believes success cannot be assessed solely by counting how many women hold executive titles. It must also be measured by whether organisations allow women to introduce different leadership styles, challenge established thinking and take ownership.

“Progress is not simply measured by the number of women in leadership positions, but by our ability to create the space and opportunity for women to redefine what leadership can look like,” she said.

Creating opportunities for others

The responsibility to create opportunities for other people emerged repeatedly from the women interviewed.

“A leader’s impact should not only be measured by what they personally achieve, but by the confidence, capability and ownership they build in the people around them,” Al Zaabi said.

Khairallah and Al Taher both identified Her Highness Sheikha Fatima bint Mubarak, the Mother of the Nation, as a source of inspiration.

Al Taher said the decision to extend the celebration across a full month demonstrated an ambition to transform the occasion into a wider platform for appreciation, action and future opportunity.

She advised aspiring leaders not to become preoccupied with having every answer or constantly attempting to prove themselves.

“Focus on your values rather than the pressure to prove yourself, because some of the most defining moments in your career will come from quiet decisions, not big ones,” she said.

Empathy must also remain central as responsibilities increase.

“Understanding those around you, what drives them and what they need from you is what makes the difference,” Al Taher said.

Technology could now lower some remaining barriers to entrepreneurship. Al Madani said one of her technology companies operates without a conventional workforce beyond herself, a business partner and its chief executive, with AI performing several other functions.

“You don’t need much money,” she said. “You just need creativity, you need the drive and you need to put yourself out there and not be scared of failing, because failure is a beautiful teacher.”

That may define the next chapter for Emirati women: not waiting for permission, not accepting artificial limits and ensuring that every achievement creates another opportunity for somebody else.

excerpt.rendered: On Emirati Women’s Day, leading figures from business, law, hospitality, energy and social development explain why the next chapter must be about influence, opportunity and women leading on their own terms
