title.rendered: The Women Keeping Sejnane’s Ancient Pottery Tradition Alive

content.rendered:
The road into the hills of Sejnane, in northern Tunisia, winds past rolling forests and scattered villages. Before long, wooden roadside stalls begin to appear, each overflowing with handmade pottery. Traditional cooking pots, water jugs and storage vessels line the shelves, adorned with delicate black speckles and intricate motifs. Elsewhere, animal figurines and sculptural dolls appear in the same distinctive style.

This type of pottery is found only in Sejnane. Dating back around 5,000 years, the craft remains deeply connected to the surrounding landscape, relying on techniques refined over countless generations. “The know-how takes years to learn,” potter Sabiha Ayari tells me. “It is passed down through the maternal line — my grandmother taught me when I was young.”

Ayari welcomes me into her courtyard, where a simple workspace has been arranged beneath a shaded terrace. Metal buckets brim with clay collected from the surrounding land, while low stools and patterned cushions are spread across the ground. Nearby, freshly moulded figurines dry in the afternoon heat, waiting for the next stage of the process. Sitting cross-legged on a cushion, Ayari reaches into a bucket, lifts a handful of clay and begins to work it between her hands with practised ease.

You might also like:

  • Dora Dalila Cheffi Returns to the Table in Tunis
  • How Refik Anadol Finds the Human in the Machine
  • In Tunis, Liên Hoàng-Xuân maps a world in flux
  • Haitham Al Busafi: The Omani artist creating immersive worlds

“Most of what I know came from watching my grandmother make pottery as a child,” she recounts, her hands slowly shaping the clay. “I then perfected my technique over the last few decades. Even today, I am still learning new shapes to mould or patterns to paint.”

Although Sejnane pottery is rooted in centuries of tradition, Ayari refuses to let the craft remain static. “The traditional pieces are the kitchen tools – the pots for couscous, or mugs for oil and water,” the potter says, gesturing towards several large vessels resting nearby. “I am always looking for something new to make, so sometimes I experiment with different styles. I have created light stands, lampshades, and even candle holders.”

Creating each piece takes several days. The process begins with sourcing the clay itself, which is gathered from nearby wadi beds. “I used to go and collect it myself,” Ayari laments. “But now I am too old and my back hurts, so I rely on some of the other women in the area to bring me the clay from the land.”

Back at the workshop, the raw clay is transformed through physical labour. Using a large rock, it is crushed, pounded and worked until it becomes soft enough to shape. “We soak it in water, then trample on it with our feet to make a paste,” she continues.

Once the clay has rested, the shaping begins. Ayari kneads the material before carefully forming each vessel or figurine entirely by hand. “We then leave the pieces to dry,” Ayari says. “Often, we will then coat the darker clay with white clay before using a shell to shine it.”

Burnishing each piece with a shell leaves behind a subtle sheen, while also creating the faint textured markings that have become a hallmark of Sejnane pottery. The pieces are then fired over charcoal before decoration begins. “To paint the pieces, we use natural dyes,” Ayari explains, holding up a bottle filled with a dark green liquid. “Leaves from local Dharou plants are ground and crushed to make a paint.”

She demonstrates the next stage by tearing apart the end of a small branch to fashion a makeshift brush. Dipping it into the natural dye, she carefully traces delicate lines across the surface of a ceramic bowl. Gradually, a bird emerges, its wings rendered in pale green. “We then fire the piece one last time,” she says. “Once it is fully cooked, the paint turns black.”

The painstaking process earned international recognition in 2018, when Sejnane pottery was inscribed by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Not only did the move bring increased demand for the pottery, but it also highlighted the importance of preserving the tradition locally. “It was a huge honour,” Ayari says proudly.

For those who continue practising the craft, pottery has become far more than a means of preserving heritage. Local potter Lamia Sadani describes the work as a form of therapy. “Whenever I touch the clay, my worries melt away,” she tells me. “So if I am having a bad day, I instantly turn to my workshop.”

Sejnane pottery also offers an important source of financial independence for the women of the region. “It was the only skill I ever had,” Ayari explains. “So I had no other option but to make a business out of it.”

The income from her work has shaped the course of her life. Ayari never married, yet pottery enabled her to support an entire family. “My brother died when he was young and left his four sons for me to take care of,” she shares. “It was not always a stable income, but I was able to provide everything for them simply from the money I made from pottery.”

For married potters, the craft often becomes a family enterprise, with responsibilities divided between making and selling the finished work. Sadani says that is how her household operates. “My husband helps me sell the pieces,” she says proudly. “When there is high demand for the products, we even hire local girls to help us with the business.”

Growing international interest in Sejnane pottery has also created opportunities for the artisans to travel for exhibitions, festivals and cultural events. “I have been able to present my work in England, France, Spain, Germany, India…” Ayari trails off. “I am always very proud to show our heritage to others around the world.”

Despite the UNESCO accolade, many artisans still worry about the future of Sejnane pottery. “A lot of the women in the village are no longer interested in working in the sector,” Ayari says sadly. “They have found other ways of earning a living.”

Sadani shares the same concern. “Fewer young girls are learning now though — they prefer to work in local factories or pursue other careers,” she says. “I have no daughters myself, so I have taught my three sons instead.”

Looking to the future, Ayari hopes the tradition will remain in her family too. “My dream is to one day teach it to one of my nephew’s daughters,” she says excitedly. “That way I can pass on the technique like my grandmother did to me.”

excerpt.rendered: In the hills of northern Tunisia, generations of women continue to shape Sejnane pottery by hand, preserving one of the country’s oldest craft traditions.

title.rendered: GEMS Education hires 1,550 new teachers as UAE school group receives 500,000 job applications a year

content.rendered:
GEMS Education is adding 1,550 new teachers for the 2026-27 academic year, taking its educator community to more than 10,000 as the UAE school group continues to recruit talent from within the country and internationally.

The organisation receives more than 500,000 job applications annually and has secured around 95 per cent of its targeted student places for the coming academic year through new registrations and re-enrolments.

The latest cohort was recruited through a global process and joins an organisation whose community spans more than 112 nationalities.

GEMS said its recruitment model draws on both UAE-based and international educators, with the organisation seeing a healthy balance between candidates already working in the country and those applying from overseas.

UAE-based teachers provide knowledge of the local education landscape, curricula and communities, while overseas recruitment gives the group access to different educational perspectives and practices from major education markets around the world.

GEMS Education adds 1,550 teachers

More than 500,000 job applications are received annually, providing GEMS with a broad global talent pool from which to recruit according to the requirements of individual schools, curricula and communities.

The 1,550 new educators were welcomed at GEMS Awareness Day 2026, the group’s annual gathering of incoming teachers, school leaders and senior leadership and advisors.

This year’s event was held under the theme Family First, reflecting the organisation’s focus on relationships between schools, students and their families.

GEMS Education workforce passes 10,000 educators

Sunny Varkey, Founder and Chairman of GEMS Education, said: “The future of education will be shaped not only by what we teach, but by the people we entrust to inspire and prepare the next generation. That is why we are investing significantly in attracting exceptional educators from around the world, developing their potential and equipping them with the tools, technology and environment to deliver the highest standards of academic excellence.

“As GEMS looks to the future, our ambition extends far beyond growth in scale. Inspired by the progressive vision and ambition of the UAE and its leaders, we are building an institution designed for the decades ahead: one that combines strong academic foundations with future skills and meaningful opportunities for students to apply their learning in the real world.

“Buildings and technology matter, but teachers remain the greatest investment we can make. When we invest in outstanding educators, we invest directly in every child’s potential and in developing the confident, capable and compassionate leaders our world will need.”

GEMS focuses on internal teacher career development

The scale of the GEMS network also allows teachers to move between schools, curricula, roles and geographies, as well as progress into leadership and other positions within the organisation.

More than 40 per cent of principal appointments during the past 12 months have been internal.

GEMS said this reflects its emphasis on developing and retaining talent from within the organisation.

More than 3,000 employees have worked at GEMS for more than a decade.

The organisation has also recorded its strongest teacher retention performance to date, with teacher turnover continuing to decline year-on-year.

Its people strategy combines professional development and leadership opportunities with internal mobility, wellbeing and employee engagement.

GEMS is also investing in local talent through its Emirati Teacher Assistant Upskilling Programme, which has trained more than 330 Emiratis within the organisation.

GEMS expands AI and future-focused learning

Alongside its recruitment programme, GEMS is expanding future-focused learning, technology and AI-enabled approaches across its schools.

The group said this will be combined with a continued emphasis on academic rigour, character, wellbeing and preparing students for the real world.

The Family First initiative is intended to strengthen relationships between schools and the communities they serve, recognising parents and families as partners in education.

The approach is designed to ensure students receive support both academically and in their broader development and wellbeing.

GEMS secures 95 per cent of targeted student places

GEMS enters the 2026-27 academic year having secured around 95 per cent of its targeted student places.

The figure includes a combination of new registrations and re-enrolments.

The group said it continues to have confidence in the UAE and its long-term education outlook while investing in schools, employees and its future-ready education offering.

GEMS Awareness Day 2026 marks the start of the new academic year for the 1,550 educators joining the organisation and takes its overall educator community beyond 10,000.

excerpt.rendered: GEMS Education welcomes 1,550 new teachers for 2026-27, taking its educator community above 10,000 as annual job applications exceed 500,000

title.rendered: UAE schools 2026-2027: 1.277m students, 11 new schools, AI training and major education changes

content.rendered:
More than 1.277m students will return to over 1,180 public and private schools across the UAE on August 31 as a series of education reforms covering assessments, digital learning, Arabic skills and school evaluations take effect.

The Ministry of Education has also opened 11 new schools and educational complexes, deployed 5,810 school buses and distributed 8 million textbooks for the 2026-2027 academic year, alongside new professional development and AI programmes for teachers and school leaders.

The Ministry of Education announced the UAE education system’s readiness for the 2026-2027 academic year at a press conference at the Zayed Educational Complex in Al Warqaa.

The briefing was attended by Sarah Al Amiri, Minister of Education; Eng. Mohammed Al Qasim, Under-Secretary of MoE; Sulaiman Al Kaabi, Assistant Under-Secretary for the Professional Development Sector; and Tariq Al Hashimi, Assistant Under-Secretary for the School Operations Sector (Dubai and Northern Emirates).

More than 1,180 public and private schools will reopen on August 31, welcoming over 1.277 million students.

UAE school preparations

A total of 26,700 new students have been registered in public schools.

The Ministry has opened 11 new schools and educational complexes, deployed 5,810 school buses and distributed 8 million textbooks.

The preparations span educational policies, curricula, human capital, infrastructure, digital services and learning tools.

The Ministry has activated the National Education Charter through six integrated pathways.

These cover linking the Charter’s principles to educational outcomes, empowering teachers to apply them, integrating them into daily practices, using classroom and extracurricular activities to reinforce them, aligning the student code of conduct with them and engaging families in their implementation.

A back-to-school campaign under the theme ‘Guided by the Charter, Building Tomorrow’ has also been launched to embed the principles into everyday life and strengthen cooperation between schools, families and the wider community.

Sarah Al Amiri said the Ministry achieved readiness for the academic year by investing in students, teachers and schools, creating a safe and stimulating learning environment and translating the National Education Charter into initiatives designed to improve educational outcomes.

She also emphasised the Ministry’s commitment to developing a more flexible, efficient and sustainable education system rooted in national identity and able to keep pace with global advances in science and technology.

UAE expands Arabic assessment

Arabic language skills assessment will expand significantly during the new academic year.

The Ministry is launching the second phase following a pilot conducted in 100 public and private schools last year to establish student baselines.

The next phase will cover all 19,000 Grade 1 students across 162 public schools and 11,000 Grade 1 students across 130 private schools.

The programme is designed to support the early development of Arabic language skills.

UAE changes digital learning for Grade 6 students

The Ministry is expanding its ‘Regulating the Use of Digital Tools in Education’ project to include all Grade 6 students in public schools.

During the previous academic year, the Ministry studied 2,500 students across nine public schools, comparing two groups to assess the impact of regulating digital tool use.

Preliminary results showed a clear improvement in academic performance in non-digital classrooms, specifically in mathematics, science and Arabic, alongside improved behaviour and increased classroom focus.

The initiative is intended to balance technology integration with fundamental skills and support academic achievement, critical thinking, cognitive development, educational interaction and discipline.

UAE changes assessment weighting for Cycle 3

Assessment weighting for Group A subjects in Cycle 3 has also been updated.

School and central assessments will now be split equally at 50 per cent each, with the Ministry saying the balance is designed to reflect actual student performance and strengthen schools’ role within a unified national framework.

Teacher-led diagnostic tests will also be implemented in schools to assess students, identify learning gaps at an early stage and use the results to guide lesson planning and targeted support.

The Ministry is expanding its Project-Based Learning and Assessment initiative to more than 129,000 students across 366 schools nationwide.

The expansion includes the first integrated project for Grade 7, combining Arabic, English, mathematics and science. It is designed to connect theoretical knowledge with practical application while developing future skills.

UAE to evaluate public and private schools

A new project will evaluate all public and Ministry-licensed private schools across the UAE over two academic years, beginning in the first semester of 2026-2027.

Schools will be measured against approved national standards, with the programme designed to identify strengths and areas for improvement and allow schools to establish sustainable development plans.

UAE teachers receive AI and professional training

The Ministry has also introduced a suite of professional development programmes for education staff.

These include the National AI Capacity-Building Programme, co-designed with Hamdan Bin Mohammed Smart University (HBSMU), the Promising School Leaders Project and the Afaq programme, delivered in collaboration with Emirates College for Advanced Education (ECAE) to equip teachers with AI skills.

Other initiatives include the Comprehensive Capacity-Building Programme for Educational Leaders, Professional Fellowship Programme and Certified Internal Trainers Programme.

The academic year began with a Specialised Training Week for more than 24,000 teachers, school leaders and specialists. It included more than 80 training programmes and workshops, as well as a dedicated programme for more than 1,700 school leaders.

No homework for UAE pupils through Grade 2

Among the other changes for the new academic year is the removal of traditional homework for students from Kindergarten through Grade 2.

The Ministry said the measure is intended to optimise classroom learning while restoring a healthy balance between school and family life.

Traditional homework will instead be replaced with daily home reading, aimed at developing early literacy, language and cognitive development and encouraging curiosity and a passion for learning.

Eng. Mohammed Al Qasim, Under-Secretary of MoE, said the Ministry has established proactive plans covering all components of the education system to ensure public schools are prepared for the new academic year.

The Ministry said it is working with public and private sector partners to provide an educational experience that meets student and parent aspirations and aligns with global best practices.

excerpt.rendered: UAE schools reopen for 1.277 million students on August 31 as new assessment, digital learning, Arabic, AI training and evaluation initiatives begin

title.rendered: Dubai to award $14.8 billion in contracts for new airport

content.rendered:
Construction on what will be the biggest airport in the entire world upon completion is starting to crank up in Dubai.

Dubai Airports have announced that they will tender out contracts to the tune of $14.8bn (AED 55 billion) by the end of 2026.

Works on the Al Maktoum International Airport continues to accelerate at full throttle.

At a media press conference on Wednesday, Dubai Airports CEO Paul Griffiths confirmed the issuing of the construction contracts and revealed some numbers around the megaproject.

“We’ve already in the last 15 months committed 10 million work hours of activity to the new project. 17,000 piles are already in the ground, and 45 million cubic metres of earth has been moved at DWC. What other proof do you need that our confidence in the future is completely unfazed by the development of the new airport,” said Griffiths.

Griffiths rejected the suggestion that construction has been impacted by the ongoing regional war.

However, he did concede that global supply chain remain under intense pressure, but argued that’s been the case ever since the start of the COVID pandemic.

He said they remain on schedule to deliver what will be the world’s largest airport.

“We’re mobilising suppliers from all the way across the world to ensure the project is completed on time. All the numbers I’ve quoted at you are actually things that are happening now, and it reinforces our confidence that Al Maktoum International is not some theoretical project; it’s actually happening,” said Griffiths.

DXB future

Griffiths outlined that the urgency to deliver the Al Maktoum International Airport comes down to a numbers game.

In 2032, DXB will be at capacity.

“By the time 2032 comes around, we will be at capacity at DXB, and the last thing the city is going to do is to allow its airport infrastructure to constrain its future growth,” said Griffiths.

DXB is a stunning airport, and undoubtedly one of the finest in the world.

Its future remains unclear, but Griffiths says what happens the iconic airport will be a decision for the government.

However, he did stress that he doesn’t see a future where two major hubs so close together would work in tandem.

“I can’t see us operating two major hubs in close proximity for any length of time, but the eventual switchover will be the world’s largest airport transition programme by a very significant margin,” said the Dubai Airports CEO.

excerpt.rendered: Dubai Airports CEO Paul Griffiths said DXB will be at capacity in 2032 – as the development of Al Maktoum International goes up the gears.

title.rendered: Checking In: Francis Hotel, Bath

content.rendered:
On Queen Square, where Bath’s Georgian story begins to unfold, seven adjoining townhouses form the Francis Hotel. Their honey-coloured façades belong to one of England’s most recognisable architectural landscapes, while behind them, a £15 million transformation has given the 98-room hotel a distinctly contemporary character. Completed with the opening of Francis Hotel Spa in April 2026, the renovation brings together design, regional food and wellness while retaining the layered history of the buildings themselves.

The hotel’s story reaches back more than 300 years. No. 9 Queen Square was once the home of John Wood the Elder, the architect whose vision helped establish Bath’s distinctive Georgian language of classical proportions and Palladian influence. No. 10 later became the lodging house of Solomon Francis, whose wife Emily expanded the business after his death, eventually incorporating neighbouring properties. The Francis Private Hotel opened in 1884.

That history is unusually visible in the architecture. Each townhouse has its own past, having housed surgeons, apothecaries, musicians, merchants, clergy and families over the centuries. During the Bath Blitz of April 1942, the hotel was bombed, with guests and staff sheltering in the basement. Its damaged façades were subsequently rebuilt, preserving the integrity of Queen Square and another chapter in the hotel’s long evolution.

You Might Also Like:

  • Checking In: Jumeirah Marsa Al Arab, Dubai
  • Checking In: Meliá Desert Palm
  • Checking in: Six Senses Zighy Bay, Oman
  • Checking In: Al Maha, a Luxury Collection Desert Resort & Spa, Dubai

Rooms and Suites

Today, the interiors by design practice 3DReid draw on this architectural inheritance without turning the hotel into a period piece. Bespoke furniture, layered textiles, artwork and tactile materials lend the rooms a residential quality, while colours and proportions reference Georgian Bath. The effect is closer to staying in an elegant private townhouse than a conventional city hotel. Rooms range from intimate spaces to larger suites, including the John Wood Suite, with contemporary comforts folded into the setting.

Dining

The same sense of place extends to Emberwood, the hotel’s British brasserie, which takes its name from John Wood the Elder and places Somerset and the wider South West at the centre of its cooking. A charcoal-fired hearth provides the focal point, with executive head chef David Hazell working with produce from the region’s farms, dairies and coastline. Porthilly oysters, West Country bavette and seasonal vegetables arrive with the warmth and informality of modern British dining.

There is a natural continuity between food and the hotel’s newest addition: Francis Hotel Spa. Set beneath the Georgian buildings, the intimate space connects contemporary wellness with Bath’s centuries-old reputation as a place of healing and retreat. Three treatment rooms and a relaxation area accompany a private thermal experience suite, the only one of its kind in Bath. At its centre is an ESPURO foam steam bath by KLAFS, alongside hot and cold experience showers, a heated relaxation bench and a steam cabin offering both foam and Rasul mud rituals.

It is an apt setting for a hotel whose story has always been intertwined with the life of the city. Bath’s Roman baths, Georgian squares, literary associations and contemporary galleries and restaurants continue to make it a destination shaped by both preservation and creativity. The Francis Hotel sits at the intersection of those histories: a collection of homes that became a hotel, a Victorian hospitality address rebuilt after wartime destruction, and now a design-led retreat for a new generation of visitors.

excerpt.rendered: A Georgian landmark in the heart of Bath enters a new chapter, bringing together architectural history, contemporary British design and the restorative spirit of the city.

title.rendered: UAE leaders mark Prophet Mohammed’s birthday with message of peace and stability

content.rendered:
UAE leaders commemorated Mawlid Al Nabawi with messages centred on mercy, unity, security and peace worldwide.

UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan reflected on the Prophet Mohammed’s legacy on August 25. Sheikh Mohamed focused on mercy, goodwill and unity while expressing hopes for stability and peace across all nations.

Mawlid Al Nabawi falls on the 12th day of Rabea Al Awwal. UAE authorities confirmed August 25 as the corresponding Gregorian date following the sighting of the new crescent moon.

Sheikh Mohamed calls for stability and peace

Sheikh Mohamed linked the religious occasion with values of compassion, humanity and goodwill. His message extended beyond the UAE to communities across the region and wider world.

Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Vice President, Prime Minister and Ruler of Dubai, also congratulated Muslims on the occasion. His message described Prophet Mohammed as a messenger of humanity and mercy. Sheikh Mohammed prayed for security, safety, stability and well-being across the Islamic world.

Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Vice President, Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the Presidential Court, focused on compassion and tolerance. Sheikh Mansour recalled a legacy built around mercy and goodness while expressing hopes for lasting peace and security.

Messages from all three leaders placed social stability and human compassion at the centre of the national commemoration.

Ajman leaders extend greetings across UAE

Sheikh Humaid bin Rashid Al Nuaimi, Supreme Council Member and Ruler of Ajman, extended congratulations to UAE citizens and residents. His message also addressed Arab and Islamic nations.

Sheikh Humaid described Mawlid Al Nabawi as an occasion representing affection and mercy. He recalled the Prophet’s example through humanity, goodness, benevolence and high moral character. His message included prayers for peace, love, security and safety worldwide.

Sheikh Ammar bin Humaid Al Nuaimi, Crown Prince of Ajman and Chairman of Ajman Executive Council, issued separate greetings. Sheikh Ammar focused on mercy and noble character as enduring elements of the Prophet’s teachings.

Ajman’s Crown Prince also expressed wishes for continued prosperity, security and tranquillity across the UAE.

UAE Council for Fatwa Chairman Abdullah bin Bayyah separately congratulated the country’s leadership, citizens and Muslim communities worldwide on August 25.

UAE holiday falls on August 28

UAE authorities have set Friday, August 28, as the public holiday for federal government employees and private-sector workers. Employees following the standard Saturday and Sunday weekend receive a three-day break through August 30.

The Federal Authority for Government Human Resources issued Circular No. 11 of 2026 covering the Mawlid Al Nabawi holiday. FAHR published the circular on August 7.

The Dubai Government Human Resources Department separately confirmed the August 28 holiday for government departments, authorities and institutions.

Dubai government operations resume on Monday, August 31. Shift workers and employees managing public services remain subject to schedules set by individual government entities. DGHR requires those entities to maintain efficient public service delivery throughout the holiday period.

Ajman Government also confirmed August 28 for government entities, with official working hours resuming on August 31.

Religious institutions hold commemorative events

General Authority of Islamic Affairs, Endowments and Zakat held a ceremony on August 25 to commemorate the occasion.

AWQAF Chairman Dr Omar Habtour Al Derei attended alongside Director General Ahmed Rashid Al Neyadi. Officials, employees and legal scholars from the UAE Council for Fatwa also participated.

UAE observances traditionally focus on reflection and religious remembrance. Public messages issued during 2026 concentrated on mercy, compassion, tolerance and social cohesion.

Government holiday arrangements also preserve operational continuity across essential public services. Dubai authorities specifically retained flexible staffing for shift-based functions and public service facilities during the August 28 closure.

Messages from the UAE leadership placed peace, security and human goodwill at the centre of Mawlid Al Nabawi commemorations across the country.

title.rendered: Sharjah announces 3 new hospitals in Kalba, Khorfakkan and Dibba Al Hisn as major development plans revealed

content.rendered:
Sharjah is moving ahead with plans for three new hospitals in Kalba, Khorfakkan and Dibba Al Hisn, as the emirate also accelerates development in Khorfakkan and updates scholarship application requirements for students.

Sheikh Dr Sultan bin Mohammed Al Qasimi, Supreme Council Member and Ruler of Sharjah, announced that work will begin on plans, studies and the tendering process for the hospitals, while approving new administrative divisions that split Khorfakkan City into four suburbs.

The three hospitals will be modelled on the University Hospital branch in Al Madam, which is nearing completion.

The Sharjah Health Authority will begin preparing plans and studies and conducting the tendering process, which is expected to take around five or six months.

The Sharjah ruler said during a phone-in on the “Direct Line” programme: “I was informed that there is overcrowding at the hospital and clinics in Kalba, so we wanted to address this matter quickly and contacted the Ministry of Health and Prevention, which responded to meet all the needs. They said they are now putting in place a mechanism to increase the number of doctors, medicines, facilities and construction. As for the three hospitals we previously announced, we decided to study the University Hospital branch in Al Madam as a model in terms of cost.

New hospitals in Sharjah

“The hospital is now nearing completion, and similar hospitals will be established in Kalba, Khorfakkan and Dibba Al Hisn. The Sharjah Health Authority will now begin preparing the plans and studies and conducting the tenders, which will take around five or six months.

“These hospitals, whether large or small, require budget funding, but we have found a solution and set out their plan midway through the year.”

His Highness has also approved new administrative divisions for Khorfakkan City.

The four suburbs are:

  • Khorfakkan City
  • Al Owainat
  • Al Sih
  • Al Sabihiyah

The Khorfakkan City suburb will extend from Khorfakkan Aqaba to Al Luluyah Aqaba, while plans include planting mountains in the area with dense, fruit-bearing trees.

The Sharjah ruler said: “We have approved the new administrative divisions for Khorfakkan City, comprising four suburbs: Khorfakkan City, Al Owainat, Al Sih and Al Sabihiyah. The Khorfakkan suburbs plan shows that the Khorfakkan City suburb extends from Khorfakkan Aqaba to Al Luluyah Aqaba.

“As this is virgin land, we will introduce some small animals and some beneficial species, such as gerbils, the mountain mouse and others. The plan also shows a yellow area called Al Owainat suburb, which is extensive and has mountains that will be levelled to create neighbourhoods.

“We also have Al Sih suburb, which has Al Aween Mountain. There is also a small mountain in this area whose name people pronounce incorrectly, calling it ‘Shuqair’, whereas its name is ‘Shukair’. This word means ‘small’, and ‘Al Shukair’ means the smallest of all things.”

Khorfakkan development set to accelerate

The approval of the administrative plan is expected to allow development in Khorfakkan to move forward more rapidly.

His Highness said: “Khorfakkan City has neighbourhoods, with each neighbourhood known by its own name, and it has a Khorfakkan City Council. Development in Khorfakkan will now proceed at a rapid pace because matters have become clear following the approval of the plan, just as happened in Kalba after we approved the city’s administrative divisions, which included the suburbs of Kalba City, Khor Kalba, Al Ghayl, Al Saf, Al Dahiyat and Al Sur.”

Plans are also moving forward to establish a mechanism for electing council members, with an extended meeting with the Sharjah Districts Affairs Department planned to determine the process.

His Highness said neighbourhood officials should be people such as mosque imams, teachers, counsellors or others known for good work, and would act as a link between residents and the Ruler of Sharjah.

The broader administrative organisation will extend beyond Kalba and Khorfakkan, with the Central Region and Sharjah City also set to be organised.

title.rendered: Oil prices rise as US threatens wider sanctions on Iran’s trading partners

content.rendered:
Oil prices have soared amidst the backdrop of ongoing threats of US sanctions against Iran, and countries who trade with Tehran.

The United States has said it will impose sanctions on countries conducting business with Iran.

However, Washington hasn’t exactly been forthcoming on the finer details of their plan, which was officially unveiled on Monday.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent formally announced Operation Economic Outcast at a press conference on Monday.

During the presser he repeatedly said the administration is preparing to act against any country that has helped Iran both export and import oil and evade the impact of economic sanctions.

As a result of this, oil prices have rose, and the trajectory is expected to remain on an upward curve.

Brent crude traded at $92.73 a barrel, up 0.6 per cent, while West Texas Intermediate is priced at $85.72, up 0.8 per cent.

Since the US-Iran war started at the end of February, both benchmarks have increased by 40 per cent.

Bessent said the US would give Tehran no breathing space, and said US President Donald Trump was already engaging with world leaders to directly request them to cease trading with Iran.

As aforementioned above, a lot of the commentary on the proposed sanctions remain vague, but Bessent did say that sanctions against a financial institution was pending.

The White House is expected to go after industry verticals such as gold, aviation and shipping when it comes to against economic campaign against Tehran.

Ali Madanizadeh, the former Iranian economic minister said his country was prepared for a fresh wave of US sanctions.

He insisted Iran had the ‘tools’ at their disposal to play the US at their own game.

He told Iranian state TV, “Our enemies intend to launch an economic terrorist attack on us, but we also have our own tools and know how to play the game. Our defence is no longer so defensive; the enemies should wait for an attack.

title.rendered: Saudi Arabia agrees €6bn Dragon Ball theme-park investment near Paris

content.rendered:
Saudi Arabia has agreed to invest €6 billion ($7 billion) in a major theme-park development near Paris as the kingdom expands its international interests in entertainment and tourism.

The agreement was announced during Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to the French capital for talks with President Emmanuel Macron.

The development will comprise three theme parks near Cergy-Pontoise, approximately 30 kilometres northwest of Paris. At least one is expected to be inspired by manga and the hit Japanese franchise Dragon Ball Z.

Saudi entertainment and investment company Qiddiya will finance the project, while French officials estimate that the development could become one of Europe’s largest new leisure destinations.

The two countries signed a memorandum of understanding covering the project, with construction expected to take place in stages over several years.

The idea reportedly emerged from discussions between Macron and the Saudi crown prince during the French president’s visit to Riyadh in December 2024, when the two leaders discovered a shared enthusiasm for manga and Dragon Ball Z in particular.

Macron described the investment as an unprecedented announcement and compared its potential scale with the arrival of Disneyland Paris.

The project represents a significant international expansion for Qiddiya, which is owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF).

Qiddiya is already developing an extensive entertainment city outside Riyadh containing theme parks, sports venues, hotels and cultural attractions.

Dragon’s Den

In 2024, the company announced plans to build what it described as the world’s only dedicated Dragon Ball theme park in Saudi Arabia through a partnership with franchise owner Toei Animation.

That separate development will cover more than 500,000 square metres and contain seven themed areas, more than 30 rides and a 70-metre-high Shenron landmark housing a rollercoaster, according to the Saudi Press Agency.

Qiddiya has not confirmed whether the proposed Paris attraction will replicate that concept or use the same designs, rides and commercial partners.

The French investment demonstrates how Saudi Arabia is taking the entertainment expertise and intellectual-property partnerships assembled under Vision 2030 into international markets.

It also gives France one of its largest foreign-backed tourism developments since Disneyland Paris opened in 1992.

For Saudi Arabia, the deal creates a prominent overseas platform for Qiddiya while extending the kingdom’s commercial influence beyond its domestic giga-projects.

Mohammed bin Salman’s French visit also included a meeting of the newly established French-Saudi Strategic Partnership Council and an appearance with Macron at the Esports World Cup closing ceremony in Paris.

excerpt.rendered: PIF-owned Qiddiya will finance a vast leisure development comprising three theme parks

title.rendered: UAE leads GCC stablecoin push as dirham-backed digital money gains ground

content.rendered:
The UAE is quickly emerging as a regional leader with the template needed to usher in a new era of regulated digital money.

More and more governments are increasingly trying to respond to the rise of US dollar-backed stablecoins by introducing and developing their own sovereign-aligned alternatives.

Global management consultancy company Arthur D. Little have created a report that explores the fundamental shift that is happening across the global stablecoin landscape.

In that report, it’s clear that the UAE has firmly established itself as the leading regional example of this emerging model.

In 2024, the first comprehensive regulatory framework for fiat-referenced tokens was established in the Middle East.

The UAE has seen regulated dollar-backed stablecoins develop alongside a dirham-denominated layer, including the launch of DDSC, backed by International Holding Company, Sirius International Holding and First Abu Dhabi Bank.

In an interview with Arabian Business, Arjun Vir Singh, Partner and Global Head of Fintech, Payments & Digital Assets at Arthur D. Little, said that the UAE is demonstrating that dollar stablecoins and a domestic digital currency ecosystem do not have to be competing choices.

“Global instruments can continue to serve international flows, while a regulated dirham layer can support domestic and regional activity. This positions the UAE not simply as an adopter of digital finance, but as a market helping define how regulated digital money can coexist across different layers of the financial system,” said Singh.

USD-backed tokens still account for approximately 97 per cent of the roughly $312 billion fiat-backed stablecoin market covered by the report.

However, non-USD alternatives are expanding rapidly, with unique holders of non-USD stablecoins increasing 2,900 per cent between January 2023 and February 2026 to reach 1.2 million.

The report argues that this does not signal the displacement of the US dollar. Instead, different currencies and instruments are likely to play different roles.

Replication not resistance

The report describes this emerging response as “replication, not resistance”, governments responding to the growth of dollar stablecoins by creating credible, regulated alternatives of their own.

Dr. Mohammad Nikkar, Principal, Financial Services practice, Arthur D. Little, Middle East, highlighted the opportunity emerging at the regional level – and examined what this shift means for financial institutions and payment providers.

“For banks and payment players, the question is no longer simply whether to participate in stablecoins. It is which currency, which payment layer, which client and which corridor they want to serve.

“The regional layer remains particularly open, creating an opportunity for the UAE and wider GCC to shape how value moves across some of the world’s most important trade corridors,” said Nikkar.

Financial Implications

The report argues that financial institutions should no longer treat stablecoins as a single market.

Instead, an emerging architecture spanning domestic, regional and international payments could see different forms of digital money serve distinct purposes.

For incumbent banks, the shift presents both an opportunity and a competitive challenge.

Institutions will need to determine where they intend to participate as banks, fintechs and infrastructure providers compete to establish the customer-facing, settlement and cross-border layers of the emerging ecosystem.

For policymakers, the next challenge will increasingly move from regulating stablecoins within individual jurisdictions toward enabling interoperability and mutual recognition between regulated regimes.

Arthur D. Little concludes that the sovereign stablecoin era does not necessarily diminish the dollar’s international role.

Instead, it points toward a more layered global payments architecture in which dollar stablecoins remain powerful internationally while sovereign-sponsored alternatives increasingly compete at domestic and regional levels.

excerpt.rendered: A report by Arthur D. Little has shown that the UAE has emerged as a regional leader in the stablecoin market

title.rendered: Saudi Arabia recalls 84,639 Toyota Camry cars over defect that could increase accident risk

content.rendered:
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Commerce has announced the recall of 84,639 Toyota Camry vehicles from the 2025 and 2026 model years over an instrument panel system defect that could increase the risk of accidents.

Owners of affected vehicles are being urged to contact local dealer Abdul Latif Jameel Motors to have their vehicle systems reprogrammed free of charge, while drivers can check their chassis number through Saudi Arabia’s Defective Products Recall Centre.

The recall covers 84,639 Toyota Camry vehicles from model years 2025 and 2026.

According to the Ministry of Commerce, the recall has been issued because of a defect in the vehicles’ instrument panel system.

The defect may prevent important information from being displayed to drivers.

Saudi Arabia recalls Toyota Camry cars

It could also result in the malfunction of turn signals, warning lights and audible alerts for the ignition key and seatbelts.

The Ministry said the problem could potentially increase the risk of accidents.

Owners are advised to check their vehicle’s chassis number to determine whether their individual Camry is included in the recall campaign.

The Ministry of Commerce urged owners of affected vehicles to contact local dealer Abdul Latif Jameel Motors. Owners can call the toll-free number 8004400055 to arrange for the affected vehicle’s system to be reprogrammed.

The work will be carried out free of charge. Owners can check whether their vehicle’s chassis number is included in the recall campaign through Saudi Arabia’s Defective Products Recall Center website, Recalls.sa.

The Ministry identified the problem as a defect in the instrument panel system.

According to the recall announcement, the defect may affect several functions important to drivers, including:

  • Display of important information
  • Turn signals
  • Warning lights
  • Audible ignition-key alerts
  • Audible seatbelt alerts

excerpt.rendered: Saudi Arabia recalls 84,639 Toyota Camry 2025 and 2026 models over an instrument panel defect that could affect warning lights, turn signals and alerts

title.rendered: Saudi Arabia-France deals: 21 agreements, $5bn credit line and $7bn Qiddiya project unveiled

content.rendered:
Saudi Arabia and France have announced 21 agreements and deals spanning energy, industry, financial services, transport and logistics, artificial intelligence, culture, health and tourism as the two countries deepen their economic and investment relationship.

The announcements during the state visit of Prince Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, Crown Prince and Prime Minister, to France included approximately $3.7bn of Saudi Aramco purchase agreements, plans for a credit line of up to $5bn and an agreement to explore a major Qiddiya entertainment-led development in France, where current ambitions envisage investment of around €6bn  ($7bn) over the development lifecycle.

Saudi and France strike deals

The Saudi-French Investment Roundtable Meeting was held in Paris in the presence of Crown Prince and President Emmanuel Macron of France.

Organised by the Ministry of Investment, the meeting brought together senior officials, business leaders and chief executives of major companies and institutions from Saudi Arabia and France.

It was designed to strengthen investment partnerships, identify opportunities in priority sectors and expand cooperation between the two countries’ business communities.

The meeting resulted in the announcement of 21 agreements and memoranda of understanding between public- and private-sector entities from both countries.

They cover:

  • Energy
  • Industry
  • Financial services
  • Transport and logistics
  • Artificial intelligence
  • Culture
  • Health
  • Tourism

Strategic discussions between business leaders focused on financing and developing transformative destinations, developing industrial partnerships and translating them into projects, expanding transport and logistics cooperation and shaping the digital future through AI and digital infrastructure.

The announcements came during the Crown Prince’s state visit to France from August 23 to 24, 2026.

During the visit, the Crown Prince and President Macron also presided over the first meeting of the French-Saudi Strategic Partnership Council and launched new initiatives aimed at strengthening cooperation between the two countries.

Saudi Aramco signs $3.7bn of French supply agreements

Among the major commercial announcements were purchase agreements between Saudi Aramco and French companies SLB and Vallourec.

The agreements cover the supply of oil and gas well drilling materials and steel pipes for oil and gas fields and have a combined value of approximately $3.7bn.

Aramco Digital separately signed a memorandum of understanding with French company Dassault Systèmes to cooperate on artificial intelligence and virtual twin technologies.

The proposed cooperation includes exploring potential applications in the oil and gas sector.

Saudi-French credit line of up to $5bn planned

Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Finance and Bpifrance Assurance Export also signed a joint statement to establish a dedicated credit line of up to $5bn.

CEO of the National Debt Management Centre Hani AlMedaini signed the statement on behalf of the ministry alongside Managing Director of Bpifrance Assurance Export Denis Le Fers.

The two sides will work to finalise operational arrangements for an initial credit line of up to $5bn.

The facility is intended to finance and refinance existing and future contracts carried out by French companies.

It will support Saudi Vision 2030 projects, with a particular focus on infrastructure, urban development, transport and healthcare.

The two sides will maintain regular and structured dialogue aimed at ensuring the credit line is implemented smoothly, efficiently and in a coordinated manner. The agreement forms part of the strategic partnership roadmap for the next decade signed by Saudi Arabia and France in December 2024.

Saudi electricity infrastructure

Cooperation also extends to Saudi Arabia’s electricity infrastructure.

Saudi Energy signed a cooperation and financing agreement with French public investment bank Bpifrance to support the development and modernisation of the Kingdom’s electricity grid.

The agreement builds on a memorandum of understanding signed in November 2025 to establish a financing facility of up to $3bn.

The framework is designed to support the company’s procurement programme and electricity infrastructure projects.

The wider Saudi-French joint statement also identified energy as an important area for future cooperation.

The two countries emphasised cooperation in oil and petrochemicals, sustainable electricity generation, energy efficiency, renewable energy, energy storage, peaceful nuclear energy, clean hydrogen and emission reduction and removal technologies.

Saudia aircraft financing agreement

The Saudi Export-Import Bank (Saudi EXIM) signed a tripartite memorandum of understanding with Saudia Group and Crédit Agricole CIB covering financing arrangements for the group’s acquisition of new Airbus aircraft.

Under the memorandum, Saudi EXIM, in its capacity as Saudi Arabia’s export credit agency, will provide insurance coverage for credit risks associated with the transaction.

The arrangement combines international bank financing with national export credit instruments.

It is intended to provide companies and projects associated with Saudi exports with greater access to international financing while supporting Saudia Group’s plans to expand and modernise its fleet and strengthen its operational capabilities in international markets.

Qiddiya explores $7bn entertainment destination in France

Qiddiya Investment Company also signed a deal with the French Government to explore the development of an entertainment-led, mixed-use destination in France.

The MoU begins a phase of joint work to define the project’s scope, development model and contractual framework in accordance with applicable procedures and approvals in France.

The Saudi-French joint statement said both countries welcomed Qiddiya Investment Company’s ambition to develop a major mixed-use, multi-park destination in Cergy-Pontoise in the Île-de-France region.

Current ambitions include up to three major entertainment anchors, hotels and complementary leisure experiences spanning entertainment, leisure, hospitality, culture and sport.

The total amount envisaged is around €6bn ($7bn) over the development lifecycle.

Qiddiya City remains Qiddiya Investment Company’s flagship project and the principal reference point for its model.

The proposed international project would provide a platform to introduce Qiddiya’s Power of Play philosophy, broaden the company’s experience and partnerships and strengthen the presence of the Saudi model in global markets.

Saudi-France trade reaches nearly $12bn

The investment announcements build on a trading relationship that has expanded over the past five years.

Trade between Saudi Arabia and France totalled approximately $53.7bn between 2021 and 2025, with Saudi exports accounting for 53.4 per cent of the total, according to data from the General Authority for Statistics.

Bilateral trade grew by approximately 43.8 per cent in 2025 compared with 2021, reaching nearly $12bn.

The joint statement issued following HRH the Crown Prince’s visit separately put bilateral trade at about $11.8bn in 2025.

Key traded commodities included boilers, machinery, equipment and mechanical appliances.

The Kingdom’s main exports included aircraft, spacecraft and their parts, while its main imports included boilers, machinery, mechanical appliances and pharmaceutical products.

French investment in Saudi Arabia reaches $17bn

French foreign direct investment stock in KSA reached SR63.9bn ($17bn) in 2024, more than double its 2021 level.

France is now the fourth-largest source of FDI in the Kingdom.

The presence of French companies in the Kingdom has also expanded, with 651 investment licences across 18 sectors.

FDI inflows into the Kingdom reached approximately SR23.9bn ($6.4bn) in the first quarter of 2026, representing year-on-year growth of 2.4 per cent.

The Ministry of Investment’s figures put KSA-French trade at SR44.2bn ($11.8bn) in 2025.

Saudi Arabia and France established political relations in 1926 and are marking their centenary in 2026.

Their economic relationship has expanded alongside the strategic partnership roadmap and the establishment of the Strategic Partnership Council in December 2024.

Saudi Arabia and France expand AI cooperation

Technology is another focus of the next phase of the relationship.

KSA and France agreed to deepen cooperation across artificial intelligence, quantum computing, emerging technologies and capacity building.

The investment roundtable’s business discussions also identified AI and digital infrastructure as one of four central themes for future cooperation.

The two countries separately agreed to extend the partnership on AlUla until 2035, covering areas including archaeology, heritage and culture.

KSA and France also highlighted cooperation around Expo 2030 Riyadh, with France participating in the event.

The expanding commercial relationship is supported by Vision 2030’s focus on economic diversification and the National Investment Strategy’s efforts to stimulate and attract investment, while sector-specific strategies are creating opportunities across value chains.

excerpt.rendered: Saudi Arabia and France deepen investment ties with 21 agreements, a planned $5bn credit line, $3.7bn Aramco deals and a potential $7bn Qiddiya project

title.rendered: Abu Dhabi issues warning over abandoned cars and boats in public spaces

content.rendered:
Abu Dhabi has urged the public not to leave vehicles and boats abandoned in public spaces, warning that the practice can hinder traffic, restrict access to public facilities and create environmental and public health concerns.

Abu Dhabi City Municipality has launched a field awareness campaign targeting vehicle and boat owners as well as residents, visitors and operators of commercial and public facilities, as part of efforts to protect the city’s appearance and quality of life.

The campaign forms part of “Our Home, Our Responsibility – Our Neighbourhood Defines Us” and is intended to strengthen shared civic responsibility across the city.

Abu Dhabi City Municipality is encouraging individuals to ensure vehicles and boats are not left unattended in public squares, parking areas, public facilities or residential neighbourhoods.

The campaign targets vehicle and boat owners, operators of commercial and public facilities, residents and visitors to public spaces.

Abu Dhabi vehicle warning

The Municipality highlighted the impact of leaving vehicles and boats unattended for prolonged periods without maintenance or cleaning.

It said the practice can affect the city’s appearance and hinder traffic flow. Abandoned vehicles and boats can also restrict access to public facilities.

The accumulation of dust, debris and waste can create environmental and public health concerns.

The campaign forms part of Abu Dhabi City Municipality’s wider efforts to address practices that detract from the urban environment and encourage behaviours that support a safe, clean and sustainable city.

Abu Dhabi City Municipality called on the public to cooperate by relocating, maintaining or disposing of abandoned vehicles and boats in accordance with approved procedures.

It stressed the importance of community cooperation in maintaining the quality of public spaces and preserving Abu Dhabi’s distinctive appearance.

The campaign also reinforces the Municipality’s message that protecting the city’s appearance is a shared civic responsibility.

It said maintaining clean, attractive and safe public spaces should be a daily practice reflecting the community’s commitment.

title.rendered: Dubai-India trade hits record $60.6bn as 85,841 Indian companies establish presence in emirate

content.rendered:
Dubai’s non-oil trade with India reached a record AED222.5bn ($60.6bn) in 2025, representing annual growth of 15 per cent as economic ties between the two markets continue to expand.

The number of Indian companies registered as active members of Dubai Chamber of Commerce reached 85,841 by the end of June 2026, while Dubai attracted approximately AED32.3bn ($8.8bn) in Indian investments between 2016 and 2025.

Mohammad Ali Rashed Lootah, President and CEO of Dubai Chambers, highlighted the scale of the economic relationship during a panel session at The Economic Times World Leaders Forum 2026 in New Delhi.

The event brought together leading investors and senior executives from India and around the world and was attended by His Excellency Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India.

Lootah revealed that Dubai’s non-oil trade with India reached a record AED222.5bn ($60.6bn) in 2025, up 15 per cent annually.

Dubai-India trade

Bilateral trade has increased by 136.2 per cent over the past decade, rising from AED94.2bn ($25.6bn) in 2016.

The growth reinforces India’s position as Dubai’s second-largest trading partner.

Lootah said relations between Dubai and India are continuing to expand and diversify in response to the evolving needs of businesses in both markets.

Trade remains a central pillar of the relationship, but cooperation is increasingly expanding into future-focused sectors including Agentic AI and the digital economy.

The number of Indian businesses using Dubai as a base for their operations is also growing.

Indian companies in Dubai

A total of 7,579 new Indian companies joined Dubai Chamber of Commerce during the first half of 2026, taking the total number of Indian companies registered as active members to 85,841 by the end of June.

That represented year-on-year growth of 15 per cent.

Lootah said: “The confidence of the Indian business community in the growth opportunities offered by Dubai is reflected in the 7,579 new Indian companies that joined Dubai Chamber of Commerce during the first half of this year. This brought the total number of Indian companies registered as active members of the chamber to 85,841 by the end of June 2026, representing year-on-year growth of 15%.

“These figures demonstrate that Indian companies increasingly view Dubai as a global hub from which to develop their international operations and expand their investments. They also reflect the Indian business community’s strong confidence in Dubai and its future growth prospects.”

Dubai provides Indian businesses with access to markets across the Middle East, Africa and beyond, supported by advanced infrastructure, global connectivity, a competitive business environment and direct links to customers, investors and partners.

Indian investment reaches $8.8bn

Dubai attracted approximately AED32.3bn ($8.8bn) in Indian investments between 2016 and 2025. That included AED8.4bn ($2.3bn) in foreign direct investment during 2025 alone.

Investment has also flowed in the opposite direction. companies invested AED34.1bn ($9.3bn) across 147 projects in India between 2016 and 2025, contributing to the creation of 55,274 jobs.

Indian companies operating in Dubai span a broad range of sectors. Trade and services account for 45 per cent of all active Indian companies registered as members of the Chamber of Commerce.

Real estate, leasing and business services account for 27.3 per cent, followed by construction at 19 per cent. Lootah also highlighted the importance of the UAE-India Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), which came into effect in May 2022.

The agreement has helped businesses reduce trade barriers, improve market access and unlock wider growth opportunities in both markets. Dubai’s non-oil trade with India increased by 35 per cent between 2022 and 2025, rising from AED164.9bn ($44.9bn) to AED222.5bn ($60.6bn).

Agentic AI opportunities

Technology is expected to play an increasingly important role in the next phase of economic relations.

Lootah identified Agentic AI, deep tech, fintech and digital services as areas expected to shape future cooperation.

He also highlighted the city’s recently announced initiative to accelerate the private sector’s transition to Agentic AI.

As part of the initiative, the Chambers has begun developing specialised training pathways and incubators for companies operating in Agentic AI.

It is also supporting the development of businesses specialising in Agentic AI solutions and promoting knowledge sharing and institutional capacity building across the Chambers.

The efforts are intended to enhance private sector competitiveness and strengthen the emirate’s position in the adoption of future technologies.

Indian technology companies see opportunities

Lootah said Dubai’s push to accelerate Agentic AI adoption is creating opportunities for Indian technology companies and innovators to bring their expertise to the emirate, develop solutions and establish partnerships with businesses.

Emerging technologies are expected to increasingly reshape commercial cooperation between Dubai and India, creating new sectors, investment opportunities and business models.

During the panel discussion, Lootah also outlined competitive advantages, highlighting the emirate’s economic foundations, resilience and ability to adapt to global developments while maintaining a competitive business environment.

He highlighted the emirate’s focus on shaping the future of business through Agentic AI and the digital economy and developing the capabilities companies need for their next stage of growth.

Lootah invited investors and CEOs participating in The Economic Times World Leaders Forum 2026 to explore opportunities across the emirate and consider the emirate as a strategic base for expansion into regional and global markets.

He also reaffirmed the Chambers’ commitment to helping businesses identify opportunities, establish partnerships and strengthen their ability to achieve sustainable growth.

title.rendered: US expands Iran sanctions in ‘economic D-Day’ as countries warned over trade ties

content.rendered:
The US on Monday announced an expansion of secondary sanctions it hopes will “sever every economic lifeline” sustaining Iran, as President Donald Trump’s administration struggles to resolve an unpopular war that has pushed energy prices higher.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled what he described as an “economic D-Day” that aims to give a final warning to countries to cut their business ties with Iran or risk having key companies and entities cut off from the dollar-based financial system.

“We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe. Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent said at a press conference.

But he declined to identify the countries that would be targeted, or when those penalties would take effect.

The move is part of US efforts to put pressure on Iran to end the attacks on ships in the Gulf and, more recently via its allies, in the Red Sea, that Tehran launched after the US and Israel began air strikes against it in February. Iran has said it will have the opposite effect.

US outlines Iran sanctions

Iran has spent decades under layers of US and international sanctions that have battered its economy but have not deterred its leadership.

Almost six months have passed since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran, sparking a conflict that has snarled shipping in the region, crimped the flow of oil and taken a toll on the US and global economies.

Oil prices easedon Monday after two weeks of gains as investors took profits ahead of the expected US announcement.

Bessent previously urged cooperation from China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil for several years, although the US blockade of Iran’s ports, renewed in mid-July, has already cut Iranian oil flows to China.

Experts say Washington is wary of Chinese retaliation for any sanctions on its banks ahead of expected talks next month between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, with any curbs on China’s exports of critical minerals especially sensitive.

China in spotlight

Asked about Chinese banks on Monday, Bessent said, “We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions.”

The Chinese Foreign Ministry said sanctions and pressure tactics do not help and Beijing would do what was necessary to protect China’s interests.

Bessent said the Treasury Department has mapped the networks, facilitators and financial channels that Iran uses to smuggle oil and evade sanctions. He said Washington would be working with US partners to target any source of Iran’s “illicit revenue.”

The department said the Iranian government was using five sectors – digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping – to prop up its economy and they were on notice for sanctions. The Treasury has also imposed sanctions on nearly 60 entities, individuals and vessels.

US President Donald Trump has threatened tariffs on goods from countries doing business with Iran, which include Turkey, Iraq and India, although the Supreme Court struck down the legal basis for such taxes.

Talks with Pakistan

Iran has dismissed the US threat and issued a new warning to shipping not to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its permission, listing 45 ships it said had violated its rules and threatening retaliation for any ship-to-ship transfers with them.

Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir, who has built a personal rapport with Trump, was in Iran on Monday for talks, regional media said. Pakistan said the visit aimed “to promote regional peace and stability”, and a Pakistani source said Munir would meet people close to Iran’s supreme leader.

Two Pakistani sources said Trump had called Munir last week, with another saying the main request was to bring Iran back to negotiations. The White House confirmed the call but did not comment on its substance.

Washington and Tehran have not conducted air strikes on each other’s militaries for weeks, but their last official direct talks to end the six-month-old conflict took place in June and strikes on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have continued.

A projectile struck a tanker west of the Saudi port city of Yanbu in the Red Sea on Monday, causing a fire on the main deck, shipping monitors from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said.

A spokesperson for Houthi allies, who last month announced they would block Saudi oil exports diverted to the Red Sea to avoid Hormuz, said they had attacked a vessel in the area. Saudi Arabia’s national shipping company confirmed that one of its vessels had been attacked.

excerpt.rendered: US expands secondary sanctions against Iran in an ‘economic D-Day’, warning countries and companies over trade ties as tensions disrupt oil and shipping

title.rendered: Innovo Group Partners with Dubai PropTech Hub to Accelerate Construction Innovation

content.rendered:
Following an MoU signing ceremony at DIFC, Dubai PropTech Hub, an initiative of Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), and Innovo Group have announced a strategic partnership.

DIFC is the leading global financial centre in the Middle East, Africa and South Asia (MEASA) region and home to the region’s first PropTech innovation hub.

Through this partnership with Innovo Group, a leading construction company across the UAE’s built environment, both entities aim to accelerate construction innovation across the UAE and the wider Global South, spanning Africa, Asia, the Middle East and Latin America.

The partnership agreement was signed by Mohammad Alblooshi, Chief Executive Officer of DIFC Innovation Hub and Simon Penney, Deputy Chief Executive Officer of Innovo and witnessed by His Excellency Arif Amiri, Chief Executive Officer of DIFC Authority and Bishoy Azmy, Chief Executive Officer of Innovo.

As a construction industry leader serving a broad portfolio of government and private-sector clients, Innovo will leverage the partnership to advance its vision of embedding innovation across how the built environment is designed, engineered and delivered.

By combining its live construction projects, engineering expertise and wider innovation ecosystem with the capabilities of Dubai PropTech Hub, Innovo will help identify, test and scale innovations that improve cost efficiency, speed and delivery certainty for the industry and its clients.

Contributing approximately 9.2 per cent to the UAE’s GDP, the construction sector is a critical pillar of the national economy and a key focus of Dubai PropTech Hub’s PropTech 2033 report.

Launched in 2025 as part of the DIFC Innovation Hub, the Dubai PropTech Hub brings together key stakeholders to accelerate innovation in the sector, with an ambition to support over 200 PropTech start-ups and attract more than USD 300 million in investment by 2030.

It now welcomes Innovo alongside its founding partners to strengthen innovation across the real estate value chain. The Dubai PropTech Hub provides customised licensing options, purpose-built physical workspaces, and a full suite of support programmes designed to fast-track innovation from concept to commercialisation.

For Innovo, the partnership advances its ambition to reimagine construction through innovations that deliver greater cost efficiency, speed and efficacy.

By opening its extensive portfolio of live projects to start-ups and future-facing innovators, Innovo provides a real-world environment in which solutions can be proven at scale.

This approach creates direct value for clients, giving them greater confidence that new technologies have been tested against genuine construction challenges before deployment, while supporting stronger productivity, safety, quality and delivery certainty.

With 50 per cent of participants in Dubai PropTech Hub’s inaugural Global Landing Pad programme focused on pre-construction and construction, Innovo’s site access will directly help these start-ups scale innovations spanning artificial intelligence, robotics, digital twins, automation, sustainable materials and new methodologies.

By developing PropTech innovations in the UAE and applying them across Innovo’s extensive footprint, the partnership will extend Dubai PropTech Hub’s impact across the Global South, where much of the world’s future urbanisation and construction growth is expected to take place.

This will help accelerate the adoption of innovative technology-enabled construction models across international markets.

His Excellency Arif Amiri, Chief Executive Officer of DIFC Authority, commented: “The Dubai PropTech Hub was established to serve as a regional platform where innovation meets industry at scale.

Innovo’s participation enhances our ability to move PropTech solutions from concept into live construction environments. By providing start‑ups with access to real projects, this collaboration accelerates commercial adoption and delivers tangible value for the industry, while reinforcing Dubai’s position as a global leader in real estate innovation.”

Bishoy Azmy, CEO of Innovo Group, said: “The construction industry is at a critical innovation juncture. As governments across the region advance ambitious infrastructure and urban development agendas, the industry must rethink how the built environment is designed and delivered.

By joining Dubai PropTech Hub, Innovo is reinforcing its commitment to reimagining construction and providing start-ups with the live project environments and engineering expertise needed to prove and scale their solutions.

This partnership will strengthen Dubai’s PropTech ecosystem and help shape an innovation-led future for the built environment.”

The strategic alliance establishes a comprehensive framework capable of tackling the construction sector’s most pressing global challenges.

By uniting visionary policy, agile technological development, and large-scale physical execution, Innovo and the Dubai PropTech Hub are laying the definitive foundation for a more resilient built environment.

The partnership ensures that Dubai remains the global epicentre for construction innovation while exporting a highly sustainable, data-driven blueprint for urban development worldwide.

title.rendered: Inside Airwallex’s $43m plan to enter the UAE payments market – EXCLUSIVE

content.rendered:
Airwallex is investing $43 million (AED158 million) in the UAE over the next five years.

The global financial technology company plans to expand its Dubai office, recruit senior executives and develop AI-powered products capable of performing financial tasks with limited human involvement.

Several UAE appointments have already been made during 2026, although Airwallex has not disclosed its current local headcount or how many jobs the investment is expected to create.

The company has secured in-principle approval from the Central Bank of the UAE for Stored Value Facilities and Retail Payment Services Category II licences.

However, it must still obtain full approval before offering those regulated services to customers. Airwallex is targeting a UAE launch during 2026.

The $43 million commitment forms part of a wider $1.135 billion investment across Europe, the Middle East and Africa announced in March.

Airwallex is targeting UAE companies that operate internationally and need to receive, hold and transfer money across multiple markets and currencies.

“Businesses in the UAE are scaling into more markets and handling more currencies than ever, but too many are still held back by financial infrastructure built for a single one,” Or Liban, Airwallex’s Managing Director for the Middle East, Benelux and Nordics told Arabian Business.

“This investment lets us close that gap. We’re growing our Dubai team and building new products to meet the needs of the region’s most ambitious companies, many of which are trading internationally from day one.

“This means embedding the right infrastructure from within the region, not around it.”

Airwallex targets UAE e-commerce growth

Airwallex cited forecasts suggesting that the UAE’s e-commerce market could reach $21 billion by 2031, creating greater demand for cross-border payment services and multi-currency financial infrastructure.

The company began establishing its Middle East presence in 2024, when it committed to obtaining the licences required to launch its products in the UAE and support local businesses.

Its regional expansion has since included establishing an entity in Saudi Arabia and signing a partnership with Tabby.

The agreement allows international merchants using Airwallex to offer Tabby’s buy-now-pay-later services to customers in the UAE and Saudi Arabia.

Airwallex has also launched three products called T:0, Airi and Kai as part of its push into autonomous finance.

The tools are designed to use AI agents to complete activities traditionally handled by corporate finance teams, including analysing information and performing certain routine financial tasks.

Founded in Australia in 2015, Airwallex provides businesses with payment, foreign-exchange, corporate-card and financial-management technology.

The company says its platform operates across more than 200 countries and territories under more than 85 licences.

It claims to serve more than 676,000 businesses worldwide, both directly and through companies that integrate Airwallex’s technology into their own platforms.
