title.rendered: Gulf economic support for Lebanon hinges on security and IMF reforms

content.rendered:
Lebanon’s improving relations with the Gulf could begin to translate into economic support, but only if Beirut advances on the disarmament of non-state actors and completes reforms through an agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), economists said.

Saudi Arabia lifted its nearly five-year ban on Lebanese imports in June, allowing the first containers of goods to leave Beirut for Jeddah on June 20. The UAE has also resumed operations at its embassy in Beirut and restored travel for Emirati citizens after a temporary wartime restriction.

The moves represent the most concrete economic signs yet of a diplomatic thaw that began after Joseph Aoun was elected president in January 2025 and Nawaf Salam formed a government the following month.

Nassib Ghobril, chief economist and head of economic research and analysis at Byblos Bank Group, said Gulf and Western envoys had been explicit about what must follow.

“The existing international political and diplomatic support for Lebanon will translate into economic and financial support” once the government advances on two parallel tracks, he said. The first is the disarmament of non-state actors and the restoration of executive authority over decisions of war and peace. The second is structural reform through an IMF agreement.

The security track remains deeply contested. Lebanon tasked its army in 2025 with establishing a state monopoly over weapons, while Aoun pledged that the state alone would hold the right to bear arms. Hezbollah has resisted full disarmament and argues that the issue cannot be settled while Israeli forces remain on Lebanese territory.

The dispute has become central to negotiations following the latest war. A US-brokered framework agreed in June links a phased Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon to the disarmament of non-state armed groups and a wider deployment of the Lebanese army. Israel has said it will not withdraw until Hezbollah is disarmed, while the group has rejected that sequence.

Saudi eases Lebanon trade restrictions

Saudi Arabia’s decision to restore imports showed how progress on a narrower security issue can produce a commercial result. Riyadh first banned Lebanese fruit and vegetables in April 2021 after more than five million Captagon pills were discovered in a shipment of pomegranates. The prohibition was later extended to all Lebanese goods during a wider diplomatic rupture.

Before the first containers departed in June, Salam and Saudi ambassador Fahd Al-Dossari inspected new cargo scanners at Beirut port. Saudi authorities said the ban was lifted after positive steps by Lebanon towards rebuilding state institutions and tighter controls against smuggling.

“The reopening of the Saudi market to Lebanese exports goes way beyond economics and technicalities, and has a very symbolic dimension,” Ghobril said. The decision reflected renewed confidence in the authorities’ willingness to impose the rule of law, protect border crossings and reconnect Lebanon with its Arab partners, he added.

Economic reforms

The economic reform track has also moved, though the most difficult decisions remain unresolved. Parliament passed further amendments to the Bank Resolution Law on August 12 after the IMF identified shortcomings in the original framework. A separate financial gap bill must determine how losses from the 2019 collapse are divided among the state, the central bank, commercial banks and depositors.

Lebanon’s real GDP fell by nearly 40 per cent between 2019 and the end of 2024. The World Bank estimated growth of 3.5 per cent in 2025, helped by tourism, remittances and private consumption, but the latest war overturned expectations of another expansion. Finance Minister Yassine Jaber said in May that the economy could contract by at least 7 per cent this year, with damage reaching $20 billion.

Leila Dagher, founding director of the Center for Policy Action and an associate professor of economics and policy at Lebanese American University, said political and security stability was the first condition for investment.

“Serious long-term investment is extremely difficult to attract when there is a persistent risk of conflict or when armed actors operate outside the authority of the state,” she said.

Banking restructuring, judicial independence, enforceable contracts, transparent procurement and predictable regulation must follow, Dagher added.

Ghobril said banking and fiscal measures would need to be accompanied by improvements to the rule of law, greater public-sector accountability and action against the shadow economy.

“Focusing only on technical issues, such as fiscal and banking reforms, despite their importance, will not restore confidence in the economy or attract investments,” he said.

excerpt.rendered: Saudi Arabia has reopened its market to Lebanese goods, but wider Gulf support will depend on progress towards state control over weapons and a credible settlement of the financial collapse

title.rendered: UAE announces major new rules for businesses starting from October 1

content.rendered:
Businesses in the United Arab Emirates are being told to start checking up on their suppliers, or risk losing money they’re owed back from the tax authorities.

From October 1, the UAE’s Federal Tax Authority (FTA) will be able to refuse to refund VAT to a business if the goods or services it bought were linked, anywhere along the supply chain, to tax evasion.

VAT is a 5 per cent charge added to most goods and services in the UAE, introduced in 2018. Businesses normally claim back the VAT they’ve paid on their own purchases but under the new rules, that claim can now be blocked.

Legal experts say the toughest part of the new rule is that businesses no longer need to have known about wrongdoing to be penalised.

Thomas Vanhee, a partner at tax firm Aurifer Middle East, said if a business genuinely knew its purchase was tied to tax evasion, the refund refusal is automatic.

But even if it merely “should have known” based on the circumstances, the authority now has the power to reject the claim too.

Under the decision, a business is treated as though it “should have known” if it simply failed to carry out proper checks on its suppliers and purchases, in line with rules the authority has now laid out.

What businesses must now do

The new checks come in two layers, according to Vanhee.

The first is checking suppliers themselves.

Businesses must verify a supplier’s identity the first time they work with them, and repeat the check every 12 months.

This includes checking official records, confirming who is authorised to act on the supplier’s behalf, and making sure the business operates from where it claims to.

Firms are also expected to watch a supplier suddenly changing address, swapping out key staff, or striking deals that look too big for a company of its size.

For bigger relationships where a supplier is providing more than AED 375,000 worth of goods or services a year businesses must also get written confirmation from a UAE bank that the supplier holds an account there, and look into their public reputation and media coverage.

Businesses must also be able to show the deal made genuine commercial sense, the price wasn’t unreasonably high or low, what they bought matched the supplier’s actual licensed business, and the goods were legitimately owned and sourced.

Cash payments will now need to be documented.

Companies will also be required to put in writing exactly who carries out these checks, who reviews them, and who is responsible for overseeing the process.

There is some relief for very small transactions. Purchases under AED 10,000 are exempt from the new checks.

Vanhee said the exemption largely disappears in practice, because it stops applying altogether once a business buys more than AED 100,000 in total from one supplier over a year.

That works out to around AED 8,300 a month.

excerpt.rendered: UAE businesses face tighter supplier checks from October 1, with VAT refunds denied when purchases are linked to tax evasion

title.rendered: Dubai property trend: Half of prospective villa buyers now search for 4-bedroom or larger homes

content.rendered:
Dubai’s villa market is seeing growing demand for larger homes, with as many as half of prospective villa buyers now searching for properties with four bedrooms or more, according to Property Finder data.

The figure has increased from 44 per cent a year earlier as Dubai’s growing population of high-net-worth individuals drives demand for larger properties, prime locations and premium finishes, while H1 2026 Dubai Land Department data points to a broader premiumisation trend.

As many as 50 per cent of prospective villa buyers are searching for homes with four bedrooms or more, compared with 44 per cent a year earlier, according to Property Finder data.

The shift comes as Dubai’s growing high-net-worth population accelerates demand for larger homes, premium finishes and properties in prime locations.

H1 2026 Dubai Land Department data also shows a premiumisation trend, with buyers increasingly prioritising quality of life over short-term value plays.

Dubai villa buyers

The changing preferences are influencing how developers target buyers seeking additional space for growing families, working from home and multi-generational living.

DAMAC Properties has responded to the trend with an initiative aimed at making it easier for buyers to move into larger properties.

Homebuyers can purchase a five-bedroom townhouse at DAMAC Islands 2 from AED3.55m ($967,000), comparable to the outlay on a four-bedroom townhouse until handover.

The initiative includes a 16 per cent down payment and waiver of the 4 per cent Dubai Land Department registration fee, reducing the initial cost of purchasing a larger property.

Amira Sajwani, Managing Director, DAMAC Properties, said: “Upsizing is not simply about acquiring a bigger property. It is about choosing a home that can accommodate the family you are becoming. An additional bedroom can serve many purposes over the life of a home; be it a study, fitness room, home office, or space for extended family. Through this initiative, we are making that long-term flexibility more accessible.”

Why are Dubai homebuyers upsizing?

The source identifies five circumstances that could encourage families to consider moving into a larger home.

  • Existing homes no longer fit everyday life: Changing family circumstances can make previously adequate homes feel increasingly constrained. Limited storage, crowded communal areas and difficulties accommodating everyday routines can increase the appeal of a larger, better-planned property
  • More generations are sharing a home: Multi-generational households can require additional bedrooms and private living areas. Homes accommodating grandparents, adult children, visiting relatives or live-in support can benefit from additional space that allows family members to live together while maintaining privacy
  • Working from home requires dedicated space: Hybrid and remote working have also changed how households use residential space. Where dining tables, bedrooms or communal areas regularly double as workplaces, an additional room can provide a dedicated home office and create greater separation between work and family life
  • Families are planning for future space requirements: Future changes such as having another child, older children requiring greater privacy or relatives moving into the household can also influence purchasing decisions. Moving into a larger home before those changes occur could reduce the need for another move later
  • The household can afford the full cost: Financial capacity remains a key consideration when moving to a larger property. DAMAC experts advise families to consider the total cost of ownership rather than the purchase price alone, including financing, service charges, maintenance, furnishing and moving costs

excerpt.rendered: Half of prospective Dubai villa buyers now seek four bedrooms or more, up from 44% a year ago, as demand grows for larger homes and premium locations

title.rendered: UAE to introduce new tax from September 1

content.rendered:
The UAE Ministry of Finance has confirmed that a new tax on electronic smoking devices will come into effect on September 1, 2026.

However, contrary to some beliefs it’s not the first time vapes and e-liquids have been subject to tax in the UAE.

An excise tax on vapes and e-liquids was first introduced on December 1, 2019.

What is new about the tax being enforced next month is a minimum excise price for vaping liquids.

The Ministry of Finance announced the issuance of a decision on the minimum Excise Price for Tobacco Products and Liquids used in Electronic Smoking Devices and Tools.

The decision aims to enhance the effectiveness of excise tax implementation and support compliance with the UAE’s tax legislation.

Under the rules and regulations of the new tax being introduced, the existing minimum Excise Price will continue to apply to Cigarettes, Water Pipe Tobacco, ready-to-use tobacco products, and similar products.

The new tax will pave the way for the introduction of a minimum Excise Price of AED 1 per millilitre (mL) for Liquids used in Electronic Smoking Devices and Tools.

As aforementioned above the new tax will enter into force on 1 September, 2026.

UAE tobacco tax rate

The UAE Ministry of Finance has also stated that the new tax has been designed to keep pace with developments in the market for excise goods and ensure the consistent application of unified standards across all categories of tobacco and electronic smoking products.

The Ministry also highlighted how it supports tax compliance and helps limit practices that may affect the effective implementation of the excise tax.

The UAE levies excise tax at a rate of 100 per cent on all tobacco products covered under the excise tax regime.

Analysts believe that the UAE has two primary aims with the introduction of the new tax.

Essentially, it wants to make the excise system more effective, but it also clearly wants to try and discourage the consumption of vaping and related products.

The country’s Federal Tax Authority explicitly describes excise tax as being intended both to reduce consumption of products considered harmful and to raise government revenue.

excerpt.rendered: The new tax being introduced by the UAE Ministry of Finance will impact vapers across the country

title.rendered: Huda: The Public Living Room

content.rendered:
At Huda, a Levantine bistro tucked into a corner of Brooklyn, dinner service shares space with film screenings, artist workshops, performance bingo fundraisers, musical performances, backgammon nights and community events. For founder Gehad Hadidi, the restaurant was never meant to be just a restaurant. “I wanted it to be a neighborhood space,” Hadidi says. “Not just a place where you come to spend money and eat food.”

The story begins decades before Huda opened its doors in 2023. Born in Michigan to an American mother and a Syrian-Palestinian father, Hadidi spent his summers in Damascus visiting extended family. He has memories of helping his grandmother prepare kibbeh naya, stealing bites as she mixed the ingredients by hand before dinner. In the evenings, relatives would gather to eat on the balcony. His family meals were rituals filled with conversation & togetherness.

After attending the American University of Beirut, Hadidi eventually moved to New York as the Syrian war intensified. He built a career in urban planning, exploring how communities form around shared spaces. Through that work,  he became interested in the role restaurants played in city life. “Restaurants define neighborhoods and are defined by neighborhoods,” he says. 

Before opening Huda, Hadidi took over La Bonne Soupe, a decades-old French restaurant in Midtown Manhattan. After navigating restaurant ownership throughout COVID and its aftermath, he felt ready to build something of his own. Together with chef de cuisine Omneyah Hassan, an Egyptian-American chef and fellow child of immigrants, the menu for Huda was built, rooted in Levantine traditions and informed by the realities of cooking in New York. The menu shifts according to the seasons, the availability of local produce and the restaurant’s relationships with nearby farms.

The name Huda itself comes from the community center Hadidi attended growing up in Detroit. From the outset, he imagined the restaurant’s back room as a space for cultural programming, inspired by the role the center had played in his own life.

You might also like:

  • How Studio Tuut is Preserving Lebanon’s Culinary Heritage
  • At Impala, Meedu Saad cooks from memory
  • Akub, the Notting Hill Restaurant That Likes to Share

In Huda’s first year, Hadidi began hosting “Summer Sundays,” transforming the restaurant into a miniature cinema dedicated to films from the SWANA region. Dining tables were removed, chairs were arranged in rows, popcorn was served, and the bar became a concession stand. These afternoons were an early attempt to put Hadidi’s vision into practice. “It’s one thing to say you want to build a community space,” he says. “It’s a totally other thing for it to actually become a community space.”

The screenings became increasingly popular, and soon artists and organisers began approaching the restaurant with ideas of their own. Among the earliest collaborations was a workshop series curated by artist Rama Duwaji. Each session centered on a season and a fruit, using food as an entry point into broader conversations about culture, memory and storytelling. One workshop focused on pomegranates, inviting participants to paint ceramic tiles while exploring the fruit’s place in mythology and regional traditions. Huda’s reputation grew with its programming, expanding to include intimate concerts, comedy nights, watch parties and other community-led events.

One of the most memorable moments so far came on New York City’s mayoral election night, when Huda hosted a watch party that drew nearly one thousand people. “It was absolutely nuts,” Hadidi says. While the turnout exceeded expectations, what stayed with him was the realisation that people had chosen Huda as the place they wanted to gather to celebrate this moment.

Hadidi remains adamant that Huda must also succeed on its own terms as a restaurant. “I don’t want people to come to the restaurant because it’s pro-Palestine,” he says. “I want them to actually enjoy the food, the service, and the ambiance.” 

His ambitions for Huda also extend beyond the present. He wants the restaurant to be a platform for younger artists, chefs, and cultural workers, a place that might help launch something larger than itself. “I hope Huda is a seed,” he says, “that grows into something much, much larger and more important.”

excerpt.rendered: At Huda, founder Gehad Hadidi is reimagining what a restaurant can be.

title.rendered: UAE weather forecast: Rain expected on 3 days as temperatures fall and winds hit 40kmph

content.rendered:
Temperatures are set to decrease in the UAE on Thursday, with the latest five-day weather forecast also showing the possibility of rainfall across parts of the country on Friday, Saturday and Monday.

Convective clouds could bring rain to eastern and southern areas, while fog and mist are possible at times and winds could reach 40kmph. Blowing dust and rougher sea conditions are also forecast in western areas on Thursday.

Conditions on Thursday, August 20 will be fair to partly cloudy, with clouds appearing in eastern areas that may become convective during the afternoon. Temperatures are forecast to decrease.

Conditions will become humid overnight and into Friday morning across some coastal areas, bringing a chance of fog or mist formation.

Winds will be light to moderate but could freshen at times in western areas, causing blowing dust. Conditions in the Arabian Gulf will be slight to moderate, becoming rough at times in the west, while the Oman Sea will remain slight.

UAE rain forecast for Friday

Friday, August 21 will be fair to partly cloudy, with the probability of convective cloud formation across eastern and southern areas during the afternoon. The clouds may be associated with rainfall.

Conditions will become humid overnight and into Saturday morning over some western areas, with a chance of fog or mist.

Light to moderate southeasterly winds will become northwesterly and could freshen at times, reaching speeds of 40kmph.

Sea conditions will be slight in both the Arabian Gulf and Oman Sea.

Chance of UAE rainfall continues on Saturday

The possibility of rainfall will continue on Saturday, August 22.

Conditions will be fair to partly cloudy at times, with the probability of convective clouds forming over eastern and southern areas during the afternoon. These clouds may be associated with rainfall.

Southeasterly winds will become northwesterly and remain light to moderate, freshening at times and reaching speeds of 35kmph.

The Arabian Gulf and Oman Sea will both be slight.

UAE weather forecast for Sunday

Sunday, August 23 is forecast to be fair to partly cloudy at times.

Clouds will appear across eastern areas during the afternoon, although the forecast does not specify a probability of rainfall on Sunday.

Light to moderate southeasterly winds will become northwesterly, freshening at times and reaching speeds of 35kmph. Sea conditions will remain slight in the Arabian Gulf and Oman Sea.

UAE rain and fog forecast for Monday

The possibility of rainfall returns on Monday, August 24. Conditions will be fair to partly cloudy at times, with the probability of convective clouds forming in eastern areas during the afternoon that may be associated with rainfall.

It will become humid overnight and into Tuesday morning over some coastal areas, with a probability of fog or mist formation.

Light to moderate southeasterly to northeasterly winds could freshen at times, reaching speeds of 40kmph.

The sea will remain slight in both the Arabian Gulf and Oman Sea.

title.rendered: Gaming habits revealed: 20% of players drive nearly 75% of spending as teenagers lead purchases

content.rendered:
A relatively small group of gamers is responsible for the vast majority of spending across the gaming industry, with the highest-spending 20 per cent of players accounting for nearly three-quarters of total expenditure, according to new research.

Bain & Company’s 2026 Gaming Report, based on a survey of more than 5,300 gamers worldwide and proprietary analysis of 100 titles released since 2023, argues that the concept of an “average gamer” is disappearing as player preferences fragment and both spending and playing time become increasingly concentrated.

Spending is heavily concentrated among a relatively narrow segment of players. The highest-spending 20 per cent account for nearly three-quarters of total spending, according to Bain.

Playing time follows a similar pattern, with the most active 20 per cent of gamers responsible for almost 60 per cent of all playing time.

Gaming habits revealed

Age also plays a significant role in spending behaviour. Bain found that 86 per cent of teenage gamers spend money on gaming each month, compared with 36 per cent of players in their 60s and 27 per cent of those in their 70s.

Gamers who create game content for public use are twice as likely to spend money, according to the survey.

Player preferences are also becoming increasingly fragmented. No single type of gaming experience attracted more than 26 per cent of respondents in Bain’s survey.

The differences become particularly apparent between generations. A third of gamers aged 13 to 17 want open, user-generated content, but that proportion falls to 15 per cent or lower among players aged 50 and above.

Anders Christofferson, partner of Bain’s Media & Entertainment practice and global head of Bain’s Video Game sector, said: “The question for gaming executives is no longer solely about reaching more players. It’s reaching the right players, in the right way, and getting more ownership over that relationship.

“The studios pulling ahead are the ones that have made a deliberate choice about who they are building for and are aligning every resource behind that answer; AI, distribution, and personalization alike.”

Games with commercial success

Bain’s analysis of games released since 2023 found a significant difference in commercial outcomes depending on how clearly developers identified their intended players.

Some 83 per cent of games built around a specific, identifiable player achieved commercial success, compared with 50 per cent of games that were not. The findings also suggest most gamers aren’t necessarily searching for radically new experiences.

Two-thirds want more of what they already play, including a franchise sequel, something similar or a focus on existing content. Only one in five is looking for something genuinely different.

Artificial intelligence could allow developers with clearly defined audiences to prototype games faster, iterate more cheaply and develop a deeper understanding of players.

Bain found that 42 per cent of gamers are more comfortable with AI in games than they were a year ago. Among teenagers aged 13 to 17, that figure rises to 59 per cent.

Anders Videbaek, partner at Bain & Company’s Media & Entertainment practice and leader of the firm’s Video Game sector in EMEA, said: “AI is changing the cost structure of game development, but it doesn’t change the fundamental question every studio has to answer first: who exactly are you building for? Without that answer, AI doesn’t lower your risk, it lets you scale the wrong bet faster. The developers pulling ahead are committing to a target player earlier than their competitors, and using AI to deepen that focus, not broaden it.”

Nearly half of gamers buy directly from developers

Another major shift identified by the report is the growth of direct-to-consumer purchasing. Nearly half of gamers surveyed had purchased virtual currency, items or in-game content directly from a developer’s web store during the previous 12 months.

Some 27 per cent had done so multiple times. The trend is particularly pronounced among younger players. Among gamers aged 13 to 17, 40 per cent had made multiple direct purchases during the past year.

Three-quarters of the world’s top-grossing mobile games now operate their own web stores, according to Bain’s analysis, compared with just 12 per cent in 2019.

For mobile publishers, converting a sale from a third-party platform to a direct channel can improve the margin on that sale by 15 to 30 percentage points, according to the report.

Personalised gaming offers influence spending

Bain argues that direct relationships also give gaming companies access to behavioural data including in-game micro-decisions, social graph connections and purchase histories.

This could increasingly be used to personalise individual players’ experiences and offers. The research found that increasing a web-store discount from 10 per cent to 30 per cent barely changed the share of gamers who preferred buying directly rather than through an app store.

Among gamers who had made multiple direct purchases during the previous 12 months, 84 per cent said a personalised offer from a game they play often would make them more likely to buy.

Bain identifies five areas where one-to-one personalisation using contextual bandit engines — machine-learning models that continuously learn from player behaviour and optimise decisions in real time — could create value.

These include in-game store and offer optimisation, reengaging lapsed players, personalised onboarding, in-game content discovery and recommendations across different titles within a publisher’s portfolio.

As overall market expansion moderates, Bain’s findings suggest gaming companies are increasingly shifting their focus from simply expanding audiences towards identifying valuable player groups, strengthening existing relationships and developing direct connections with those players.

title.rendered: Dubai events calendar 2026: GITEX Global, Arabian Travel Market, Big 5 and 50+ major shows announced

title.rendered: UAE President Sheikh Mohamed receives phone call from Donald Trump

content.rendered:
UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan spoke to US President Donald Trump on Tuesday.

During the call the two leaders spoke about the challenges facing the Middle East as the conflict between the US and Iran edges closer towards the six-month mark.

Huge issues persist in both the Strait of Hormuz and The Red Sea.

The two leaders also reinforced their commitment to enhance bilateral ties between the UAE and United States.

The most pressing issue regional is undoubtedly the continued war between Washington and Tehran.

A two-month window aimed at resolving the war and finding a peace settlement has now passed, but many diplomats remain hopeful that a deal can be struck.

On Monday, the UAE leader met Sultan Haitham of Oman for talks that took place in Abu Dhabi.

Those talks rather inevitably also focused on the ongoing war, and the need to build robust and resilient partnerships.

Oman has been locked in talks with Iran over the management of the Strait of Hormuz, and was subjected to threats by US President Donald Trump, who said they would bomb the country if it didn’t play ball with Washington.

It was also reported on Tuesday that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with the UAE’s National Security Adviser and Deputy Ruler, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed,

“The two discussed a number of regional security issues, including Lebanon, as well as continued US-UAE co-ordination to hold Iran and its terrorist proxies accountable for ongoing attacks,” the US State Department said.

UAE blasts latest Iran attacks

On Tuesday, the UAE Foreign Ministry also condemned a drone attack on Iraq’s Kurdistan region that was carried out by Iran.

Two explosives-laden drones targeted the office of Masrour Barzani, Prime Minister of the Kurdistan Regional Government, and the home of a senior security official in Erbil.

The UAE Ministry said in a statement, “This act of aggression constitutes a flagrant violation of the sovereignty of the Republic of Iraq and the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, and a threat to their security and stability.”

excerpt.rendered: The two leaders both agreed to continue to cooperate closely over the regional challenges currently facing the Middle East region.

title.rendered: Dubai’s wealthy buyers drive demand for bigger, higher-end homes

content.rendered:
DAMAC Properties has launched an offer targeting Dubai homebuyers seeking larger family homes at DAMAC Islands 2. Five-bedroom townhouses start at about $966,600 (AED 3.55 million), according to company material.

Buyers can secure a unit with a 16% down payment and receive a waiver on the 4% Dubai Land Department registration fee. DAMAC designed the offer to reduce upfront capital requirements for households moving into larger properties.

Dubai recorded $68.62 billion (AED 252 billion) of real estate transactions during Q1 2026, up 31% year on year. Luxury real estate investment reached $23.88 billion (AED 87.71 billion), representing 26% growth.

Larger homes attract family buyers

Dubai’s expanding private wealth base is adding demand across larger residential formats. UAE attracted about 9,800 new millionaires during 2025, with most settling in Dubai, according to Henley & Partners estimates cited by DIFC.

Property Finder data cited in DAMAC’s announcement puts larger villas at the centre of buyer searches. Some 50% of prospective villa buyers are searching for homes with at least four bedrooms. That compares with 44% one year earlier.

Household requirements are also changing alongside wealth and population growth. Families seeking extra bedrooms increasingly need dedicated offices, storage, fitness rooms and accommodation for relatives.

Multi-generational households create another requirement for additional private space. Grandparents, adult children and live-in support can require separate bedrooms and living areas.

Hybrid working adds pressure when dining rooms or bedrooms regularly serve as workspaces.

DAMAC cuts upfront cost for larger homes

DAMAC’s 16% down payment equates to about $154,700 (AED 568,000) on the stated starting price. A 4% registration fee on that value would equal about $38,700 (AED 142,000).

Waiving that registration charge reduces cash required when buyers secure the property.

DAMAC says the five-bedroom townhouse offer requires an outlay comparable with a four-bedroom townhouse until handover. Buyers still need to assess financing costs and future payment obligations across the full acquisition period.

Amira Sajwani, Managing Director of DAMAC Properties, said larger homes can accommodate changes in household structure over several years.

“Upsizing is not simply about acquiring a bigger property. It is about choosing a home that can accommodate the family you are becoming.”

Sajwani said an additional bedroom can operate as a study, fitness room, home office or accommodation for extended family.

Household changes drive upsizing decisions

DAMAC identifies several household conditions that can trigger demand for more space. Crowded shared areas, limited storage and increasingly difficult daily routines can indicate that an existing property no longer meets requirements.

Family planning also affects purchase timing. Another child, teenagers requiring more privacy or relatives joining the household can alter bedroom requirements quickly.

An earlier purchase can reduce the likelihood of completing two separate property transactions within a relatively short period. Moving costs, furnishing requirements and financing expenses all affect that calculation.

Financial capacity remains central to any upsizing decision. DAMAC advises buyers to calculate total ownership costs rather than focusing only on the purchase price.

Financing, service charges, maintenance, furnishing and relocation expenses can materially increase household expenditure after acquisition.

Dubai Land Department data also recorded 60,303 real estate transactions during Q1 2026, up 6% year on year.

DAMAC Islands 2 expands larger housing supply

DAMAC Islands 2 includes several formats aimed at buyers requiring larger internal areas.

Five-bedroom townhouses span approximately 293 square metres and 263 square metres. Four-bedroom townhouses measure about 203 square metres.

Six-bedroom luxury villas extend to approximately 583 square metres. Five-bedroom twin villas provide around 324 square metres.

DAMAC has positioned the development around landscaped areas, lagoons and wellness facilities. Design references draw from Antigua, Bahamas, Barbados, Bermuda, Cuba, Maui, Mauritius and Tahiti.

Current DAMAC listings for Antigua at DAMAC Islands 2 include four- and five-bedroom townhouses and twin villas. Company listings also indicate a 2030 handover schedule for units within that part of the development.

Dubai’s wider luxury segment continues to absorb substantial capital. DLD recorded a 26% annual increase in luxury real estate investment during Q1 2026.

title.rendered: UAE approves 10 new drugs, from weight-loss pills to gene therapy

content.rendered:
The UAE is continuing to accelerate its efforts to become a global leader in healthcare.

The Emirates Drug Establishment has approved a whole host of new drugs over the last 12 months.

In June 2026, the UAE became the first country outside the United States to introduce an oral GLP-1 treatment for weight management.

It was a big step forward in the country’s efforts to really expand obesity care.

The UAE weight loss and obesity management market is valued at $1.2 billion.

However, a number of new other drugs and medicines have been granted regulatory approval in the last year.

The UAE has approved medicines that tackle conditions from obesity and heart disease to cancer, dry eyes, vitiligo, cholesterol, and nasal spray for severe allergies.

Below is an overview on the new medicines that have entered the UAE healthcare market over the last 12 months.

Weight loss management

Oral Wegovy

As aforementioned above, the UAE is only the second country in the world to greenlight Wegovy, also known as semaglutide.

It is essentially a needle-free option for patients that don’t want to inject themselves to manage their weight loss.

Medical practitioners have stated that it should be used alongside a change in lifestyle, with healthier eating and increased physical activity encouraged.

The treatment also claims to reduce the risk of major heart-related events in high-risk patients.

Foundayo

Foundayo has also been introduced to the UAE over the last year.

That treatment is a once daily pill used for patients with obesity.

However, it can also be prescribed to people with other issues such as diabetes and high blood pressure.

Cholesterol/Blood Pressure/Heart Failure

Lipfendra

High cholesterol remains a big problem across the UAE.

Despite the availability of cholesterol treatments, it is high across the board.

The big selling point with this particular drug Lipfendra is convenience.

Traditional treatments for cholesterol have largely been injections, but Lipfendra is a once-daily pill.

Baxfendy

Baxfendy has been introduced to the UAE in a bid to tackle high blood pressure.

It is providing practitioners with another treatment if existing options are not shifting the dial.

Interestingly, the UAE became the first country in the world to approve Baxfendy.

Inpefa

Inpefa is an oral drug that has been designed to tackle the issue of heart failure.

Cardiovascular disease is the biggest killer in the UAE.

It accounts for 30 per cent of all deaths.

The UAE became only the second country globally to authorise it.

Allergies/Dry Eyes

EURneffy

EURneffy has been introduced to help patients overcome severe allergies.

The nasal spray delivers epinephrine, or adrenaline, during severe allergic reactions.

Instead of having to inject the medicine, eligible adults and children can receive it through the nose.

Miebo

Dry eyes is also a condition that has become more common across the UAE.

Miebo is a prescription eye drop drug for dry-eye disease.

However, instead of simply adding moisture, it targets excessive tear evaporation.

That gives doctors another option for patients suffering symptoms such as burning, irritation, blurred vision and discomfort, particularly when tear evaporation is driving the condition.

Breast Cancer/Gene Therapy/Skin Disease

Etcamah

Etcamah is a treatment for breast cancer, but it is not for every person with breast cancer.

It is a very specific drug aimed at certain breast cancer patients.

Patients with advanced or metastatic breast cancer whose cancer develops a genetic change known as an ESR1 mutation are eligible while they are receiving hormone treatment.

Itvisma

A new drug has been introduced for patients suffering from spinal muscular atrophy (SMA).

Spinal muscular atrophy is a rare genetic disease that results in muscle wastage and weakness.

Itvisma is a one-time gene therapy for eligible patients with spinal muscular atrophy.

Rather than only treating symptoms, the therapy targets the underlying genetic cause of the disease.

RINVOQ

The UAE also became the first country globally to approve RINVOQ.

The medicine itself already existed; what is new is its approval for vitiligo.

The once-daily pill provides a treatment that works throughout the body, giving eligible patients another option, particularly when treating individual skin patches may not be enough.

title.rendered: Former Majid Al Futtaim CEO warns companies are ‘negotiating their own decline’

content.rendered:
Companies risk “negotiating the terms of their own decline” by chasing immediate profits at the expense of investment, talent and customer trust, former Majid Al Futtaim chief executive Alain Bejjani has warned.

Bejjani, who led the Dubai-based retail and property group from 2015 to 2023, said the pressure on chief executives to deliver short-term results had intensified as artificial intelligence transforms businesses, supply chains fragment and capital becomes more expensive.

However, he rejected the idea that leaders must choose between meeting today’s targets and preparing their companies for the future.

“Today’s performance is not the enemy of the long term. It is what funds it,” Bejjani told Arabian Business.

“Results earn you credibility with capital investors, patience from your board, the ability to attract the best talent and the right to invest through a downturn.

“A company that misses its numbers does not get to hold philosophical debates about its future. Its future will be decided by markets, by creditors or by an acquirer.”

Bejjani said the more important question was how companies produced their financial results.

Two businesses could report identical quarterly numbers while moving in entirely different directions, he argued. One may be strengthening its operations and relationships, while the other may be protecting profits by postponing investments and placing unsustainable pressure on employees.

“Building means customers who come back and capabilities that deepen; it means technology absorbed into how the company actually works, and leaders developed faster than the business grows,” he said.

“Borrowing, however, looks like deferred investment dressed up as efficiency, talent sweated rather than grown, and the brand exploited rather than nurtured. The income statement cannot tell the difference for a surprisingly long time. And then, suddenly, it can.”

Short-term performance

Bejjani described the distinction as one between “extraction and construction”, rather than the traditional debate between short- and long-term thinking.

Businesses focused on construction use current performance to develop their people, technology and customer relationships. Companies pursuing extraction generate results by consuming capabilities and goodwill that may be difficult to replace.

The former chief executive said the pace of disruption made those underlying strengths increasingly important.

“When disruption hits, and it now hits every industry in shorter cycles, the companies that adapt are the ones that have built capacity in the calm quarters: financial resilience, institutional trust and people who know how to learn,” he said.

“Adaptability is accumulated in good times and spent in bad ones. You cannot find it in the middle of the storm.”

During his tenure at Majid Al Futtaim, Bejjani said the group worked towards a 25-year strategic direction. This was not based on an attempt to predict economic or technological conditions decades in advance, but on the long lifespan of the company’s malls and other major assets.

“The direction never told us what would happen. It told us what to do when anything happened,” he said.

Four priorities for CEOs

Bejjani identified four capabilities that companies should develop regardless of which economic or technological scenario emerges: adaptable talent, a resilient balance sheet, customer and stakeholder trust, and strong investor relationships.

He said these represented investments that would retain their value even when corporate forecasts proved wrong.

Looking at businesses from an investor’s perspective, Bejjani said he now paid less attention to ambitious visions for 2040 and more attention to how companies generated their present-day performance.

“No single quarter can tell you a company’s future. But the way results are made, sustained over time, invariably shapes what the company is becoming,” he said.

“The ‘how’ of today conditions the ‘what’ of tomorrow. A company that delivers by building is compounding towards relevance. A company that delivers by extraction is negotiating the terms of its own decline, however healthy this year’s numbers might look.”

Bejjani said uncertainty about the future could not become an excuse for weak performance—but neither should immediate targets be met by weakening the business.

“The leaders still in business in 2040 will not be the ones who made predictions,” he said. “They will be the ones who never bought a single today at the expense of their tomorrow.”

excerpt.rendered: Alain Bejjani says businesses that protect short-term profits by neglecting investment, talent and customer trust may appear healthy while quietly weakening their future

title.rendered: Saudi jobs surge as HRDF helps 329,000 citizens find employment in first half of 2026

content.rendered:
Saudi Arabia’s Human Resources Development Fund (HRDF) contributed to the employment of 329,000 Saudi citizens during the first half of 2026, an increase of 23 per cent compared with the same period last year.

The fund also provided around SR4.9bn ($1.3bn) in direct support to individuals and establishments benefiting from its training, empowerment and guidance programmes and products, while the number of Saudi citizens benefiting from its services and programmes exceeded 1.69 million.

Saudi HRDF supports employment of 329,000 citizens

The Human Resources Development Fund contributed to the employment of 329,000 Saudi citizens in the labour market during the first six months of 2026. The figure represents an increase of 23 per cent compared with the first half of 2025.

The results highlight the scale of HRDF’s employment and development activity across Saudi Arabia’s labour market.

Total direct support provided to individuals and establishments benefiting from HRDF’s training, empowerment and guidance programmes and products amounted to around SR4.9bn ($1.3bn) during the first half of the year.

More than 1.69 million citizens benefited from the fund’s services and programmes during the period. The figures reflect the fund’s expanding developmental impact on individuals, establishments and the labour market.

171,000 Saudi establishments receive support

The number of establishments benefiting from HRDF services in KSA exceeded 171,000 across different regions and economic sectors of the Kingdom. That represented an increase of 25 per cent compared with the same period last year.

Small, medium-sized and micro enterprises accounted for 95 per cent of all beneficiary establishments.

The new figures underscore the fund’s continued and significant support for private-sector growth, enabling businesses to attract and qualify national talent and strengthening their contribution to economic development and job creation.

title.rendered: UAE launches new SEO satellite into space aboard China’s Long March 2C rocket

content.rendered:
The UAE has successfully launched the SEO satellite into space aboard a Long March 2C carrier rocket from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Centre in China.

The satellite, developed as part of the National Space Science and Technology Centre’s (NSSTC) efforts to expand national space projects, will provide data to support environmental protection, natural resource management, planning and decision-making.

The project will also provide Emirati researchers and engineers with practical experience in satellite design, development and operations in cooperation with international partners.

UAE SEO satellite

The SEO mission will support scientific research and technology applications related to sustainability and future development.

Data provided by the satellite is intended to support four areas identified by the National Space Science and Technology Centre:

  • Environmental protection
  • Natural resource management
  • Planning
  • Decision-making

The mission forms part of efforts to develop UAE capabilities in the space sector and expand the country’s work in science, technology and innovation.

UAE satellite launches aboard Long March 2C

The SEO satellite was launched aboard a Long March 2C carrier rocket from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Centre in China.

The National Space Science and Technology Centre is based at the United Arab Emirates University (UAEU).

The project is also intended to develop national talent by giving Emirati researchers and engineers practical experience in the design, development and operation of satellites.

The work is being carried out in cooperation with international partners.

UAE develops national space capabilities

Salem Al Qubaisi, Director-General at UAE Space Agency, said the successful launch was in line with the UAE’s vision and National Space Strategy to strengthen the country’s position among global leaders in the sector and expand the contribution of advanced science and technology to sustainable development and the knowledge economy.

He said the mission highlighted the importance of cooperation between national and academic institutions in building an advanced space ecosystem and developing Emirati capabilities.

Dr. Nabil Mohammed Al Bastaki, Director of the National Space Science and Technology Centre, said the SEO project is part of the Centre’s ongoing efforts to advance national space projects and strengthen UAE capabilities.

He said the project also provides researchers and engineers with practical expertise in satellite design, development and operations.

title.rendered: FCA appoints new UAE attaché as UK deepens financial ties with Gulf

content.rendered:
The UK’s Financial Conduct Authority has appointed a new Financial Services Attaché for the UAE as Britain seeks to deepen financial and investment ties with the Emirates and the wider Gulf.

Darine Obeid will take up the Abu Dhabi-based position on August 31, operating from the British Embassy.

Obeid has spent more than a decade at the FCA, working across retail and wholesale banking and fintech. Her experience includes financial crime, operational resilience, artificial intelligence and customer outcomes.

“The UAE has firmly established itself as a dynamic and strategically important market, offering significant opportunities in fintech, sustainable finance and financial crime,” Obeid said.

“I’m looking forward to working closely with counterparts across the Gulf to deepen engagement on investment and innovation.”

Expanding ties

Her appointment comes as economic ties between Britain and the UAE continue to expand.

Total trade in goods and services between the two countries reached £25 billion ($33.8 billion) in the 12 months to the end of 2025, according to the latest UK government figures, up 3.7 percent year-on-year.

UK exports to the Emirates accounted for £15.8 billion of that total, making the UAE Britain’s 18th-largest export market. More than 5,000 British companies operate in the Emirates, according to UK government estimates.

The investment relationship has also grown significantly.

In 2021, the UAE committed £10 billion to the UAE-UK Sovereign Investment Partnership, established between Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala and the UK’s Office for Investment. The programme targeted investment in technology, infrastructure, energy transition and life sciences.

From AI to clean energy

The two countries have subsequently expanded cooperation into areas including artificial intelligence, clean energy and financial and professional services.

The FCA appointment also comes months after the UK concluded a landmark free trade agreement with the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council, which includes the UAE.

Agreed in May, the deal made Britain the first G7 country to conclude an FTA with the GCC. The UK government estimates the agreement could increase British GDP by £3.7 billion annually in the long term, although it must still complete ratification procedures before entering into force.

The FCA said its new Gulf presence would support its wider international strategy, including efforts to attract investment into the UK.

“Our new Financial Services Attachés in India and the UAE will advance the UK’s interests on financial services policy and help drive investment into our open market,” said Ruairi O’Connell OBE, the FCA’s director of international.

“Just as the UK is a global financial services centre, the FCA is a globally connected regulator and international leader in financial regulation.”

The FCA is simultaneously expanding its presence in India, appointing Sabina Saini as Financial Services Attaché based at the British Deputy High Commission in Mumbai.

For the UAE, however, the appointment adds another institutional link to an economic relationship increasingly focused not simply on bilateral trade, but on investment, fintech, AI and the future of financial services.

excerpt.rendered: Darine Obeid will be based at the British Embassy in Abu Dhabi as regulator targets greater cooperation on fintech, sustainable finance and investment

title.rendered: Trump cuts South Korea drills after declaring ‘very good relationship’ with Kim Jong Un

content.rendered:
US President Donald Trump has ordered a “substantial” reduction in joint military exercises with South Korea, due to his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Seoul’s refusal to join US action against Iran.

The decision came hours before the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises were due to begin on Monday, August 17, with the drills set to run until August 27.

“Based on the fact that it is too late to cancel, I have instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises!” Trump said.

The US President based the move in part on his “very good relationship with Kim Jong Un”, describing the exercises are “not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile,” Trump said.

Alongside his relationship with Kim, Trump pointed towards South Korea’s refusal to join US action against Iran as another factor behind the decision, “I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, ‘No thanks!'” he said.

South Korea’s defence ministry has maintained that the exercises will proceed as scheduled, despite Trump’s order to reduce US participation.

North Korea gains experience in Ukraine

Ulchi Freedom Shield was expected to include around 18,000 South Korean troops alongside US forces and personnel from 11 of the 18 member states of the United Nations Command. Some 28,500 American military personnel are stationed in South Korea.

The reduction comes as North Korea’s military capabilities continue to develop, driven in part by direct battlefield experience gained through its involvement in Russia’s war in Ukraine. US and South Korean military officials had planned for this year’s exercises to reflect changing threats including drones, GPS disruption and cyberattacks.

More than 14,000 North Korean troops have fought alongside Russian forces in the Kursk region, whilst Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that a further 30,000 could be deployed.

“They’ve taken those lessons they learned there and brought them back to North Korea, that changes the DPRK capability,” US military spokesman Col Ryan Donald said.

North Korea has meanwhile continued its own military activity, carrying out ballistic missile tests in the days leading up to the exercises and describing the drills as “a rehearsal for an aggressive war”.

Military readiness

Trump’s reduction has raised concerns over military readiness at a time when North Korea is gaining battlefield experience and strengthening its military relationship with Russia.

Leif-Eric Easley, professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, warned that scaling back the exercises could damage alliance coordination, slow South Korea’s move towards taking greater responsibility for its defence and weaken deterrence against potential conflict in Asia.

“The cost savings from downsizing drills are marginal, whilst the diplomatic benefits for relations with North Korea are doubtful,” Easley said.

Trump previously took a similar approach following his 2018 summit with Kim, suspending major US-South Korean exercises as Washington pursued denuclearisation negotiations with Pyongyang.

Those negotiations collapsed in 2019, with North Korea since expanding its nuclear and missile programmes whilst deepening military ties with Russia.

excerpt.rendered: The US President ordered the exercises scaled back hours before they began, calling them costly and an unnecessarily ‘hostile’ signal to Pyongyang

title.rendered: Dubai property market rebounds as sales rise and investors return

content.rendered:
Dubai’s residential property market saw sale transactions rise, a pause in price reductions and the return of buyers, according to the latest data from Property Finder and Mortgage Finder.

Activity was largely concentrated within the secondary segment as well as apartments. Investors have seemingly returned through the mid-market, seeking value in homes before pricing stabilises higher.

Speaking on the matter was Cherif Sleiman, Chief Revenue Officer at Property Finder, who summarised July’s market behaviour as “a market that has moved back into growth, with transaction volumes and values rising together and buyers returning with real intent […] we expect that momentum to carry through the second half of the year.”

Dubai property sales rise in July

Looking at the numbers, sale transaction volumes rose from 8,887 in June to 9,217 in July, a climb of 3.8 per cent. Transaction value climbed 5.2 per cent from AED 33.2 billion to AED 34.9 billion.

This increase came near entirely from the secondary market, which saw volumes grow roughly 18 per cent from 4,100 to 4,800. This figure suggests an appetite for ready stock. Commercial activity volume grew a substantial 24.8 per cent to 397 deals, achieving a value of AED 5.8 billion.

As buyer sentiment continues to normalise, so does the demand among home seekers, those planning to buy within six months grew from 66 to 68 per cent.

Those expecting further price declines fell from 56 to 52 per cent, a correction from the previous peak of 73 per cent at the start of the conflict. Those expecting prices to remain flat or rise rose from 44 to 48 per cent.

Moving with demand, Property Finder’s sale-listing price index settled at 2.5 per cent of the pre-conflict baseline for the second consecutive month.

Advertised and final transacted prices began to narrow between 5.5 and 11 per cent in July. A sign of convergence when compared with 6 and 12 per cent seen in May.

Apartment activity

Apartments gained ground over villas and townhouses, growing from 59.5 to 62 per cent of sales. Studios and one-bedroom units drove this. Property Finder suggests this illustrates a sign of stronger investor appetite for higher-yield, more liquid stock.

Mortgage Finder data demonstrates a similar return of investor confidence, as mortgage transactions rose from 9 per cent in June to 12.8 per cent in July. These mortgages were largely of the middle-income bands.

Applicants earning between AED 20,000 and AED 59,999 a month made up 62.4 per cent of the share. Higher earners, above AED 60,000, observed a tighter villa and townhouse pipeline, which has likely limited conversion.

According to Dubai Land Department data, of 2,887 mortgages registered in July, apartments accounted for 81.9 per cent of volume despite only 20.3 per cent of all apartment sales involving a mortgages at all. This shows how differently the segments behave and interact with the financial market. Apartments are largely transacting in cash, whilst villas tend to require financing with an owner-occupied mindset.

On a final note, rental activity too grew. New leasing transactions rose 2 per cent when compared with the pre-conflict baseline, supported by tenants using softer rents to move into larger homes.

excerpt.rendered: New data points to improving sentiment across Dubai, with investors targeting apartments and ready homes as expectations of price declines ease

title.rendered: Abu Dhabi wealth fund targets full control of $8.66bn Abu Dhabi Ports

content.rendered:
Abu Dhabi sovereign investor L’IMAD has proposed acquiring all remaining shares in AD Ports Group through wholly owned subsidiary ADQ. The cash offer values the port and logistics operator at about $8.66 billion (AED31.81 billion).

L’IMAD intends to offer shareholders $1.70 (AED6.25) per share. ADQ already controls 75.42 per cent of AD Ports Group, leaving about 24.6 per cent held by other investors.

Offer prices AD Ports at $8.66 billion

AD Ports Group has 5.09 billion ordinary shares outstanding. Applying L’IMAD’s proposed price values the company’s equity at approximately $8.66 billion (AED31.81 billion).

L’IMAD submitted notification of its intention on August 17 2026. ADQ will conduct the voluntary conditional cash offer for shares it does not already own.

AD Ports Group will present the proposal to its Board of Directors. Required procedures will follow UAE Capital Market Authority rules covering acquisitions and mergers of public joint stock companies. AD Ports Group confirmed it will disclose further material developments as the process advances.

Full ownership would place the ports operator entirely within L’IMAD’s investment structure through ADQ. L’IMAD describes itself as a sovereign investment platform of the Government of Abu Dhabi.

Minority investors receive 23 per cent premium

Abu Dhabi’s L’IMAD’s $1.70 (AED6.25) offer represents a 23 per cent premium to AD Ports Group’s August 14 closing price of about $1.39 (AED5.10).

Offer pricing also sits 25 per cent above the one-month volume-weighted average price of about $1.37 (AED5.02). L’IMAD calculated a 31 per cent premium against the three-month volume-weighted average price of about $1.30 (AED4.76).

ADQ’s 75.42 per cent holding already gives the Abu Dhabi investment company controlling ownership. AD Ports Group records approximately 1.25 billion shares, equal to 24.6 per cent, as free float.

Proposed consideration gives minority shareholders a cash exit above recent market pricing. Completion remains subject to the conditions and regulatory procedures attached to the offer.

Q2 earnings strengthen financial position

Abu Dhabi Ports Group reported record second quarter results three days before L’IMAD announced its offer.

Revenue increased 47 per cent year on year to $1.93 billion (AED7.08 billion) during Q2 2026. EBITDA climbed 49 per cent to $474 million (AED1.74 billion), producing a 24.5 per cent EBITDA margin. Total net profit rose 88 per cent to about $228 million (AED836 million).

Maritime and Shipping generated 53 per cent of quarterly group revenue. Cluster revenue increased 62 per cent year on year to about $1.04 billion (AED3.82 billion). EBITDA reached about $280 million (AED1.03 billion), up 79 per cent.

Economic Cities and Free Zones recorded revenue of about $351 million (AED1.29 billion). A warehouse transaction contributed $177 million (AED650 million) to group revenue and about $80 million (AED294 million) to EBITDA.

AD Ports continues capital deployment

Abu Dhabi Ports Group ended June with net debt of about $6.19 billion (AED22.73 billion). Net debt to EBITDA declined to 3.7 times from 3.9 times during Q1 2026.

Quarterly operating cash flow reached about $583 million (AED2.14 billion), an 88 per cent year-on-year increase. Organic capital expenditure totalled about $395 million (AED1.45 billion).

Abu Dhabi Ports Group also invested $300 million (AED1.1 billion) during June to acquire another 30 per cent of Global Feeder Shipping. Ownership in the container feeder operator rose to 81 per cent.

L’IMAD’s proposed acquisition would consolidate ownership of an operator spanning ports, maritime shipping, logistics and industrial infrastructure. AD Ports Group remains listed on the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange while the offer proceeds through corporate and regulatory review.

title.rendered: From Dubai to Istanbul by rail? The 120-year-old route making a comeback

content.rendered:
Completed in stages between 1900 and 1908, the Hejaz Railway Line (HRL) created a direct rail connection between Damascus and Madinah.

Upon its completion, Hajj journeys that had previously taken around 40 days by camel could now be completed in five. For the Ottoman Empire the line offered not only faster pilgrimage but a peninsula spanning vein serving commerce, administration and military movement across its Arabian territories.

Over a hundred years on, the HRL has returned to focus to address ever growing maritime insecurity. Türkiye, Syria and Saudi Arabia are examining rail connectivity along the former route, while the UAE and Oman have emerged in discussions around possible extensions into the GCC Railway project.

Several transport agreements have been concluded over the past year concerning this, including a railway cooperation agreement between Saudi Arabia and Türkiye. No construction programme has yet emerged, but the agreement establishes significant political willingness.

What is the Hejaz Railway

Ottoman Sultan Abdulhamid II commissioned the Hejaz Railway project in 1900 under the guise of pilgrimage. Its value however, stretched further, giving the Ottoman administration a faster means of transporting soldiers, government officials and supplies into Arabia, reducing the time and difficulty involved in reaching territories far from the imperial heartland.

Financing the project was itself unusual for a major infrastructure undertaking of the period. Instead of depending on traditional European capital, the railway drew contributions from Muslim communities across Ottoman territories and beyond. Donations arrived from locations including India, Egypt and Southeast Asia, tying the project to Abdulhamid II’s efforts to cultivate Islamic solidarity.

Madinah was reached in 1908. By then, approximately 1,300 kilometres of track connected the city with Damascus, while a separate branch provided access to the Mediterranean through Haifa. The intended continuation south to Makkah was never completed.

Its importance naturally made the railway a wartime target. During the Arab Revolt, forces led by Sharif Hussein and his sons repeatedly attacked the line with support from British officers, including T.E. Lawrence, better known as Lawrence of Arabia.

The Ottoman Empire’s subsequent collapse fragmented the railway across the newly established states of the region. Sections remained in use around Damascus and in Jordan, while the southern portion in Saudi Arabia gradually ceased operating.

Physical traces of that network remain. Historic stations and railway infrastructure survive in Madinah, Tabuk and AlUla, alongside preserved locomotives from the original line.

Modern attention

“Three years running, from the Red Sea crisis to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, have taught the region something it had not previously priced: that the cost of not being able to move is far higher than the cost of moving expensively,” Dr Lijo John, Assistant Professor, Logistics and Supply Chain Management at Heriot-Watt University Dubai, says.

A second motivation is peace in Syria. Years of civil war left cross-border railway with little prospect of implementation. The country’s political transition and renewed attention to domestic transport infrastructure have changed that thus presenting an “opportunity to transform post-war Syria into a transit corridor connecting Türkiye to Jordan, Saudi Arabia, and the Gulf markets”, in the words of Yeghia Tashjian, Regional and International Affairs Cluster Coordinator at IFI.

Diplomatically, Türkiye, Syria and Jordan agreed in April to deepen transport cooperation and examine cross-border railway connections. Saudi Arabia and Türkiye followed two months later with an MoU establishing a framework for railway cooperation. Türkiye’s willingness can be explained by “Ankara’s ambition to establish a north-south trade axis linking Europe to the Gulf,” Tashjian says.

Following talks with his Saudi counterparts, Türkiye’s Transport and Infrastructure Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu estimated that reconstruction of the railway connection between Türkiye and Aleppo would require around $100 million. Uraloğlu has also suggested that a railway linking Türkiye and Saudi Arabia through Syria and Jordan could be developed over the next three or four years.

Parts of the necessary infrastructure already approach either end of the proposed corridor. Saudi Arabia’s railway system today reaches the Jordanian border, while Türkiye has rail connections at Islahiye, Kilis and Gaziantep near the Syrian frontier.

The tracks do not necessarily end in Saudi Arabia. Uraloğlu has raised the prospect of connecting the modernised Hejaz route with the GCC Railway and extending connectivity towards the UAE, Oman and Yemen, providing another land alternative alongside to the areas contested waterways.

The economics of a modern corridor

A rebuilt railway would share the geography of its Ottoman predecessor, but little else about its commercial purpose. Pilgrimage and imperial administration drove the original project. A modern network would instead have to justify itself through freight, tourism, reliability and connectivity between Arabia and Europe.

“Railways operate best under three conditions: high payload, predictable, recurring demand, and inland origin-destination pairs. Distance also plays a decisive role in making railways an attractive option. Under 500 kilometres, trucks win. Above 3,000, shipping wins. The corridor’s commercial sweet spot lies between,” John explains.

Potential cargo markets would include Turkish machinery, automotive components and white goods moving towards Gulf markets, while minerals and petrochemicals, including Jordanian phosphate and potash and Saudi polymers, could travel north towards Europe. Construction materials and agrifood would provide further sources of demand.

Even then, rail can not contest the volumes carried by sea. “Even in a crisis scenario, this corridor might absorb a tenth of diverted volume, amounting to 15 to 25 million tonnes annually at full operation,” John says whilst adding that “Under normal conditions, the displacement comes from road haulage and Ro-Ro feeders, not deep-sea shipping,”

Where the UAE enters

The UAE is not party to the current agreements between Türkiye, Syria, Jordan and Saudi Arabia. Its connection instead rests on another infrastructure programme, the GCC Railway. Linking the two systems would effectively extend the north-south corridor deeper into the Gulf, connecting UAE rail infrastructure with Saudi Arabia before continuing north through Jordan and Syria towards Türkiye.

John notes that “The UAE connection is credible but indirect. It is not an extension of the HRL, but rather the GCC Railway, which is roughly half-complete, targeted for 2030, running through the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait into Saudi Arabia and Jordan, meeting the HRL alignment there,”

“Two projects converging into one network, making a Jebel Ali–Istanbul movement conceivable,” John adds, referring to the UAE’s expanding Etihad Rail network.

A southern extension towards Yemen would reach the Arabian Sea and thus provide access to shipping without requiring cargo to pass through Bab-el-Mandeb or the Suez Canal. John describes that “without Yemen, the axis is incomplete. Only a southern terminus on the Arabian Sea allows cargo to bypass Bab-el-Mandeb and Suez entirely. Reaching the UAE makes the corridor useful. Reaching Yemen is what would make it decisive,”

“In this sense, the railway is not merely a transport project but part of a larger Turkish strategy to position itself as the indispensable connector between Europe, the Levant, and the Persian Gulf,” Tashjian observes. Freight moving between the Gulf and Türkiye would cross multiple national borders, placing customs procedures, transit agreements and border processing alongside track construction as a central issue.

More than a reconstruction

The Hejaz Railway is remembered as one of the Ottoman Empire’s greatest engineering achievements. Its modern revival could grow to become an economic workhorse.

The Saudis are particularly interested considering Vision 2030, the Kingdom’s goal of becoming a global logistics base linking Asia, Europe and Africa, a modern Silk Road if you will. Türkiye too has a similar objective in mind.

For Syria, this would mean what Tashjian describes as “reclaiming its historical role as a land bridge”, while contributing to the country’s post-war reconstruction.

The Gulf states will benefit from diversified energy pipelines in an era where shipping lanes can be treacherous.

Together, those ambitions have given new life to a railway many assumed long buried.

excerpt.rendered: Over a century after the Hejaz Railway reached the end of the line, it may be back on track

title.rendered: LEAP 5 returns to Riyadh as Saudi Arabia cements its role at the centre of the global technology ecosystem

content.rendered:
As the global technology sector searches for its next frontier of growth, investment and collaboration, LEAP will return to Riyadh for its fifth edition from 31 August–3 September 2026, reinforcing the Kingdom’s ambition to position itself at the heart of the global innovation economy.

Co-organised by Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, the Saudi Federation for Cybersecurity, Programming and Drones (SAFCSP) and Tahaluf, LEAP has evolved into what organisers describe as the world’s most attended technology event. Since its launch in 2022, it has attracted more than 688,000 attendees, 2,480 startups, 6,200 companies and over 5,000 investors across four editions.

Now entering its fifth year, the event reflects Saudi Arabia’s expanding influence within the global digital economy under Vision 2030, with Riyadh increasingly positioned as a convening ground for policymakers, founders, investors and multinational technology leaders.

Global technology leaders head to Riyadh

This year’s edition is set to bring together senior executives and innovators from companies including Google, Amazon Web Services, AMD, Qualcomm, Cisco and Huawei, alongside Saudi champions such as Saudi Telecom Company (stc) and Saudi Aramco.

The speaker line-up includes Matt Garman, CEO of AWS; Justin Hotard, President and CEO of Nokia; and Tareq Amin, CEO of HUMAIN, highlighting themes spanning cloud infrastructure, connectivity and applied artificial intelligence. Frontier technology leaders from AI, data and advanced computing are also expected to address the event, underscoring LEAP’s positioning as a platform where strategy meets execution.

Beyond attendance figures, LEAP’s organisers argue that the event’s growing impact lies in its dealmaking power. At the 2025 edition alone, $14.9bn in deals and announcements were recorded, contributing to an estimated $820m in economic impact.

As it marks its fifth anniversary, LEAP is increasingly framed as a global launchpad for partnerships and cross-border investment, rather than simply a showcase of emerging technologies.

“Over the past four years, LEAP has evolved at a rocket-fuelled pace, playing a critical role in nurturing talent, creativity and investment,” said Faisal Alkhamisi, Chairman of the Saudi Federation for Cybersecurity, Programming and Drones. “Yet, this is just the beginning. LEAP will continue to reflect the ever-changing tech landscape and inspire pioneers from across the globe.”

Expanding platforms and sector focus

LEAP 5 will feature more than twenty stages covering sectors including climate tech, health tech, fintech, space tech and smart cities, reflecting the breadth of digital transformation underway across industries.

DeepFest will return as the region’s dedicated platform for AI and deep technology, convening global leaders to explore applied artificial intelligence and next-generation systems. An expanded Tech Arena will host live demonstrations and practical AI use cases, signalling a shift towards implementation and real-world adoption.

New zones will also spotlight the convergence of technology with creative industries and sport. GameX Creative, backed by players such as Savvy Games Group and ESL FACEIT Group, will focus on gaming, esports and digital storytelling.

Meanwhile, the Sports Tech Hub will convene organisations including Juventus FC and Tottenham Hotspur FC to examine how AI, data and immersive technologies are transforming athlete performance, fan engagement and commercial models.

A new initiative, LEAP Connect, has been introduced as a curated matchmaking platform designed to accelerate partnerships between founders, investors and policymakers, with the aim of converting on-stage dialogue into tangible commercial outcomes.

Capital at scale

Central to LEAP’s positioning is its Investor and Startup Programme, anchored by a $1m Rocket Fuel Pitch Competition. With participation from domestic and international investors, the programme spans 60 technology verticals and seeks to reinforce Riyadh’s status as a global capital hub for innovation.

Mike Champion, CEO of Tahaluf, said: “LEAP has become a place where the future is not just discussed but built. The momentum in Saudi Arabia is extraordinary, and as LEAP enters its fifth edition, it will take this ambition into new worlds, unlocking investment and shaping the technologies that will define the next decade.”

With more than 201,000 visitors, 600+ startups, 1,000+ speakers, 1,800+ global technology brands and 1,900+ investors expected, LEAP 5 signals not only the scale of Saudi Arabia’s digital ambitions, but its determination to convene the global technology ecosystem in Riyadh as it shapes the next phase of the intelligent age.

excerpt.rendered: LEAP 5 returns to Riyadh, convening global technology leaders, investors and innovators to shape the next era of digital transformation
