title.rendered: Dubai Airport Express Line draws bids from six groups

content.rendered:
Dubai has received proposals from six consultant groups for the planned 55km Airport Express Line.

Road and Transport Authority(RTA) is seeking study and design services for a rail corridor linking Dubai International Airport with Al Maktoum International Airport. Proposals were reported on August 13 2026 after consultants received the tender earlier this year.

Planned infrastructure includes five stations across the route. Passenger facilities include remote airline check-in, baggage drop-off and security screening.

Six groups compete for design contract

AECOM has partnered with Singapore’s Surbana Jurong for the consultancy competition. Parsons has submitted a joint proposal with Arup.

France’s Systra is bidding with Egis. AtkinsRéalis, Jacobs and WSP have submitted separate proposals for the contract.

RTA initially gave consultants until June to submit proposals for the study and design package. Industry reports have not disclosed a preferred consultant or contract value.

Airport Express Line plans place the eastern terminus at the existing Red Line station serving DXB in Al Garhoud.

Trains would run through Al Jaddaf before following the Al Khail Road corridor towards Jumeirah Village Circle. A new JVC station forms a central interchange within the proposed alignment. Services would continue south towards DWC in Jebel Ali.

Branch lines extend airport rail coverage

MEED reported that RTA’s proposed alignment also includes two branch connections from the main airport corridor.

One branch runs from the planned JVC station towards Al Fardan Exchange station at Emirates Golf Club. Another branch serves Business Bay through a separate new station.

Passenger processing facilities give the project a broader operating scope than a conventional urban metro connection. Remote check-in would allow eligible travellers to complete airline processing before reaching airport terminals.

Baggage drop facilities would transfer part of the passenger handling process into the rail network. Security screening facilities also form part of the proposed station specification.

RTA has not announced a construction programme or operational launch date for the Airport Express Line. Current procurement activity covers the study and design stage.

Dubai expands rail infrastructure pipeline

Airport Express Line procurement sits alongside major investment across Dubai’s metro network.

Dubai Metro Blue Line construction is progressing across a 30km alignment with 14 stations. RTA launched primary tunnelling works in May 2026. Scheduled opening remains September 9 2029.

RTA also approved the Dubai Metro Gold Line in April 2026 with investment of about $9.26bn (AED34bn). Plans cover 15 locations between Al Ghubaiba and Jumeirah Golf Estates, including Business Bay and JVC.

Gold Line construction is scheduled to follow contract award in 2027. RTA has set September 9 2032 for inauguration.

Dubai Metro carried 295 million passengers during 2025, recording seven per cent annual growth. RTA expects network demand to exceed 300 million passengers during 2026.

Airport capacity raises transport requirements

Dubai Airports handled a record 95.2 million passengers at DXB during 2025. Operator forecasts put 2026 traffic at about 99.5 million passengers.

Al Maktoum International Airport forms the centre of Dubai’s long-term aviation capacity programme.

Dubai Airports confirms investment of $35bn (AED128.5bn) in DWC expansion. Planned capacity reaches 150 million passengers annually within the next decade and 260 million at full development. Cargo capacity is planned at 12 million tonnes annually.

Airport Express Line design work would connect that aviation capacity with DXB, established metro infrastructure and major residential and commercial districts across Dubai.

title.rendered: UAE drivers can have four black points removed under new rule

content.rendered:
UAE motorists can have four black points removed from their traffic records by joining a nationwide road safety campaign on August 31 2026. Registration for Accident Free Day opens on August 17 through the Ministry of Interior.

Motorists must complete an online pledge and comply with traffic rules throughout August 31. Authorities scheduled the campaign for the first day of the new academic year, when school traffic raises vehicle volumes across UAE roads.

Registration opens on August 17

Ministry of Interior registration requires motorists to access its online platform and identify themselves using their Emirates ID. Drivers then sign a pledge covering specific road safety requirements before participating.

Participants must respect speed limits, maintain sufficient following distance and use seatbelts. Mobile phone use while driving breaches the pledge conditions. Drivers also need to exercise caution during lane changes and overtaking.

Emergency vehicles and pedestrians receive priority under the commitment. Motorists must yield to ambulances, police vehicles and other authorised emergency traffic when required. Pedestrian crossing priority also forms part of the campaign requirements.

Ministry systems handle registration electronically, allowing participation without a physical visit to a traffic department. Eligible motorists who complete the campaign requirements receive the black point reduction automatically.

Four black points removed on September 25

Ministry of Interior will deduct four black points from successful participants on September 25 2026. Drivers do not need to submit a separate application after completing Accident Free Day requirements.

UAE traffic regulations retain black points on a motorist’s record for one year. Accumulating 24 points can result in licence suspension, with suspension periods ranging from three to six months according to the driver’s record.

Accident Free Day therefore gives motorists carrying existing points a defined route to reduce their balance through verified driving behaviour.

Ministry of Interior authorities used the same four-point incentive during the 2025 campaign. Participants who complied on August 25 2025 subsequently received SMS notifications confirming that four black points had been removed from their records.

Authorities linked that 2025 campaign with the opening of the academic year and the wider Safe School Year traffic programme.

School traffic drives August 31 campaign

August 31 coincides with the start of the 2026 academic year for most UAE schools. Authorities expect heavier flows around schools as parents, buses and staff return to regular morning transport schedules.

Brig Juma bin Suwaidan, Head of Dubai Traffic Police, urged motorists to adjust driving behaviour around education zones.

“Drivers should follow speed limits around the schools, not be distracted and give priority to pedestrians,” he said.

Dubai Police expects concentrated traffic flows near schools at the beginning of term. Speed compliance, pedestrian priority and reduced driver distraction form central requirements during that period.

Campaign conditions also target following distance and overtaking behaviour, two operational factors affecting traffic flow when road utilisation rises during school drop-off periods.

Accident Free Day continues national road safety drive

Accident Free Day operates across the UAE through coordination between the Ministry of Interior, Federal Traffic Council and local police authorities. The 2025 campaign used the same nationwide structure to align enforcement and driver participation across individual emirates.

Ministry authorities position the one-day campaign as a behavioural intervention tied to everyday traffic rules rather than a temporary exemption from penalties. Drivers receive the four-point reduction after fulfilling the pledge requirements during the designated period.

Brig Juma indicated that longer-term driving behaviour remains the principal measure of campaign performance. Authorities want motorists to retain the same speed discipline, following distances, pedestrian awareness and mobile phone restrictions beyond August 31.

Registration opens on August 17, giving motorists two weeks to complete the pledge before Accident Free Day on August 31. Successful participants will see four black points removed electronically on September 25.

title.rendered: AD Ports posts record profits despite Hormuz remaining shut

content.rendered:
Abu Dhabi Ports Group rerouted cargo through UAE east coast terminals and expanded multimodal capacity during Q2 2026. Measures reduced exposure to wider regional maritime disruption and kept regional supply chains operating.

Abu Dhabi-based AD Ports reported total net profit of $227.6 million (AED836 million), up 88 per cent year on year. Revenue increased 47 per cent to $1.93 billion (AED7.08 billion). EBITDA advanced 49 per cent to about $474 million (AED1.74 billion), producing a 24.5 per cent margin.

East coast routes absorb rerouted cargo

AD Ports shifted cargo operations and feeder services to Fujairah Terminals and Khor Fakkan Port on the Gulf of Oman. Operations used 27 container vessels and five bulk vessels across alternative shipping corridors during the quarter. Services connected UAE cargo with India, Pakistan, Oman, Red Sea ports and Upper Arabian Gulf markets.

Land corridors linked Fujairah and Khor Fakkan with Khalifa Port, Jebel Ali Port and Sharjah through bonded customs transit. AD Ports added 400 trucks during Q2 and increased rail service frequency with Etihad Rail.

Six chartered aircraft carried critical commodities including food and pharmaceuticals. Warehousing and storage capacity exceeded 54,000 square metres, with further capacity scheduled during 2026.

AD Ports had already activated cargo rerouting during Q1. Earlier operations used land, rail and air capacity alongside regional feeder shipping to maintain cargo flows across the UAE.

Shipping rates offset lower feeder volumes

Container feeder volumes reached 740,000 TEUs during Q2, down 11 per cent from a year earlier. Higher freight rates offset the volume contraction.

Gulf and Indian Subcontinent services accounted for 30 per cent of quarterly feeder volumes. Average rates across those services increased 96 per cent year on year and 103 per cent from Q1.

Red Sea services represented 24 per cent of feeder volumes. Average rates increased 37 per cent from Q2 2025 and 56 per cent sequentially. AD Ports doubled its bulk, multipurpose and RoRo vessel fleet to 72 vessels from 36 a year earlier.

Maritime and Shipping generated $1.04 billion (AED3.82 billion) in revenue, up 62 per cent. Cluster EBITDA increased 79 per cent to about $280 million (AED1.03 billion). Maritime and Shipping supplied 53 per cent of group revenue during Q2.

UAE logistics capacity limits disruption

UAE container throughput reached 573,000 TEUs during Q2 as regional maritime disruption constrained conventional cargo flows. Bulk and general cargo volumes totalled 3.1 million tonnes. AD Ports channelled traffic through east coast facilities and international terminals to maintain cargo connectivity.

International container capacity utilisation reached 61 per cent, compared with 22 per cent across UAE container capacity during the quarter. Ports revenue reached about $166 million (AED609 million), while EBITDA totalled almost $64 million (AED234 million).

Logistics recorded stronger earnings as alternative transport capacity absorbed redirected cargo. Cluster revenue rose 30 per cent to about $400 million (AED1.47 billion). EBITDA increased 154 per cent to approximately $25.6 million (AED94 million), despite a 23 per cent decline in quarterly UAE polymer volumes.

Asset sales and shipping investment support earnings

Economic Cities and Free Zones contributed further earnings growth. KEZAD completed a warehouse sale worth about $177 million (AED650 million) during Q2.

Cluster revenue reached roughly $351 million (AED1.29 billion), up 132 per cent from a year earlier. Revenue increased 15 per cent excluding the warehouse transaction.

AD Ports also completed a $300 million (AED1.1 billion) purchase of an additional 30 per cent stake in Global Feeder Shipping on June 23 2026.

Group ownership increased to 81 per cent. Net leverage declined to 3.7 times from 3.9 times in Q1, while net debt reached $6.19 billion (AED22.73 billion).

Free Cash Flow to the Firm reached negative $280 million (AED1.03 billion) after the GFS investment. Excluding that transaction, AD Ports generated positive quarterly free cash flow of about $19.9 million (AED73 million).

title.rendered: Saudi Arabia’s AI push comes with a $42 billion price tag

content.rendered:
Saudi Arabia’s planned AI and cloud infrastructure expansion requires up to $42bn (AED154.2bn) in project capital by 2030. Alvarez and Marsal estimates the requirement applies if developers energise about half of publicly announced data centre capacity.

Saudi operators would deliver between 2.5GW and 3GW under that scenario. Debt financing would range from $14bn (AED51.4bn) to $32bn (AED117.5bn).

Saudi banks can finance significant capacity, while larger delivery volumes require broader lender syndication and institutional capital participation.

Saudi data centre capacity heads towards 1GW

Alvarez and Marsal estimates Saudi Arabia operates about 410MW of data centre IT load. Base case capacity reaches approximately 1GW by 2030.

That expansion requires roughly 620MW of additional capacity. Project capital ranges between $7bn (AED25.7bn) and $9bn (AED33.1bn).

Debt requirements under 50 to 75 per cent gearing range from $3.5bn (AED12.9bn) to $7bn (AED25.7bn). Alvarez and Marsal calculates that requirement at less than one per cent of Saudi banks’ private sector loan book.

S&P Global recorded 222MW of Saudi IT power capacity during the first quarter of 2025. Its December 2025 assessment projected 29 per cent annual capacity growth through 2030. Planned additions totalled about 760MW at that point.

Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah account for the principal data centre clusters as hyperscale, cloud and AI infrastructure deployment accelerates.

Bigger pipeline changes financing requirements

Saudi Arabia’s announced pipeline substantially exceeds the 1GW base case used in the financing analysis.

Delivery of 2.5GW to 3GW by 2030 raises estimated capital expenditure to between $28bn (AED102.8bn) and $42bn (AED154.2bn). Required debt rises to between $14bn (AED51.4bn) and $32bn (AED117.5bn).

Alvarez and Marsal identifies contracted offtake as a central condition for project financing. Lenders assess contracted cash flow, lease rates, power costs, utilisation and ramp-up periods before allocating debt.

Developers also need fixed-price construction contracts, defined grid connection schedules and phased mechanical and electrical deployment. Those structures transfer delivery risk and align capital drawdowns with energised megawatts.

Saudi sponsors can access bank lending, sukuk and private credit channels. Larger projects require capital structures covering construction, stabilisation and refinancing periods rather than initial development costs alone.

Humain expands Saudi AI infrastructure pipeline

Humain has emerged as a major capacity developer since its establishment by the Public Investment Fund in 2025.

Saudi Arabia’s National Infrastructure Fund agreed financing terms worth up to $1.2bn (AED4.4bn) with Humain in January 2026. Proposed financing covers up to 250MW of AI data centre capacity.

Humain is targeting around 6GW of capacity by 2034 and has agreements involving xAI and Blackstone-backed AirTrunk. National Infrastructure Fund and Humain are also examining an investment platform designed to attract local and international institutional capital.

Humain selected Goldman Sachs in May 2026 to advise on financing for data centres and GPU infrastructure supporting 2GW of capacity. Financing requirements were estimated at at least $5.33bn (AED19.6bn), with planned facilities located around Riyadh.

Hyperscalers add demand for Saudi capacity

Global cloud providers are adding substantial committed infrastructure demand across Saudi Arabia.

AWS announced a Saudi cloud region scheduled for 2026. Microsoft has developed three data centres supporting availability zones in the Eastern Province. Oracle operates cloud regions in Jeddah and Riyadh.

Humain’s partnerships add another layer of compute demand. Nvidia has committed technology supporting an announced 500MW of capacity, including 18,000 Blackwell processors. S&P Global records a related investment plan at $10bn (AED36.7bn).

AWS and Humain also announced a partnership valued at $5bn (AED18.4bn), according to S&P Global.

Saudi developers consequently face a financing requirement tied directly to energised capacity, contracted customers and grid connection schedules. Alvarez and Marsal calculates the 1GW base case remains within existing banking capacity. Delivery approaching 3GW expands the funding requirement into institutional debt, sukuk and private credit markets.

title.rendered: Contractor awarded Sphere Abu Dhabi project sees net profits soar to $58.2m

content.rendered:
ALEC Holdings, the UAE contractor that successfully tendered and won the deal for The Sphere Abu Dhabi has saw revenues and profits soar in the first-half of 2026.

It released its H1 results for 2026, and they made for good reading.

Year-on-year revenue growth is up by a staggering 67.7 per cent to $2.4 billion (AED 8.99 billion).

Earlier this year, ALEC Holdings was announced as the main contractor for the coveted Sphere Abu Dhabi project, valued at a cool $1.7 billion.

ALEC was also awarded a number of project’s on ADNOC’s Das Island.

In addition to the above, other key highlights from their results include $58.2 million (AED 213.8 million) in net profit.

Its balance sheet also remained very strong, despite the economic headwinds as a result of the US-Iran war.

ALEC Holdings had $272m (AED 1 billion) in net cash and $148m (AED 544.8 million) in Free Cash Flow to Firm, up 49.9 per cent year-on-year.

In line with its dividend policy, ALEC has announced an $27m (AED 100 million) interim cash dividend for its H1 results, that us payable in October 2026.

Barry Lewis, CEO of ALEC Holdings, attributed the securement of new megadeals as a factor in their strong financial performance.

“H1 2026 was a period of strong growth for us, with revenue increasing 67.6 per cent year-on-year to reflecting the scale of activity and strength of delivery across our portfolio.

“We also secured significant new work, including our appointment to deliver Sphere Abu Dhabi and three EPC awards on Das Island for our Energy Services subsidiary, TARGET, with a combined value exceeding $490 million.”

At the height of the regional conflict, extended stoppages to offshore work temporarily curtailed activity their Energy Services business, limiting its potential revenue contribution, while the Group continued to carry the cost of idled manpower.

“We actively managed these pressures through disciplined cost control and project and workforce planning, while maintaining execution momentum across the wider portfolio,” said Lewis.

He added that the demand backdrop across the UAE and Saudi Arabia remains constructive, supported by continued investment in large-scale urban development, aviation, energy, hospitality and digital infrastructure.

“Our $8.8 billion (AED 32.5 billion) backlog provides strong visibility over future activity, and we continue to deploy our capacity selectively, prioritising complex, large-scale projects that align with our capabilities and where our integrated platform delivers the greatest value to clients.”

John Deeb, CFO at ALEC Holdings, echoed the sentiments expressed by Lewis.

“Our net profit reached $52.8 million in H1, which demonstrates the scale and resilience of our business model.

“Our Q2 profitability impacted by operational disruptions in Energy Services related to regional geopolitical developments and the associated absorption of fixed costs, partially mitigated by disciplined cost management,” said Deeb.

title.rendered: UAE firm sees profits surge 693% to $997 million despite disruption of war

content.rendered:
UAE’s ADNOC tankers have come under attack by Iranian forces over the last few days, but its shipping business is expertly navigating the choppy waters of war.

ADNOC Logistics & Services have saw their profits soar in the first-half of 2026.

Despite the outright chaos being caused by the US-Iran war, higher charter rates and growing demand for energy transport have yielded record returns for UAE company.

Incredibly, net profit rose by 693 per cent year-on-year, which amounts to $997 million.

ADNOC is the UAE’s national oil company, but ADNOC Group has a whole host of publicly-listed companies, and ADNOC Logistics and Services is one of them.

Shipping revenue rose by 132 per cent, which will come as a surprise to many due to the issues on both the Strait of Hormuz and in the Red Sea over the last few weeks.

132 per cent in brass tax amounts to $2.45 billion (AED 9 billion).

The revenue from the logistics segment declined by 20 per cent as costs increased, but net profit once again jumped on the balance sheet, rising to $1 billion (AED 3.7 billion) in the first-half of the year.

Abdulkareem Al Masabi, chief executive of ADNOC Logistics & Shipping expressed his delight at the earnings in a statement they issued to the press.

“The improved outlook is supported by our efforts to support ADNOC Group and favourable shipping market fundamentals.”

It has also been disclosed that ADNOC Group board of directors have approved a sizeable interim dividend for the remainder of the year.

An interim dividend of $85.2 million (AED 313 million) will be issued, which is in line with its medium-term payout strategy.

ADNOC’s subsidiary is seeking to expand its fleet and has committed to spending $5.7 billion – and vessel acquisitions and new-build commitments in the year-to-date are valued at $2.3 billion.

In addition to the above, ADNOC Logistics & Services raised its shipping guidance to mid-80 per cent growth, from a previous forecast that was estimated around the mid-to-high teens.

title.rendered: Abu Dhabi Customs warns of fake notices seeking customs fees

content.rendered:
Abu Dhabi Customs has warned customers and companies against fraudulent electronic messages impersonating the authority. The alert, issued on August 12, covers notices using official language to request shipment information, customs classifications or payments.

Fraudulent communications include notices carrying the wording “Official Customs Hold Notice”. Messages reference customs tariff classification requirements under the Harmonised System and present recipients with apparent customs procedures. Abu Dhabi Customs confirms these communications do not originate from the authority.

Fraudulent notices mimic customs processes

Fraudulent messages include reference numbers, dates and times designed to resemble formal customs documentation. Senders also claim that shipments have been placed on hold pending action by the recipient.

Messages seek information linked to customs tariff classification and request payment of fees. Abu Dhabi Customs identifies these elements as attempts to give fraudulent correspondence an official appearance.

Criminal operators can use such communications to obtain personal, commercial or financial information from recipients. Fraudulent payment instructions can also direct businesses towards unauthorised transactions.

Abu Dhabi Customs has asked recipients to verify shipment-related requests before taking any action. Companies handling regular import and export volumes face particular exposure when fraudulent correspondence imitates routine customs documentation.

Reference numbers and shipment terminology alone do not authenticate a customs request. Verification through official channels remains required before companies disclose information or initiate payments.

Abu Dhabi Customs directs users to official channels

Abu Dhabi Customs confirms that official customs procedures and transactions operate through approved systems and authorised digital channels. Customers should use those channels when checking payment demands, shipment instructions or customs requirements.

Authority guidance instructs customers not to respond to suspicious messages. Recipients should also avoid links and attachments contained in unverified correspondence.

Businesses should not provide personal details, company information or banking credentials following requests from untrusted sources. Abu Dhabi Customs also advises customers against making payments based on such messages.

Digital verification gives importers and logistics operators a direct method for checking whether a customs instruction originated from an approved channel. Operators can compare requests against existing shipment records and transactions held within authorised systems.

Abu Dhabi Customs places customer data protection and secure digital transactions among its customs service priorities. The authority continues to maintain official channels for customs processing and customer interaction.

Companies urged to report suspicious messages

Abu Dhabi Customs has instructed customers receiving fraudulent messages to avoid replying or sharing information with the sender. Recipients should report suspicious communications through approved official channels.

Reporting provides the authority with information on active impersonation attempts targeting customs users. Companies can also isolate suspicious correspondence before staff process payment requests or disclose commercial records.

Importers, freight operators and other businesses regularly exchange documentation linked to tariff classifications, shipment status and customs charges. Fraudulent communications imitate those established transaction categories to appear credible.

Internal payment controls can prevent staff from processing requests received outside recognised customs systems. Company procedures can also require independent verification when messages introduce unexpected shipment holds or requests for tariff information.

Abu Dhabi Customs continues awareness activity focused on safe digital practices and protection against fraud and impersonation attempts. Its August 12 warning directs users back towards authenticated customs channels for transaction handling.

Digital safeguards protect customs transactions

Abu Dhabi Customs operates digital channels as the authorised route for customs procedures and transactions. That distinction gives companies a clear authentication point when questionable communications reach procurement, finance or logistics teams.

Businesses can treat unexpected requests for banking information, company credentials or direct payments as verification triggers. Staff responsible for customs clearance can cross-check the underlying shipment through approved systems before releasing information.

Shipment holds also require verification when correspondence arrives outside established transaction channels. Fraudulent senders rely on operational urgency to encourage recipients to respond before checking authenticity.

Abu Dhabi Customs advises customers to avoid engagement with suspicious correspondence entirely. Reporting through approved channels allows the authority to maintain visibility over impersonation attempts while protecting legitimate customs transactions.

title.rendered: Abu Dhabi Finance Week 2026 announces 200 global leaders as speakers

content.rendered:
Abu Dhabi Finance Week (ADFW) has confirmed more than 200 international speakers for its 2026 edition, with senior figures from some of the world’s largest financial institutions, investment groups and technology companies set to attend.

Hosted by ADGM from December 7 to 10, the fifth edition is expected to feature more than 800 speakers across over 70 thematic events. The programme will include leaders from Standard Chartered, Morgan Stanley, State Street, Allianz, Temasek Holdings, Binance and Franklin Templeton alongside senior UAE government and business figures.

ADFW 2026 will take place under the theme “The Capital Community, Powered by Partnerships”.

ADFW said more than 200 international speakers from government, financial services, investment, technology and innovation have already been confirmed.

The four-day programme is ultimately expected to feature more than 800 speakers across more than 70 thematic events.

Abu Dhabi Finance Week 2026

Ahmed Jasim Al Zaabi, Chairman of ADGM, said the early commitment from global financial leaders reflects growing confidence in Abu Dhabi as a destination for capital, investment and long-term partnerships.

“The strength of ADFW lies not only in the conversations that happen here, but in what they lead to. By bringing together the world’s leading investors, policymakers and innovators, Abu Dhabi creates an environment where dialogue translates into investment and relationships become long-term partnerships. That is what distinguishes Abu Dhabi as the Capital of Capital,” he added.

Government representatives announced for the event include Ahmed Jasim Al Zaabi, Chairman of ADGM and the Abu Dhabi Department of Economic Development; Dr Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi, Minister of Foreign Trade; Mohamed Ali Al Shorafa, Chairman of the Department of Municipalities and Transport; and Dr Sultan bin Saif Al Neyadi, Minister of State for Youth Affairs.

Also participating are Shamis Ali Khalfan Al Dhaheri, Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Department of Community Development and Second Vice Chairman and Managing Director, Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce and Industry; Salem AlNuaimi, Managing Director of Abu Dhabi Pension Fund; Majid Al Suwaidi, CEO, ALTÉRRA; Dr Tariq bin Hendi, CEO of Botim; Mohamed Abdelbary, GCEO of Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank; Hamad Al Ameri, CEO of Alpha Dhabi; and Antonoaldo Neves, CEO of Etihad.

Senior executives from major international financial institutions will also take part.

Standard Chartered, Morgan Stanley and Allianz executives confirmed

They include Oliver Bäte, Chairman of the Board of Management and CEO, Allianz SE; Tan Su Shan, CEO, DBS Group; Ron O’Hanley, Chairman and CEO of State Street; Bill Winters, CEO, Standard Chartered; and Clare Woodman CBE, CEO, Intl, Morgan Stanley.

Other confirmed speakers include Stefan Bollinger, CEO, Julius Baer; Dilhan Pillay Sandrasegara, Executive Director and CEO, Temasek Holdings; Andreas Berger, Group CEO, Swiss Re; Charles R. Kaye, Chairman, Warburg Pincus; Hendrik du Toit, Founder and CEO, Ninety One; Tarek Sultan, Chairman, Agility; and Steven Desmyter, President, Man Group.

The asset management, alternatives, infrastructure, commodities and institutional investment programme will feature another group of senior executives.

Confirmed participants include Jenny Johnson, CEO, Franklin Templeton; Katie Koch, President and CEO, TCW; Tobias C. Pross, CEO, Allianz Global Investors; and Marc C. Ganzi, CEO, DigitalBridge.

Dmitry Balyasny, Co-Founder, Managing Partner and Chief Investment Officer, Balyasny Asset Management; Mike Freno, Chairman, President and CEO, Barings; David Druley, CEO, Cambridge Associates; and Stefan Hoops, CEO of DWS are also scheduled to participate.

Global investment leaders head to Abu Dhabi

Digital assets, fintech and technology will form another major component of the programme.

Speakers announced include Chamath Palihapitiya, Founder of Social Capital; Richard Teng, CEO of Binance; JoeBen Bevirt, Founder and CEO, Joby Aviation; Robert Smith, Founder & CEO of Vista Equity; Pascal Gauthier, Chairman and CEO, Ledger; Lily Liu, President, Solana Foundation; and Charles Cascarilla, Co-Founder and CEO, Paxos.

Their participation reflects the event’s coverage of fintech and digital assets alongside traditional global markets and asset management. ADFW 2026 will introduce an expanded programme intended to provide more focused engagement.

New additions include the inaugural Abu Dhabi Real Estate Summit, AIMA Global Hedge Fund Leaders Platform, The Hub71 Startups Campus and A Healthcare and BioTech Forum.

The event will also stage multiple Global Strategy Roundtables and expanded private forums. Across the week, the programme will be organised around four main thematic days.

Topics will cover Abu Dhabi’s economic strategy, global markets, asset management, fintech, digital assets, sustainable finance and Islamic finance.

ADFW 2026 takes place from December 7 to 10 and marks the fifth edition of the event hosted by ADGM.

title.rendered: Saudi Arabia ranks among world’s top 10 for AI investment as tech workforce hits 426,000

content.rendered:
Saudi Arabia ranks among the world’s top 10 countries for private artificial intelligence investment, according to the World Bank Group, as the Kingdom expands data centre capacity, attracts specialist AI talent and builds its technology workforce.

The World Development Report 2026, The Promise of Artificial Intelligence, also highlights Saudi Arabia as a model for government data integration, with a Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA) platform connecting more than 60 government entities. The findings come as Saudi Arabia marks 2026 as the “Year of AI”.

The World Bank Group report assesses the impact of artificial intelligence on developing economies and examines the opportunities it creates for individuals, businesses and governments, alongside the requirements for maximising its development impact and managing associated risks.

The report is structured around three dimensions: Capabilities, Concentration and Complements.

Capabilities considers how AI can broaden access to expertise and support decision-making, while Concentration examines how advanced models, chips and data centres are concentrated among a limited number of countries and companies.

Saudi Arabia AI investment

Complements covers the infrastructure, data, skills and institutions required to maximise the potential of the technology.

Within its examination of Concentration, the report highlights Saudi Arabia’s use of tax incentives and special economic zones to attract investment in data centres and develop compute capacity.

The approach connects capital investment with a wider ecosystem encompassing talent, startups, energy and infrastructure supporting AI applications.

Saudi Arabia’s data centre capacity increased from 68MW in 2021 to 440MW in 2025 before reaching 467MW in the first quarter of 2026.

That represents growth of more than 6 per cent since the beginning of 2026 and an increase of nearly sevenfold compared with 2021.

Saudi data centre capacity rises

The expansion has been accompanied by increased connectivity.

Coverage from 4G and 5G networks reached 99 per cent by the end of 2025, while average internet speed reached 216Mbps.

The infrastructure provides key foundations for expanding cloud services and artificial intelligence applications across the Kingdom.

Saudi Arabia is also attracting specialised international AI talent while expanding its domestic technology workforce.

The World Bank report found that the Kingdom was among the economies recording the highest net inflows of AI professionals per 10,000 LinkedIn members in 2025, alongside Luxembourg, Australia and Switzerland.

Saudi Arabia recorded a net inflow of 3.08 among leading AI authors and innovators in the same year. The Kingdom’s overall technology workforce has meanwhile increased to approximately 426,000. That represents cumulative growth of 186.6 per cent compared with 2018, when the workforce stood at 150,000.

Women now account for 35 per cent of participation in communications and information technology professions.

World Bank highlights Saudi government data model

Under the Complements dimension, the report highlights Saudi Arabia’s approach to government data infrastructure.

A platform operated by SDAIA enables data integration across more than 60 government entities while allowing the data to remain within the respective entities’ systems.

The World Bank presents the experience as a model for structured and secure data exchange across government.

The system enables government entities to develop applications while strengthening governance, trust and data protection.

The findings reinforce the role of SDAIA in developing an integrated data ecosystem as part of Saudi Arabia’s wider approach to data and artificial intelligence.

Digital economy reaches 16% of GDP

The development of Saudi Arabia’s AI ecosystem comes alongside broader growth in its digital economy. The digital economy’s contribution has reached 16 per cent of GDP, according to the supplied information.

Saudi Arabia’s communications and information technology market reached SAR199 billion ($53.07 billion) in 2025.

The Kingdom also ranked second globally in the World Bank Group’s 2025 GovTech Maturity Index.

The figures form part of Saudi Arabia’s broader efforts under Saudi Vision 2030 to develop an economy supported by data, compute and innovation.

World Bank outlines three stages of AI development

The World Development Report sets out a progressive pathway for economies seeking to capture the benefits of artificial intelligence. It begins with adopting available AI tools before moving towards adapting technologies to local languages, data, institutions and requirements.

The final stage involves developing cutting-edge technologies and the infrastructure required to support them.

The report emphasises that capturing the benefits of AI depends not simply on developing the largest models but on creating an interconnected ecosystem encompassing connectivity, compute, data, skills and institutions.

Locally tailored solutions can, according to the report, broaden access to expertise, raise productivity, improve public services and support economic growth.

Saudi Arabia marks 2026 as ‘Year of AI’

The report was prepared with participation in the Kingdom in the international discussion surrounding artificial intelligence policy.

Minister of Communications and Information Technology Abdullah Alswaha served on the report’s High-Level Advisory Panel.

The report team also held consultation sessions involving the Saudi Competitiveness and Business Center and the WBG–Saudi Arabia Knowledge Hub, alongside national government, private-sector and research entities contributing expertise across data, telecommunications, compute and innovation.

Its release follows the Cabinet’s approval on March 10, 2026 to designate 2026 as the “Year of AI”.

excerpt.rendered: Saudi Arabia ranks among the world’s top 10 for private AI investment as data centre capacity hits 467MW and its technology workforce reaches 426,000

title.rendered: Coinbase gets Abu Dhabi licence to launch international tokenisation hub in ADGM

content.rendered:
Coinbase has received Financial Services Permission from the Financial Services Regulatory Authority (FSRA) of Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM) to establish an international tokenisation hub in the UAE capital.

The approval allows Coinbase to arrange deals in investments and provide custody to facilitate the launch of tokenised securities, forming the regulatory foundation for a new Abu Dhabi operation focused on tokenised securities and onchain capital markets.

The move forms part of a wider UAE expansion that Coinbase says will establish two of its most ambitious global businesses outside the United States across Abu Dhabi and Dubai.

Coinbase secures ADGM approval for tokenised securities

The Financial Services Permission gives Coinbase approval from the FSRA to arrange deals in investments and provide custody.

Coinbase said this will facilitate the launch of tokenised securities and provide the foundation for its international tokenisation hub in ADGM.

According to the company, tokenised securities registered and issued in ADGM will be fully backed by underlying shares under FSRA supervision.

The structure provides rights connected to the underlying shares, although the precise rights available depend on conditions detailed in the relevant prospectus.

Coinbase’s supplied disclosure states that only “Vested Holders”, as defined in the prospectus, may exercise certain rights, including voting in relation to the underlying shares.

Dividends are automatically reinvested, with both vested and unvested holders potentially benefiting economically from that feature. Only vested holders may be eligible for redemption rights.

How Coinbase’s Abu Dhabi tokenised securities will work

Coinbase said transactions limited to the digital securities will not require investors to establish a brokerage or bank account.

However, there is an important qualification for investors seeking to exercise certain redemption rights.

A vested holder exercising redemption rights must have an applicable brokerage or bank account capable of receiving the proceeds, subject to the terms and conditions in the relevant prospectus. The company also said every transfer will be subject to ongoing sanctions screening.

Coinbase said it will have the ability to freeze or seize assets at wallet level where required, as it seeks to combine decentralised finance capabilities with regulatory requirements.

Abu Dhabi framework combines blockchain and capital markets

Brett Tejpaul, Co-CEO of Coinbase Institutional, said: “ADGM issued one of the world’s first regulatory frameworks for virtual assets in 2018. That reflected a genuine institutional commitment to innovation-forward regulation, executed with the rigor that global financial markets require. No major financial center has yet built a framework that treats tokenized equities simultaneously as securities, blockchain-native tokens, and DeFi-composable assets.”

ADGM has positioned digital assets and tokenisation as part of the development of its financial services ecosystem.

Arvind Ramamurthy, Chief Market Development Officer, ADGM, said: “Coinbase’s establishment of its international tokenisation hub in ADGM is a strong endorsement of Abu Dhabi’s growing role in shaping the future of global finance. It reflects the strength of ADGM’s progressive, robust and internationally aligned regulatory framework, which continues to provide leading global institutions with the confidence to develop responsible, blockchain-enabled financial services at scale.

“As tokenisation becomes an increasingly important part of capital markets infrastructure, ADGM remains committed to supporting innovation that enhances market access, transparency and investor confidence, while upholding the highest standards of regulatory oversight.”

Coinbase expands across Abu Dhabi and Dubai

The Abu Dhabi launch forms part of Coinbase’s broader commitment to the UAE. Through investments in Abu Dhabi and Dubai, the company said it is establishing two major global businesses outside the United States.

Abu Dhabi will serve as a hub for tokenised securities and onchain capital markets, while the second operation will be a global hub for derivatives.

Coinbase said the two businesses reflect its confidence in the UAE as a location for the next generation of financial infrastructure.

The company also argues that tokenisation could broaden access to capital markets globally, citing an estimated four billion people worldwide who currently cannot access them.

The supplied material does not provide the underlying source or methodology for that four-billion figure, so it should be treated as a Coinbase claim rather than an independently established statistic.

The Financial Services Permission provides Coinbase with the regulatory basis in ADGM to arrange deals in investments and provide custody in connection with its planned tokenised securities offering.

The structure combines regulated securities with blockchain-based ownership and transactions, while applying sanctions screening and other regulatory controls.

Coinbase described the approval as its most significant step yet towards building infrastructure for a more open and accessible global financial system.

The international tokenisation hub will sit alongside the company’s planned derivatives operation as Coinbase expands its presence across the UAE.

title.rendered: UAE targets $697bn Islamic finance sector by 2031 under global hub strategy

content.rendered:
The UAE is targeting AED2.56tn ($697bn) in local Islamic finance assets by 2031 as it seeks to strengthen its position as a global hub for Islamic finance and the Halal industry.

Islamic finance assets in the country have already reached AED1.4tn ($381.2bn), with the UAE ranked third globally on the 2025 Islamic Finance Development Indicator and 43 licensed Islamic financial institutions operating in the country.

The expansion forms part of the UAE Islamic Finance and Halal Industry Strategy 2025–2031, approved by the UAE Cabinet in May 2025 to capture global growth opportunities in the two sectors and support economic diversification.

The Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE) plays a central role in coordinating efforts with federal and local entities to integrate Islamic finance and the Halal industry into the UAE’s economic agenda.

The strategy seeks to increase local Islamic finance assets to AED2.56tn ($697bn) by 2031, with the broader ambition of establishing the UAE as a global hub for Islamic finance and the Halal industry focused on impact and advanced innovation.

UAE Islamic finance assets

It aims to capture opportunities in global Islamic markets by establishing an ecosystem supporting international Islamic financial transactions, investment and trade in halal products.

The plan also seeks to increase the production of high-value halal products and enhance the social and environmental impact of the sectors in support of sustainable development.

Its strategic objectives include increasing the competitiveness and global scale of the Islamic finance industry, strengthening local production and re-export of halal products, and expanding the contribution of Islamic philanthropy to sustainable development.

The UAE’s strategic initiatives include developing large-scale, competitive Islamic financial institutions and promoting their internationalisation.

The strategy also seeks greater integration between Islamic finance and the Halal industry and the development of a global ecosystem in the UAE for sukuk, money markets and Islamic funds.

Sukuk and Islamic funds

Other initiatives focus on creating an environment for innovation in Islamic finance and establishing a mechanism for impactful Islamic sustainable finance through international collaboration.

For the Halal industry, the UAE plans to develop an ecosystem capable of scaling up local production of high-value halal products.

The strategy also includes establishing a halal traceability system to support re-exports and creating an environment that allows local SMEs and technology startups in the sector to scale.

Halal tourism, modest fashion and Islamic-themed media are also identified as areas for development.

UAE plans expansion of Islamic philanthropy

Islamic philanthropy forms another element of the strategy. The UAE plans to encourage adoption of a waqf mechanism in philanthropic activities across the public and private sectors.

The strategy also seeks to establish solutions enabling transparent monitoring of the impact of Islamic philanthropy.

The UAE has developed an integrated legal, Shari’ah and regulatory framework intended to provide greater certainty for Islamic financial institutions and their customers.

The Commercial Transactions Law (Federal Decree by Law No. 50 of 2022)  became the first commercial law to regulate Islamic finance contracts and provide a specific legal reference for Shari’ah-compliant transactions.

The law includes a full chapter covering Islamic finance, including forms and provisions governing contracts and financing.

It also links its provisions to Shari’ah standards issued by the Higher Shari’ah Authority, establishes a method for interpretation and dispute resolution, and empowers the CBUAE to issue regulations following approval by the Higher Shari’ah Authority.

New Central Bank law regulates Islamic finance institutions

The Central Bank Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025) regulates the business activities of Islamic finance institutions and their supervisory and Shari’ah frameworks.

Among its provisions, Islamic financial institutions are excluded from the prohibition on trading in real estate and goods on a bank’s own account to the extent required to implement financing structures compliant with Islamic Shari’ah.

Islamic financial transactions are also exempt from registration requirements or similar fees or costs.

The framework is intended to enhance legal certainty, protect customer rights and support innovation within the financial system.

The CBUAE established the Higher Shari’ah Authority in 2018 to standardise Shari’ah aspects of Islamic financial institutions and unify their practices in line with internationally recognised Shari’ah standards.

More than 280 standards and resolutions regulating Islamic financial transactions have since been issued to minimise differences in Shari’ah views.

More than nine Shari’ah governance standards have also been issued, establishing rules intended to ensure compliance with Shari’ah and prudential standards covering financial integrity, risk management and the stability of Islamic financial institutions.

According to the supplied information, the resulting framework provides clearer rights and obligations, supports the implementation of Shari’ah-compatible contracts and provides standardised interpretations through the Higher Shari’ah Authority.

It is also intended to support stable Islamic financial transactions through an integrated supervisory and Shari’ah framework and reduce legal and Shari’ah disputes.

UAE ranks third globally for Islamic finance

The UAE’s Islamic finance assets currently stand at AED1.4tn ($381.2bn).

The country ranked third globally on the 2025 Islamic Finance Development Indicator and has 43 licensed Islamic financial institutions.

The UAE is seeking to build on that position through the combination of legislation, Shari’ah standards, regulatory measures and initiatives connecting Islamic finance with the wider Halal economy.

The 2031 strategy ultimately seeks to expand the international competitiveness of both sectors while increasing their economic, environmental and social impact.

title.rendered: Iran says Strait of Hormuz under its control after Trump claims US has ‘total control’

content.rendered:
The Strait of Hormuz is “under Iran’s control and management”, the recently appointed head of Iran’s Basij paramilitary unit said on Thursday, a day after US President Donald Trump said the United States had “total control” of the strategic waterway.

Hossein Taeb said the US had sought to disrupt what he described as the Islamic Republic’s popularity in the region by launching another war in the Strait of Hormuz, but had once more been defeated despite claiming Iran had neither an air force nor a navy.

“Today you see that the Strait of Hormuz is under the management and control of the Islamic Republic,” Taeb said, according to the semi-official Fars news. He added that Iran was continuing on its course in complete security.

After the start of the war, which began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, Tehran effectively shut the strait, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas was previously shipped.

The US subsequently imposed a naval blockade on Iranian shipping and ports, while saying it would protect freedom of navigation for vessels travelling to and from non-Iranian ports.

Strait of Hormuz control disputed

Iran’s joint military command, ​Khatam al-Anbiya Central ‌Headquarters, said later on Thursday that no vessel could transit the Strait of Hormuz without Tehran’s permission.

“The baseless claims made by the United States regarding the normal passage of vessels through the Strait of Hormuz … are nothing more than lies and falsehoods,” the command said in a statement published by state media.

In June, the two countries reached an interim agreement declaring a permanent ceasefire and calling for a swift return to freedom of navigation in the Gulf.

The deal unravelled a few weeks later, with both sides accusing the other of violations. Iran resumed limited attacks on vessels that it said were sailing contrary to the arrangements under the agreement, and the US restarted strikes on Iran’s southern provinces, which Washington said were aimed at degrading Tehran’s ability to target vessels in the Gulf.

In a post on X on Thursday, Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, said that Mojtaba’s strategy would be “offensive war”, if Tehran’s conditions were not met.

“The most enduring path to a new regional order lies in implementing the Hormuz economic-security mechanism, independent of Washington’s military guarantees,” Mokhber wrote, in an apparent reference to an expected deal between Iran and Oman to organise transit through the Strait of Hormuz.

Separately on Thursday, senior military political official Rasoul Sanaei-Rad said Iran would not reopen the strait unless the other side fulfilled its commitments under the interim deal, adding that the reopening of the waterway was not something the US could achieve unilaterally, according to Fars news.

excerpt.rendered: Iran says the Strait of Hormuz is under its control, rejecting Donald Trump’s claim of US “total control” as tensions continue over the vital energy route

title.rendered: UAE A-Level results 2026: Top schools reveal grades after cancelled exams

content.rendered:
Students at some of the UAE’s leading British-curriculum schools have recorded strong A-Level results in 2026, with high proportions securing A* and A grades and graduates winning places at universities around the world.

Results released by GEMS Education, Horizon International School, the Repton Family of Schools, Cranleigh Abu Dhabi, Brighton College and Arcadia British School show the performance of the Class of 2026 following a disrupted academic year in which A-Level examinations across the UAE were cancelled due to regional circumstances.

Horizon International School said its students were assessed through alternative evidence-based measures following the cancellation of examinations, while Repton said its results carried particular significance after exams were cancelled across the UAE due to regional conflict.

Across the schools announcing results, students have secured places and offers from universities including:

  • Imperial College London
  • Columbia University
  • Brown University
  • University College London
  • London School of Economics
  • University of Toronto
  • Northwestern University
  • New York University

GEMS Education A-Level results 2026

Across 22 GEMS Education schools in the UAE and Qatar, 2,388 students sat 6,312 A-Level examinations.

Of all entries, 39 per cent achieved A*–A grades, while 67 per cent were awarded A*–B.

Jumeirah College recorded 67 per cent of entries at A*–A, while GEMS Wellington Academy, Al Khail recorded 86 per cent at A*–B and GEMS Metropole School, Motor City recorded 84 per cent at A*–B.

At GEMS Al Barsha National School, 100 per cent of entries were awarded A*–C.

Dino Varkey, Group CEO of GEMS Education, said: “This has been another exceptional year for our students across both A-level and BTEC pathways. These results reflect the ambition, determination, and resilience of young people who have worked tirelessly to achieve their goals, supported throughout by exceptional educators and families working together in partnership.”

Students have secured offers at universities including Imperial College of London, University of Toronto, Kings College London, University of Bath, University of Manchester and University of Sydney.

GEMS also reported strong results for its vocational pathway.

A total of 564 students completed BTEC Level 3 qualifications, with 46 per cent achieving the highest Distinction Star grade and 72 per cent achieving Distinction Star or Distinction. The overall pass rate was 99.8 per cent.

Horizon International School records 44% A*–A

At Horizon International School, 44 per cent of students achieved A*–A grades, while 84 per cent achieved A*–B and 95 per cent achieved A*–C.

The school said students were assessed through alternative evidence-based measures following the cancellation of A-Level examinations across the UAE.

Its A-Level students achieved an average of 1.57 grades above their expected outcomes across all subjects, according to the school’s Value-Added measure.

Among the strongest individual performances was Andreas Palmos, who secured five A* grades. Aly Abouelhassan achieved A*, A, A and B, while Yahya Abuzakuk achieved A*, A* and B.

Stephen Quinn, Principal of Horizon International School, said: “Despite the challenges of this year, our students demonstrated remarkable resilience and commitment to their learning. Supported by our dedicated teachers, families, and wider HIS community, they achieved strong results that reflect their hard work and determination. We are incredibly proud of their accomplishments and look forward to seeing them continue to thrive and make a positive impact in the future. Congratulations to all our students and their families on this achievement.”

Repton schools reveal A-Level results

The Repton Family of Schools also reported strong performances across its three UAE schools following the cancellation of examinations.

Repton Al Barsha marked a milestone with the results of its first A-Level graduating cohort.

Half of all A-Level entries at the school were awarded A*–A, while 87 per cent achieved A*–B.

Haniya Mirza achieved three A* grades, while Iasonas Romanos achieved A*, A* and A. Graduates have secured places at universities including Imperial College London, New York University and University of Toronto.

Chandini Misra, Principal of Repton Al Barsha, said: “Today marks a truly special moment in the history of Repton Al Barsha as we celebrate our first A-Level graduating class. That this inaugural cohort has achieved such impressive outcomes during a year marked by significant disruption makes their success even more remarkable. They have demonstrated resilience, ambition and a commitment to excellence throughout their studies, setting a wonderful standard for future generations of Repton Al Barsha students. We are incredibly proud of everything they have achieved.”

At Repton Dubai, 39 per cent of entries received A*–A grades and 73 per cent were awarded A*–B.

Qasim Khan achieved five A* grades and will join Columbia University, while Zeineldein Abdelwahab achieved four A* grades and will join Northwestern University. Kyra Behl achieved three A* grades and an A and has secured a place at University of Warwick in the UK.

Repton Abu Dhabi recorded 37 per cent of entries at A*–A and 71 per cent at A*–B.

Students secured offers from universities including Wageningen University & Research, University of Groningen and University of Manchester.

Brighton College reports strong A-Level results in Dubai and Abu Dhabi

Brighton College Dubai and Brighton College Abu Dhabi also reported strong A-Level results following the exceptional 2026 examination cycle, during which alternative assessment arrangements were implemented across the UAE.

Brighton College Dubai recorded its strongest A-Level results to date, with 33 per cent of grades awarded A* and 61 per cent at A-A. A* was the most common grade awarded at the school.

Pupils secured places at universities including the University of St Andrews, University College London, King’s College London, the University of Bristol, the University of Manchester, University of Exeter, London School of Economics and the University of Edinburgh. The school said a record number of pupils are progressing to study Medicine this year.

Simon Crane, Head Master of Brighton College Dubai, said: “These exceptional results are a source of immense pride for our entire College community. With 33% of grades at A* and 61% at A*–A, these are our strongest A Level results to date and rank amongst the very best in the UAE.

“They reflect a culture where it is cool to care about learning, ambition is celebrated and excellence is the norm. My congratulations go to our brilliant pupils, dedicated staff and supportive families on these remarkable achievements. We could not be prouder!”

Brighton College Abu Dhabi reported 63 per cent of grades at A-A* and 84 per cent at A-B*.

In 15 of the 22 A-Level subjects offered, at least 75 per cent of grades were A-B. A*-A attainment reached 82 per cent in Biology, 77 per cent in Psychology and 76 per cent in Mathematics.

Through UCAS, Sixth Form pupils applied to 55 UK universities and received offers from 49. More than three-quarters received an offer from their first-choice university, while 67 per cent of all UK offers came from Russell Group universities, covering 21 of the 24 Russell Group institutions.

Barney Durrant, Head Master of Brighton College Abu Dhabi, said: “Our pupils have done exceptionally well, in the face of significant adversity, and it is testament to their resilience, flexibility and commitment that they have secured such excellent grades. We are all very proud of them – not just for the grades they have achieved, but for the skills they have developed in doing so, and there is no doubt that these achievements will give them greater confidence in the future.

“Our excellent results are also indicative of an incredibly committed teaching staff and the strong support of our parents – and we are very grateful for both.”

Following the cancellation of external examinations, Brighton College Abu Dhabi said alternative assessment arrangements were implemented through a Portfolio of Evidence process, using a broad range of evidence gathered throughout pupils’ courses.

Brighton College Dubai similarly said alternative assessment arrangements were implemented during the exceptional UAE examination cycle, with grades based on evidence gathered throughout pupils’ courses.

Cranleigh Abu Dhabi records strongest A-Level results

Cranleigh Abu Dhabi, established in partnership with Aldar Education, recorded its strongest A-Level performance to date, with a 100 per cent overall pass rate across 310 examination entries.

The proportion of entries achieving A* increased to 32 per cent, compared with 22 per cent in 2025 and 13 per cent in 2024.

A total of 65 per cent of entries were awarded A*–A, representing a 13 per cent increase year-on-year and a 23 per cent increase since 2024. Overall, 89 per cent achieved A*–B.

Students are heading to universities across the UAE, UK, US, Canada, Australia, Europe, South Africa and Hong Kong.

Destinations include Imperial College London, University College London, the London School of Economics, Durham University, King’s College London, University of Saint Andrews, University of Edinburgh, University of Toronto, McMaster University, Brown University, New York University, MBZUAI, NYU Abu Dhabi, University of Manchester and IE University.

Among the standout performers, Hamza O’Brien achieved four A* grades in Biology, History, French and Mathematics and an A in EPQ, and will study Mathematics and History at Brown University.

Deema Al Athba achieved four A* grades in Chemistry, Maths, Further Maths and EPQ and will study Mechanical Engineering at NYU Abu Dhabi.

Millie Matheron secured three A* grades in Economics, Mathematics and EPQ and will study Management at the London School of Economics.

Sarah Matthews, Principal of Cranleigh Abu Dhabi, said: “At Cranleigh, we are boldly ambitious for our students in every sense as they develop the knowledge, skills and habits of mind that ensure they are ready to thrive beyond our gates and become worthy leaders in any field they choose. Today we celebrate their phenomenal success and are incredibly proud of the excellent results achieved, which are a just reward for the hard work they have committed to their studies, alongside the dedicated efforts of their teachers and the careful support of their parents.”

The results come ahead of an expansion of the school.

Aldar Education announced in June an AED385.8m ($105m) investment in a new purpose-built Prep and Senior campus on Saadiyat Island, scheduled to open during the 2027–2028 academic year.

The new campus will have capacity for up to 2,178 pupils and expand academic, Sixth Form, sporting and creative facilities.

Arcadia British School celebrates first A-Level graduates

Arcadia British School is also celebrating its first graduating cohort.

Across 48 examination entries, 13 per cent were awarded A* grades, 25 per cent achieved A*–A, 75 per cent achieved A*–B and 96 per cent received A*–C.

Students also recorded strong BTEC Level 3 results, with 45 per cent securing Distinction*, 18 per cent Distinction, 18 per cent Merit and 18 per cent Pass grades.

Giles Pruett, Executive Principal at Arcadia British School and Member of the Board of Governors at Arcadia Education, said: “We are incredibly proud of what our first graduating cohort has achieved, especially during unprecedented times faced at the beginning of the year when they adapted to distance learning. These results reflect the hard work, agility and determination of our students, the dedication of our teachers, and the support of parents throughout their journey at Arcadia British School. As they prepare to make their next steps into the world, we are confident they will carry themselves with curiosity, confidence and resilience.”

UAE students head to universities around the world

The results show graduates progressing into a wide range of disciplines, including medicine, engineering, artificial intelligence, computer science, economics, law, business, management, mathematics, politics, architecture and the creative arts.

They also highlight differing academic and vocational pathways, with GEMS Education and Arcadia British School reporting BTEC Level 3 results alongside their A-Level outcomes.

For some schools, the Class of 2026 represents an additional milestone. Repton Al Barsha and Arcadia British School are both celebrating their first graduating A-Level cohorts, while Cranleigh Abu Dhabi has reported its strongest A-Level performance to date.

excerpt.rendered: UAE schools reveal 2026 A-Level results after exams were cancelled, with students at GEMS, Repton, Cranleigh, Horizon, Brighton and Arcadia securing top grades

title.rendered: AI being adopted faster than security frameworks can keep pace, warns Saudi IT leader

content.rendered:
A leading figure from the IT industry in Saudi Arabia has issued a stark warning over the state of play in the country when it comes to AI deployments.

Wasna Ben Gassem, Managing Director, Saudi Arabia at TrendAI has said that closing the gap between AI ambition and AI security is becoming harder.

A recent global study from Trend Micro showed that 57 per cent of organisations believe that AI is advancing faster than they can secure it.

Of the 3,700 business and IT leaders surveyed, only 38 per cent had comprehensive AI policies in place, while 67 per cent admitted feeling pressure to approve AI deployments despite active security concerns.

In an interview with Arabian Business, Gassem said the findings closely mirror the conversations taking place in boardrooms across Saudi Arabia.

“Regardless of sector or organisational size, there is a growing sense that AI is being deployed faster than security frameworks can keep pace. Enterprises are embedding AI into critical systems without the adequate visibility, control, or integration required to manage risk in real time.

“In many cases, competitive urgency is quietly overtaking operational readiness. For a country that is rapidly establishing itself as one of the world’s most ambitious and intentional digital economies, that tension is worth examining carefully,” said Gassem.

Investing in the future

Saudi Arabia has rapidly emerged as one of the most active global players in AI adoption.

The kingdom ranks fifth globally and first in the Arab world in AI sector growth, according to the Global AI Index.

The Saudi leadership has also revealed plans to grow the national AI market to $9.17 billion by 2030.

Gassem said that continued investment in infrastructure, talent and sector-specific applications will help diversify the economy and modernise public services.

“Saudi Arabia has recognised earlier than most countries the importance of not only adopting quickly, but adopting securely. Recently, Saudi Arabia ranked first globally in artificial intelligence security, privacy, and cryptography according to the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI) AI Index Report 2026.

“With this strong foundation laid, it is now imperative that Saudi enterprises ensure their own operational maturity evolves just as rapidly,” said Gassem.

Security challenges

Gassem also highlighted that translating progressive AI ambition into secure, scalable execution starts with recognising that many existing enterprise architectures were not designed for the complexity that AI introduces.

“Autonomous systems, generative tools, and increasingly intelligent business applications are creating new operational dependencies that demand far greater governance maturity than most organisations currently have in place.

“Security teams are now confronting risks that extend well beyond traditional cybersecurity, including data misuse, shadow AI, regulatory uncertainty, and reduced oversight over sensitive systems,” said Gassem.

The Managing Director of TrendAI’s business in Saudi Arabia, believes this is why the conversation around enterprise AI must evolve quickly.

“Security can no longer function as a reactive control point introduced after deployment decisions are made. It must become an integrated architectural layer spanning infrastructure, governance, compliance, data protection, and operational oversight from the very beginning.”

Securing the future

Gassem argues that for enterprises across Saudi Arabia, the next phase of AI maturity will depend on moving beyond adoption speed to enable secure scalability.

Fragmented point solutions and disconnected governance frameworks are increasingly insufficient in an environment where AI is reshaping every layer of enterprise operations.

“What organisations require now is unified, platform-driven security that delivers real-time visibility, lifecycle governance, proactive threat intelligence, and integrated risk management across the full AI ecosystem.

This is why organisations are increasingly prioritising unified cybersecurity platforms that can provide a single view of risk across infrastructure, data, applications, and AI environments,” said Gassem.

She concluded the interview, by stressing the need for consolidating visibility and strengthening governance.

“Enterprises can better manage emerging threats, maintain compliance, and ensure that innovation is supported by security at every stage of the AI lifecycle. Saudi Arabia has already demonstrated that meaningful AI leadership is about building securely, governing responsibly, and scaling sustainably.

“To ensure long-term success, enterprises need to match that national ambition with security architectures capable of sustaining it,” concluded Gassem.

excerpt.rendered: Saudi Arabia plans to grow its domestic AI market to $9 billion by 2030.
