title.rendered: One of Africa’s Longest Waves is Reshaping a Moroccan Fishing Village

content.rendered:
I’m in the front seat of a dusty SUV, windows down, hurtling along an empty road cut into a mountain high above the Atlantic. My friend is in the back, sharing her seat with surf leashes, wax and a stack of damp wetsuits. Driving us is Momo, short for Mohamed Idabbou, 29, who promised us a sunset spot completely blocked from the wind in a Moroccan surf town — as good a reason as any to get in a car with someone.

Our original plan was to paddle out for a sunset surf, but a sudden onshore wind had other ideas. So did Momo.

“Do you guys always drive in the middle of the road?” My friend’s face pokes between our headrests.

“What do you mean?” He addresses her reflection in the rear view.

I’d actually been wondering the same thing. The taxi driver who took us from the airport to the coast also cruised smack down the centre line.

“I mean, why drive in the middle? Why not stay in the right lane?”

He shrugs as we round a hairpin turn. “Don’t you think it’s more comfortable this way?”

Debatable.

We met Momo the way we meet most local surfers on our travels: slowly, then all at once. A polite good morning became a daily chat about the conditions, then an impromptu invitation to a sunset spot right outside of town, where we’ve just arrived.

The trail up the mountain is not made for flip flops. Loose sand gives under each step as we climb, with Momo moving at twice my pace. The wind, so relentless back in town, is still. The Atlantic stretches silver and enormous below. It smells strongly of salt and faintly of fish.

We’ve barely settled in before a pulsing, electronic beat makes its way up the mountain several minutes before four newcomers do. Momo warmly greets the first arrival, who’s followed shortly by three others, one with a speaker slung over his shoulder. Names are exchanged followed by the routine questions: Where are you from, when did you get in, did you paddle out today, what time are you going tomorrow?

In Imsouane, a small town situated between Agadir and Essaouira, a spontaneous invitation has a way of becoming a full evening. The group grows from three to seven to 10, someone passes around a flaky, honey-soaked pastry, wood is gathered for a small fire, and we talk about waves. The waves here, the waves back home, the waves we surfed today and the waves we hope to surf tomorrow.

After sunset, we follow the festive sound of rhythmic clapping layered over intricate drum beats down the mountain, becoming more distinct until we spot a drum circle that’s formed near the parked cars. Our local friends fall into step immediately, adding their voices to the hypnotic melody and artfully stomping in dusty unison. I scoop up one of the puppies milling about, doing my best to match the steps of the dance.

Then comes the inevitable: going out for tagine. It takes hours, and no one’s particularly concerned. Tea is served and then served again. Small plates of marinated olives and spiced carrots appear and are swept away. The order is made for us. Finally it arrives, three clay dishes with wide, circular bases and tall, cone-shaped tops that barely fit on the huge corner table we’ve been occupying for half the night.

The tops are whipped off with a flourish, heady scents of cumin, cinnamon and turmeric wafting off the simmering stews. I take the cue from our hosts to grab a piece of the seemingly never-ending stack of bread and pinch up bites of fish, lemon, lamb and apricot.

By the time we return to our rented room, it’s almost 1 am, our hair smokey and stomachs full of tagine. The alarm is already set for a sunrise surf. That’s when the hierarchy will shift. Tonight, we are guests. Tomorrow at dawn, we will have to earn our place.

The smoke of tagine still clings to my hair as I race down the staircase into Imsouane’s bay, 9-foot-2 longboard tucked under my arm at just the right angle to keep it from scraping the rough stone of the steps. The sun is barely up, but I’m far from the first one out. Even from shore, I can pick out familiar figures by the way they move through the ocean. There’s Houssine Badaoui, 24, unmistakable as he pumps powerfully down the line. On the wave just behind, Omar Oukhair, 28, elegantly wraps all 10 of his toes around the tip of his board.

It would be hard not to be impressed by this place, whether you’ve ever stepped foot on a surfboard or not. The water shifts colour with the light, this morning a soft, glassy blue. The Bay curves inward beneath towering cliffs on one side, glowing gold in the morning sun. The village stretches onto a slim rocky outcropping on the other. A tiny sliver of crescent moon hangs in the dark pink sky.

And then there’s the wave.

The first time I saw it, peeling in perfect lines from one end of the Bay to the other, I knew I was in trouble. Imsouane boasts one of the longest waves in Africa, on a good day you can ride it for hundreds of metres. It’s a wave to rearrange your life around, which is what I ended up doing. Other trips were cancelled, going home was deprioritised. I hurried to come back as soon as I left.

That’s the way surfing works. You schedule your life around the wave, not vice versa.

I’m not the only one who feels this way about the storied coastlines of Morocco — if anything, I’m late to the party. Surfers have been coming to this stretch of coast for decades, with Taghazout long established as the center of it all. Imsouane’s rise in popularity still feels somewhat new, its fishing village roots more visible than Taghazout’s, where surf tourism has already had decades to reshape the town.

That doesn’t mean you’ll find an empty wave here. The Bay fills early every day, especially during the peak winter season. Surf camps bus in beginners from up and down the coast. Travellers fly in from all over, chasing the longest ride of their lives. Moroccan surfers from Rabat and Casablanca relocate to Imsouane during the winter. And threading through it all is the local crowd, the surfers who grew up here before the Bay became a destination.

From the beach it looks like anarchy, a seemingly unlimited number of surfers jockeying for a very limited amount of waves. But no matter where on the globe you are, surfing has rules. Lots of rules.

The main one is that the surfer with the longest potential ride has priority to take the wave, but it’s rarely that simple. There is a hierarchy that supersedes the rules. Beginners sit at the bottom, locals are at the top. The more skilled the local, the more respect they command.

If you can earn the trust of the locals in the water, you’ll be rewarded with waves. Ignore the rules, and the ocean can suddenly become a very small place.

My first weeks in Imsouane, I stayed on the shoulder, waiting for waves no one else wanted. It’s the most reliable path to not ruin your own morning when you’re new to a surf break. I smiled and greeted everyone, both in the water and around town, until the regulars in the lineup started to recognise me. A little goes a long way.

From there, life in the water gets easier.

This morning, I’m surrounded by familiar faces plus dozens I don’t know. I’ve caught a couple of small peelers, but I’m still waiting for my wave of the day, chatting with whoever happens to be floating nearby. Then it arrives.

“This one is you, go! Yalla, go!” Mustapha Meskouri, 25, always smiling, yells from somewhere behind me.

I don’t waste the time to second guess him. A brief look over each shoulder is all I need, followed by three long paddles and I’m up. The wave rises in front of me, a perfect wall of water continuously rebuilding itself. The first part of the ride is an obstacle course, swerving and dipping around countless surfers bobbing in the water on their boards. I enjoy this part, the test of my reaction time, the board responding to the slightest shift of my bare feet.

Then the crowd clears out. All that’s left is me and the wave, hurtling toward the golden cliffs on the far side of the Magic Bay. That’s why I’m here. That’s why I come back.

The ride is so long that I’ve taken to singing to myself to pass the time, squeezing every last second out of the joyride by walking lightly up and down the board. I finally dig my back foot into the tail, halting momentum right at the sandy shore. At a normal surf break, I would turn back to the horizon, flop on my stomach, and begin the paddle back to the lineup.

But the Bay is no normal break. By then, the lineup is a distant cluster of bodies and boards at the far end of the bay. The most logical way back is to climb onto shore, prop my board on my head and hoof it back to the surf break. Other than the crushing weight of the longboard on my neck and the salty bind of my wetsuit, it’s a nice walk.

The beach is alive with a mix of international tourists, Moroccan vacationers, surf instructors rallying their groups of giddy beginners and fishermen setting off in small, blue boats. I smile and nod at two women around my age, one in bright yellow, the other vibrant in head-to-toe orange. A soccer game is in full swing, teenagers in swim trunks yelling and spraying sand in every direction. The ball bounces my way, spinning in the water lapping at the shore. I kick it back as their faces turn expectantly toward me.

High above, the village perches on the cliffs. There are cafes, guesthouses, surf shops and homes all crowded together, life teeming among the structures. Just beyond that, a long stretch of town remains bare, desert dust visible through skeletal grey concrete block walls. The huge construction project faces the coastline opposite of the Bay. It looks strangely empty.

In the water, the village locals hold all authority. Here on land, the rules are more blurred, the hierarchy harder to see.

The vacant lots in the middle of town make that uncertainty visible. In early 2024, authorities began demolition in Imsouane, reportedly giving residents and business owners just 24 hours to evacuate before bulldozers arrived to raze a central section of the village. Authorities cited unauthorised structures built along the maritime public domain. Petitions to stop the demolition moved quickly through the global surf community, but not quickly enough.

By the time I arrived in 2025, the town was rebuilding. Some businesses and homeowners had relocated, others weren’t as fortunate. People in town talked about the demolitions carefully, some angry, others resigned, many still hopeful.

“Imsouane has changed so much since the demolitions,” Momo told me. “The vibes are not the same. People come back but they don’t find the same feeling as before.”

He continued, suddenly serious: “I think they want to make Imsouane like a resort with nice places and restaurants. It could be good, but we don’t know. We don’t know what’s coming.”

One afternoon, Momo pointed out a bustling seaside café, his uncle’s place. It had been torn down in the demolitions, then rebuilt and reopened for business, though it likely won’t stay that way. He thought they have one year, maybe two, before they’re shut down again. After that, I began noticing how much of Imsouane seemed built on borrowed time.

Despite this, Momo remained relentlessly cheerful. “As long as the wave in the Bay is working, people will come.”

That’s the simple truth beneath every surf town. Great waves bring the surf world to your door, whether the community is ready or not. They start as a secret, then a rumour. From there they become a pilgrimage for the ultra-committed, and eventually a full blown economy. An hour and a half south, Taghazout and nearby Tamraght offer a glimpse of surf tourism after it has had more time to organise itself.

I visited Taghazout for the first time, somewhat reluctantly, between two trips to Imsouane. On my first pass through Morocco, I blew right through the famous surf town on the way to the Magic Bay. It’s not that I doubted the quality of the waves or the charm of the seaside town. It’s that I have an aversion to the obvious choice.

For those who don’t surf, a Moroccan town of only a few thousand residents may be far from obvious. For us, it’s legendary, a bucket list destination.

The map looks different to surfers, we care about swell and wind patterns and which season will bring the perfect alignment of the two. Tiny towns where the perfect conditions reliably meet serve as our capitals: Taghazout, Ericeira, El Tunco, Siargao, Sayulita, to name a few.

Every surf traveller seems to be on some version of the same tour. It’s not unusual for me to run into someone I surfed with in the Philippines walking down a street in El Salvador, or see someone typing away at a cafe in Mexico whom I met in Portugal. These towns are far from interchangeable, but they have been on the surf circuit long enough to build reputations that they, for the most part, live up to.

Taghazout is confident in its position as the Moroccan surf town, home to Anchor Point, World Surf League qualifying events and an iconic skatepark perched high above the sea that comes alive each evening at sunset with a mix of travellers, local kids, seriously good skaters and people who just come to watch. The edge of the bowl buzzes with the camaraderie of a hometown football game, everyone rooting for the skaters soaring above graffiti-covered concrete waves set against the pastel Atlantic.

In the distance I spot Houssine Badaoui, 24, part of a new generation of Moroccan surfers who have honed their skills on the country’s Atlantic coastline. Largely self-taught, the Oualidia native divides his time between competition, coaching and pursuing some of Morocco’s most challenging waves. He ranked among the country’s top five junior surfers in 2021 and went on to compete internationally the following year. He was 10 when his father died; the family sold their house, and school gave way to selling sweets on the beach to make ends meet. Surfing followed, then competitions, then teaching for other schools, until he and his brother Abderrahim saved enough to open a surf school of their own.

“My brother is my role model and surfing together became a form of therapy,” says Badaoui. “I feel the same way about riding horses in our hometown, Oualidia. Makes me feel like a king.”

We moved on to Tamraght, Taghazout’s sleepy neighbour that caters to travellers who prefer to end their day at a yin class over a bar. A design-forward crowd has moved in during recent years, cafes with beautifully styled interiors share the sidewalks with small, family-run eateries. One afternoon, I queued up for coffee among a crowd that wouldn’t look out of place in Venice Beach, everyone busily working their remote jobs. The illusion shattered when a power outage shut down every espresso machine and Wi-Fi router in town. Luckily, the more interesting alternative was waiting right outside: An entrepreneurial barista with an espresso machine rigged into the hatch of his car. He promptly made me an excellent “car-ppuccino” and enthusiastically explained the sourcing of his glazed ceramic mugs.

Taghazout and Tamraght were full of surprises. The waves were fast, the people were kind, the food was spicy and memorable. Still, I left without the nagging pull to return. I found myself counting the days until it was time to take the taxi back to Imsouane, back to the regulars I’d come to look forward to seeing each morning, back to the wave that has occupied my thoughts since I first laid eyes on it. The energy in Imsouane is different from any surf town. The wave has already made the town a destination. The question now is what kind.

On my first evening back, I went to watch the sunset above Cathedral, a stretch of beach on the other side of the village from the Bay. It lacked the iconic spectacle of Taghazout’s skatepark. There was no bowl, no clear place to sit, no obvious separation between performer and audience. We simply gathered along the side of the road, looking out over the Atlantic from a stretch of cliff now unobstructed after the demolition of the small homes and businesses that once stood there.

By late afternoon, it felt like the whole town had arrived. The mix of people was familiar by now: Beachgoers wrapped in towels, tourists smoking cigarettes on the curb, shopkeepers ambling over from their stalls, cafe workers busily refilling glasses of mint tea. Boards leaned against cars, wetsuits drying on the side mirror. Kids and still-wet surfers took turns on skateboards passed around in the street. Below, the sunset turned the waves briefly gold, as if just for us.

For a few minutes, we all faced the same direction, gathered at the edge of a place still deciding what it would become. Then the sun dropped, the wind changed, and the town began rearranging itself again.

excerpt.rendered: On Morocco’s Atlantic coast, one of Africa’s longest waves has drawn surfers from around the world, and left a small fishing village negotiating what kind of destination it will become.

title.rendered: Buying a home in UAE? Your mortgage offer could vary by more than $272,000 between banks

content.rendered:
UAE homebuyers can receive significantly different mortgage approval amounts from different banks despite having the same income, employment and financial circumstances, with around one in ten applicants in a new analysis seeing a gap of more than AED1m ($272,000).

PRYPCO Mortgage found that among buyers assessed by more than one of its banking partners, the median difference between the lowest and highest approved loan amount was approximately AED100,000 ($27,200), or around 7 per cent of the total loan value.

Half of applicants received approval amounts that differed by at least AED100,000 ($27,200), while a quarter saw variations exceeding AED500,000 ($136,000).

The findings were released as PRYPCO Mortgage, the home-financing arm of PRYPCO, launched a new self-service platform for homebuyers.

UAE mortgage offers can vary by more than AED1m

Analysis of mortgage applications processed through PRYPCO Mortgage found significant differences in how much individual banks were prepared to lend to the same applicants.

Among buyers assessed by more than one banking partner, the median difference between their lowest and highest approved loan amount was approximately AED100,000 ($27,200), equivalent to around 7 per cent of the total loan value.

Half of applicants received approval amounts that differed by at least AED100,000 ($27,200).

A quarter experienced variations exceeding AED500,000 ($136,000), while around one in ten saw a difference of more than AED1m ($272,000).

In most cases, the approvals were issued within weeks of each other, according to PRYPCO Mortgage, meaning the buyer’s income, employment and financial circumstances remained unchanged.

The difference was the bank assessing the application.

Why UAE banks can offer different mortgage amounts

Banks in the UAE apply their own credit policies when assessing the same mortgage application.

According to PRYPCO Mortgage, banks can differ in how much of a variable salary, commission or bonus they count as income.

They can also differ in which employers they regard as lower risk, how they assess existing credit card and loan commitments, and where they set loan-to-value limits according to property type and buyer profile.

As a result, an application that appears marginal under one bank’s policy can clear comfortably under another’s.

The variation can be particularly significant for buyers at the lower end of the property market, where affordability margins are tighter and many first-time homebuyers have limited flexibility if they receive a lower-than-expected approval.

The practical consequence, according to the analysis, is that there is no single answer to the question of how much a buyer can borrow. Instead, there can be a range depending on the lender.

PRYPCO said most buyers begin by approaching the bank that holds their salary account, take the figure it provides and search for a home based on that single number.

Essa Ibrahim, Co-founder and President, PRYPCO, said: “Most buyers treat their borrowing capacity as a fixed number. It is closer to an opinion. In our data, half of the applicants who approached more than one lender found a gap of at least AED 100,000 between them. For some it ran past a million. That gap decides which homes are on the table and which are not. Different banks will naturally assess the same buyer differently. The problem is that buyers commit to a property long before they ever see the disagreement.”

PRYPCO launches UAE mortgage platform

PRYPCO Mortgage has also launched a self-service platform designed to bring affordability checks, matched offers, digital KYC, document collection and application tracking into a single journey.

UAE homebuyers receive a personalised affordability estimate before creating an account or uploading a document.

Rather than returning a single borrowing figure, the platform surfaces offers for which a buyer qualifies across PRYPCO Mortgage’s network of more than 20 banking partners and explains why each has been matched to the buyer’s profile.

Eligible salaried UAE residents and nationals purchasing individually can complete digital KYC and receive an instant pre-approval through InstaMortgage, PRYPCO Mortgage’s instant pre-approval product delivered through its partnership with Appro.

Buyers who do not yet qualify receive specific next steps towards eligibility rather than a rejection.

“We built the platform so that the full range is where a buyer starts, not something they have to ask for,” Essa added. “You should know what the market will lend you before you fall in love with a home. Not after.”

How the UAE mortgage analysis was conducted

The findings are drawn from pre-approvals issued through PRYPCO Mortgage between September 2023 and August 2026.

The comparison covers thousands of applicants who received a recorded pre-approval amount from more than one of the company’s banking partners. For each applicant, the analysis compared the lowest and highest approved amounts.

Medians are reported rather than averages because, according to PRYPCO Mortgage, a small number of very large differences skew the average upwards.

Individual banks are not identified and no bank-level approval data is disclosed.

PRYPCO Mortgage has facilitated more than AED22bn ($5.99bn) in home financing since launching in 2023 and works with more than 20 banking partners across the UAE.

excerpt.rendered: UAE mortgage approvals can vary significantly between banks, with one in ten applicants seeing differences of more than AED1m, according to PRYPCO data

title.rendered: Young Emiratis pour $1.2bn into Sharjah property as 5,314 invest in real estate

content.rendered:
Young Emiratis aged between 18 and 35 have invested a cumulative AED4.3bn ($1.17bn) in Sharjah real estate, with 5,314 individuals trading 7,052 properties as of August 2026.

New figures from the Sharjah Real Estate Registration Department show the scale of property investment among younger UAE nationals, including a relatively balanced investor base between men and women.

The statistics were released to coincide with International Youth Day on August 12 and highlight the growing investment activity of Emirati youth in Sharjah’s property market.

The cumulative value of real estate investments by Emirati youth reached AED4.3 billion ($1.17 billion) as of August 2026.

A total of 5,314 young individuals were responsible for trading 7,052 properties, according to the Sharjah Real Estate Registration Department.

Sharjah real estate market

The figures cover the target age group of 18 to 35 years. The department said the data reflects the growing position of young Emiratis as strategic partners in the real estate sector and their confidence in Sharjah’s economic and legislative environment.

It also highlighted growing investment awareness among younger Emiratis and their interest in building sustainable capital assets.

The report showed the gender distribution across properties, investors and investment value.

Men accounted for 61.3 per cent of traded properties, representing 4,325 properties. Women accounted for the remaining 38.7 per cent, representing 2,727 properties.

Among individual investors, men represented 59.5 per cent of the total, with 3,162 investors. Women accounted for 40.5 per cent, representing 2,152 investors.

Emirati women invest in Sharjah property

Investment values were split 64.6 per cent for men and 35.4 per cent for women. Male investment amounted to AED2.8bn ($762.4m), while female investment reached AED1.5bn ($408.4m).

Together, the figures account for the AED4.3bn ($1.17bn) cumulative investment value recorded among Emirati investors aged 18 to 35.

Saud Al-Khayyal, Chairman of the Youth Council at the Sharjah Real Estate Registration Department, emphasised that the statistical results clearly reflect the success of the emirate’s developmental approach. Al-Khayyal said: “The outstanding investment performance of Emirati youth, which we highlight today on the occasion of international youth day, reflects the growing base of national investors in the emirate. We do not view these figures as merely representing real estate transactions, rather as evidence of the growing investment culture and awareness among the younger generations regarding the importance of building assets.

“This enhances our vision of making Sharjah’s real estate sector a preferred and sustainable investment choice for individuals and families seeking to build their wealth and achieve financial stability.”

excerpt.rendered: Young Emiratis aged 18-35 have invested $1.2bn in Sharjah real estate, with 5,314 investors trading 7,052 properties as of August 2026

title.rendered: Muslim travel market to hit $310bn as 262m international arrivals forecast by 2030

content.rendered:
International Muslim arrivals are projected to reach 262m by 2030 and generate an estimated $310bn in annual expenditure as artificial intelligence, digital services and changing travel patterns reshape the global tourism market.

The 2026 Global Muslim Travel Index (GMTI), released by Mastercard and CrescentRating, projects international Muslim arrivals will increase to 208m this year, up from 196m in 2025, as destinations compete to make services more accessible, reliable and digitally discoverable.

The 11th edition of the Global Muslim Travel Index evaluates 150 destinations representing more than 98 per cent of global Muslim visitor arrivals.

Destinations are evaluated using the Access, Communications, Environment and Services (ACES) framework.

GMTI 2026 places a stronger focus on AI readiness, digital visibility, smart destination infrastructure, traveller confidence and resilience planning amid a more volatile global environment.

Muslim travel market

The report projects international Muslim arrivals to increase from 196m in 2025 to 208m in 2026 before reaching 262m by 2030.

Annual expenditure is estimated to reach $310bn by 2030.

Bahrain climbed five places to rank seventh among the top travel destinations for Muslims, with a score of 74.

The country also ranked second among destinations providing a safe, sustainable and accessible environment where Muslim travellers can explore with confidence and peace of mind. Jordan retained its position among the top 15, ranking 12th with a score of 72.

The country also moved into the top five most accessible destinations, with the report highlighting modernised visa facilitation and increased flight connectivity.

Bahrain and Jordan both recorded a perfect score of 100 for the availability of prayer places and airport services.

Saud Swar, country manager, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Jordan, and other Levant, at Mastercard, said: “In line with our long-standing commitment to supporting the growth of the travel and tourism industry, we are pleased to collaborate with CrescentRating to develop GMTI, which identifies the key trends and destination leaders shaping the future of halal travel. Jordan’s and Bahrain’s continued presence among the top 15 Muslim-friendly travel destinations testify to their rich tourism offerings, modern amenities and abundant halal facilities”.

AI transforms Muslim travel planning

Artificial intelligence is becoming an increasingly important part of how travellers research and plan trips.

According to GMTI 2026, 80 per cent of travellers worldwide now use AI tools for travel purposes.

AI-powered platforms can help travellers identify halal dining options, locate prayer spaces, compare transport routes, receive personalised recommendations and navigate destinations.

The report argues that this shift has particular significance for Muslim travellers, who can need to verify multiple faith-based requirements before and during a journey.

It warns that destinations which fail to digitise their Muslim-friendly offerings risk being excluded from AI-driven recommendation systems regardless of the quality of their physical infrastructure.

As a result, the competitive landscape is shifting from simply having services available to ensuring that reliable information about those services is digitally visible.

Technologies including e-visas, biometric border systems, AI chatbots, digital travel assistants, real-time translation and smart destination management are also helping reduce uncertainty and improve ease of travel, according to the report.

Fazal Bahardeen, CEO, CrescentRating and HalalTrip, said: “The Muslim travel market is expanding at an unprecedented pace, driven by the continued growth of the global Muslim population. With 70 per cent of Muslims worldwide now digitally native, GMTI 2026 highlights a profound evolution in how travel is consumed. As travellers move from active searching to AI-assisted decision-making, destinations must ensure that Muslim-friendly services are not only available but also digitally visible”.

Reional destinations

The report also identifies changing travel patterns amid global volatility.

Rising fuel costs, geopolitical tensions, airspace disruptions and security concerns are prompting more travellers to favour closer, safer and more predictable destinations, according to GMTI 2026.

The report describes the trend as a shift towards “home-continent” mobility.

Rather than cancelling travel altogether, travellers are adjusting itineraries and choosing regional corridors offering greater stability, lower friction and stronger confidence instead of relying on long-haul journeys through complex transit hubs.

Muslim-friendly destinations move beyond halal food and prayer spaces

GMTI 2026 also introduces a Destination Activation Stack designed to assess the changing requirements of Muslim-friendly tourism.

The model integrates three frameworks. ACES measures foundational destination preparedness, while RIDA assesses responsible, immersive, digital and assured travel experiences. TRUST evaluates the signals that convert traveller interest into bookings.

The framework reflects the evolution of the global faith-based travel market from a niche segment into what the report describes as a mainstream economic powerhouse.

Destinations are consequently no longer assessed solely on whether baseline services such as halal food and prayer spaces are available.

The report says those services must also be accessible, visible, reliable and digitally discoverable, while meeting traveller expectations around safety, sustainability, inclusivity and experience quality.

excerpt.rendered: Global Muslim travel is projected to reach 262m international arrivals and $310bn in annual spending by 2030 as AI reshapes how travellers plan trips

title.rendered: The ‘Humanmaxxing’ trap: Why spending more on longevity might not make you live longer

content.rendered:
‘Humanmaxxing’ has taken over among longevity enthusiasts, while lacking a single definition, the concept refers to maximising ways to improve health, fitness and performance. But is this simply the next wellness trend or is it an evidence-based way to live longer?

“Good science tends to be more comfortable with uncertainty than good marketing is. Marketing speaks in absolutes. Real evidence almost always arrives with caveats,” Ali Hashmi, Co-Founder and CEO of Metabolic, told Arabian Business.

“Oddly enough, it’s usually that hedging that gives me the most confidence in it. The science of longevity is real. It just isn’t sold in a bottle,” he said.

Traditionally, healthcare has been based on “getting it fixed” after “something breaks.”

However, longevity takes a different approach, one that is generally centered on optimisation before the problem occurs.

“There’s an old line in medicine that prevention beats cure,” Hashmi said, but on the contrary, for most of modern history “healthcare has been organised around disease. Something breaks, we become patients, we get it fixed, we go home.”

“That model has very little to say to a healthy fifty-year-old who wants to know how the next thirty years are likely to go, partly because there has never really been a reimbursement code for that conversation,” he explained.

Now, longevity enthusiasts are getting are looking ahead. Instead of waiting for disease, a growing group of health-conscious consumers are tracking sleep, glucose, fitness and biological markers while experimenting with supplements, scans and therapies designed to improve healthspan.

This allows a person who already tracks their steps, sleep and screen time to track parts of their biology that were once visible only during a medical appointment. But the problem is that the ability to measure more has arrived faster than the ability to understand what all of those measurements mean.

“It’s easy to file it [longevity] under a social media trend, or a generation that has become obsessed with optimisation. There’s some of both. But I suspect something more basic is going on underneath. This is a generation that grew up quantifying everything, steps, sleep, screen time, and has simply turned that same lens on its own biology,” Hashemi said.

The expensive side of longevity

The modern longevity consists of treatments, wearables, clinics and methods that often come with a hefty price tag.

However, experts are concerned that spending often moves in the opposite direction to the strength of the evidence.

“The spending tends to run in the opposite direction to the evidence. The interventions with the strongest support are mostly free or nearly so, and the ones with the weakest support tend to be the ones with a price tag and a nice interface,” he said.

This usually creates an appealing shortcut. Changing habits like sleep, food or exercise requires consistency over months and years while buying another supplement or test takes a few minutes.

Hashmi believes that this is the reason that complicated interventions become easier to sell. “The basics are hard because they are behaviours, not purchases. Sleeping eight hours means renegotiating your whole life. Buying NMN means entering a credit card,” he said.

For consumers, that can make spending money feel like progress even when the biggest health risks remain unchanged. Someone may invest heavily in supplements and annual screening while continuing to sleep poorly, exercise too little or leave high blood pressure untreated.

“If your longevity routine costs more than your rent and you’re still sleeping five hours, you have bought yourself a very expensive distraction,” Hashemi said.

“The more aggressively something is marketed, the weaker its evidence tends to be. Squats don’t have an affiliate program.”

What actually has evidence behind it?

Alongside longevity trends, there is an evidence-based version of the concept. Experts emphasise on the importance of strength and muscle mass, cardiorespiratory fitness, sleep and long-term metabolic health.

“The evidence-based list is shorter and more boring than the internet suggests, which is inconvenient for the people selling the interesting version,” he said.

Muscle, in particular, is often overlooked in a health culture that remains heavily focused on weight. Hashemi argues that preserving strength becomes increasingly important with age because it affects metabolic health, resilience during illness and the ability to remain independent.

“We spend enormous energy talking about weight and far too little on body composition. As we age, preserving muscle matters for metabolic health, for resilience through illness and for independence, not only for how much you can lift.”

Walking, particularly after meals, also forms part of the basic approach, alongside regular strength training, enough sleep, whole foods, stress management and strong social relationships.

Hashemi advised, “There’s a fairly boring consensus list, and the reassuring thing is that it hasn’t moved much in years. Treat sleep like a job rather than a luxury. Eat mostly whole food, and if your grandmother wouldn’t recognise it, be a little suspicious. Walk often, especially after meals, which is about the cheapest glucose control on earth. Lift heavy things, because strength is the currency of old age.”

That is where one of the biggest contradictions in humanmaxxing begins. The interventions with the strongest evidence are often the least expensive, while the products attracting the most attention can cost significantly more.

“My sense is that the constraint was never information. It’s adherence, and adherence is a systems problem far more than a willpower problem,” he said.

GLP-1 drugs bring stronger clinical evidence

One major development does stand apart from much of the longevity market. GLP-1 drugs, which are used to treat diabetes and obesity, have produced evidence that extends beyond weight loss.

The SELECT trial studied more than 17,000 adults who were overweight or obese and had established cardiovascular disease but did not have diabetes. Weekly semaglutide reduced the risk of cardiovascular death, a non-fatal heart attack or a non-fatal stroke by 20 per cent compared with a placebo.

“For the right patient it is the most significant metabolic tool of our generation, and unlike most of what gets called longevity science, it arrives with hard outcome data,” Hashemi said.

However, he cautioned against treating the drugs as replacements for exercise, nutrition and continuing medical support.

Research involving Metabolic’s care model found that patients receiving GLP-1 treatment alongside continuous behavioural support achieved better metabolic results when they remained engaged with their care teams. Hashemi said the most engaged patients were around 60 per cent more likely to reverse metabolic syndrome than those with the lowest engagement.

A separate 2025 study of 125 patients in GluCare’s hybrid diabetes programme found that patients with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes recorded an average 2.4 point reduction in HbA1c over 12 months. Higher levels of virtual interaction with the care team were associated with better blood sugar control, although the researchers noted that the observational study could not establish that engagement alone caused the improvement.

“The medication creates the opportunity. What people do with it decides the outcome,” Hashemi said.

Supplements are running ahead of the science

The evidence becomes far less clear across many popular anti-ageing supplements.

Nicotinamide mononucleotide, known as NMN, and nicotinamide riboside, known as NR, are sold as ways to increase levels of NAD, a molecule involved in energy production and other cellular processes. Hashemi said the biological mechanism and animal research are interesting but human studies have yet to show that these supplements help people live longer or remain healthier.

Resveratrol, another supplement promoted for anti-ageing benefits, has also failed to produce the outcomes once expected from early research.

“The human data is thin, mostly short studies showing that a blood marker moves, with nothing yet showing that people live longer or better. Resveratrol had its moment and quietly did not survive contact with larger trials. Most anti-ageing stacks are combinations of things at that same tier of evidence, sold with a confidence the evidence does not support.”

Hashemi applies similar caution to whole-body MRI scans for healthy young adults. These scans can identify unexpected abnormalities, but some findings may never have caused harm. The result can be further imaging, biopsies and anxiety without clear evidence that the screening improves lifespan.

Consumers can test health claims by asking what human evidence exists, whether an intervention improves a real outcome and who benefits financially from the claim.

A change in a biomarker does not automatically mean a person will become healthier. Stronger evidence would show that an intervention reduces illness, disability or death in human trials.

“Anyone taking responsibility for your health should be able to answer one question: where are your outcomes published? Claims without published data are just marketing with a stethoscope,” he said.

Wearables need interpretation

Wearables and home testing devices have made personal health data easier to collect. Smart rings and watches can track sleep, movement, heart rate and recovery, while continuous glucose monitors show how glucose changes throughout the day.

The data can help people understand their bodies, but Hashemi warns that measurements without medical context can also create unnecessary anxiety.

A continuous glucose monitor will show blood sugar rising after a meal, including in a healthy person. Someone unfamiliar with normal glucose patterns may interpret that increase as a sign of illness and make restrictive dietary changes that are not needed.

“A measurement on its own does very little. It has to be interpreted to become information, the information has to change a decision to be worth anything, and the decision has to change an outcome to matter. Most consumer devices hand you the measurement and stop there, which is where the anxiety comes from.”

Constantly checking health scores can become counterproductive. A person who loses sleep because they are worried about a poor sleep score has gained data without improving their health.

“We live in a world that is data-rich and insight-poor. A number without context is noise. A number with clinical interpretation is knowledge.”

Dubai moves to regulate longevity medicine

The debate is becoming increasingly important in Dubai following the creation of the Dubai Longevity Authority in June 2026.

Established under Law No. 17 of 2026, the authority will regulate longevity, wellness and advanced healthcare. Its mandate covers research, clinical trials, manufacturing, delivery and patient clinics. It will also use a science-led framework that adjusts regulation according to the level of risk involved in a treatment.

Hashemi believes clearer rules could help separate healthcare providers that publish clinical outcomes from businesses relying on untested claims.

“For serious operators it means a clear pathway and rules worth building against. For patients it’s the difference between a regulated therapy and a leap of faith. For providers already running clinical research and publishing outcomes, it raises the floor of the whole market to a standard some of us have been arguing for over years.”

The authority could also support Dubai’s ambition to become a global centre for longevity medicine. Hashemi said the emirate has capital, clinical infrastructure, regulatory capacity and the ability to move quickly. The region’s high burden of metabolic disease also gives the sector a clear public health role.

“I’d temper my enthusiasm in one respect, and I mean it as a compliment to the idea rather than a criticism. The entire value of a regulator like this comes down to the evidentiary bar it sets and then holds. Set it high and it becomes a genuine mark of quality, the thing that separates medicine from wellness theater,” he said.

The real goal is staying healthier for longer

The promise behind Humanmaxxing can easily become tangled in the idea of extending life as far as possible but longevity experts argue otherwise.

“The biggest one is that living longer is mostly about adding years at the end. It isn’t. It’s about the middle,” Hashemi said.

“Most people picture longevity as extending the tail of life, more time in the stretch nobody actually wants more of. The real work is compressing morbidity: pushing the onset of decline so late that you’re at more or less full function into your eighties and then go quickly, rather than fading for two decades,” he explained.

In recent times, people are treating longevity as “something you buy at sixty, ideally somewhere expensive and far away,” which he described as a “misconception.”

Hashemi argues that longevity decisons “don’t require a plane ticket or a five-figure membership. What they need is a care model that watches the data continuously and keeps you consistent.”

‘By the time most people start caring about longevity, they’re negotiating with compound interest they’ve already run up. The good news is that the same math runs in your favour if you start early. Stay boringly consistent and the returns compound into something outsized. Longevity isn’t really an intervention. It behaves more like a portfolio, and like any portfolio, time in the market beats timing the market,” he concluded.

excerpt.rendered: From supplement stacks and full-body scans to peptides, wearables and GLP-1 drugs, the race to optimise the human body has become a booming industry but the evidence to a longer life is in simpler answers

title.rendered: UAE Jaywan cards to work in more than 183 countries under UnionPay deal

content.rendered:
UAE Jaywan cardholders will be able to use mono-badged cards at more than 100 million points of sale and 1.8 million ATMs across more than 183 countries and regions under an agreement between Al Etihad Payments and UnionPay International.

Al Etihad Payments (AEP), owner and operator of the UAE’s national switch and Jaywan domestic card scheme, has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with UnionPay International to facilitate the global acceptance of Jaywan mono-badged cards through the UnionPay network.

The agreement is designed to expand the international use of the UAE’s domestic payment scheme and improve the efficiency of cross-border payments.

Where will UAE Jaywan cards work internationally?

Under the collaboration, holders of Jaywan mono-badged cards will be able to use them across UnionPay’s international network.

This includes more than:

  • 100 million points of sale
  • 1.8 million ATMs
  • 183 countries and regions

The agreement significantly expands the potential international reach of Jaywan mono-badged cards.

The source does not provide a specific date for when the expanded global acceptance will become available to cardholders.

How will Jaywan cards work outside the UAE?

Under the MoU, UnionPay will route Jaywan card transactions made outside the UAE to the UAE National Switch.

The National Switch is operated by Al Etihad Payments. Settlement arrangements will be governed by a separate MoU.

That agreement will include the provision of settlement, liquidity and foreign exchange services to support the international expansion of the Jaywan scheme.

UAE Jaywan expands global reach

The agreement was signed at UnionPay International’s headquarters in Shanghai.

Saif Humaid Al Dhaheri, Chairman of Al Etihad Payments, and Dong Junfeng, Chairman of China UnionPay and UnionPay International, signed the MoU. Al Dhaheri said the agreement represents an important step in supporting the global expansion of Jaywan and enhancing the efficiency of cross-border payments.

The collaboration is intended to facilitate trade, tourism and economic cooperation while creating more opportunities for Jaywan cards to be used internationally.

It is also designed to strengthen Jaywan’s position among global payment schemes.

UAE-China cross-border payments

Junfeng said the strategic partnership between China and the UAE continues to deepen, creating growing demand for seamless cross-border payment services across trade and tourism.

“Building on the MoU on cross-border payments signed by the two central banks in 2025, these agreements will strengthen the global competitiveness and operational resilience of the UAE’s domestic payment brand. Furthermore, this partnership will significantly improve local currency settlement efficiency and support bilateral trade ties,” he said.

How do Jaywan-UnionPay cards currently work?

The latest collaboration builds on an existing partnership between Al Etihad Payments and UnionPay for the issuance of co-badged Jaywan–UnionPay cards by financial institutions in the UAE.

Under that existing arrangement, domestic transactions are processed through the Jaywan scheme.

International transactions are processed through the UnionPay International network. The new MoU relates specifically to facilitating international acceptance of Jaywan mono-badged cards through the UnionPay network.

excerpt.rendered: UAE Jaywan cardholders will be able to pay at more than 100m points of sale and use 1.8m ATMs across 183-plus countries and regions under a UnionPay deal

title.rendered: Dubai property foreign investment jumps 26% to $40.4bn as 29,312 new investors enter market

content.rendered:
Foreign investment in Dubai real estate reached AED148.35bn ($40.4bn) in Q1 2026, jumping 26 per cent year on year as international capital continued to flow into the emirate’s property market.

Dubai attracted 48,448 property investors during the quarter, including 29,312 new investors, while total real estate transactions reached AED252bn ($68.6bn), rising 31 per cent in value.

The figures reinforce the increasing importance of international investment to Dubai real estate, with Provident Estate arguing that the market is moving beyond cyclical recovery towards a deeper phase of structural growth.

Foreign investment in Dubai property reached AED148.35bn ($40.4bn) during the first three months of 2026. That represented a 26 per cent year-on-year increase.

The number of foreign investments also increased 11 per cent to 48,445.

Dubai real estate foreign investors

Dubai attracted a total of 48,448 property investors during Q1, including 29,312 new investors.

The number of new entrants increased 14 per cent compared with the same period a year earlier.

Together, the figures show growth in both international capital and the number of new participants entering Dubai’s real estate market.

Total real estate transactions reached AED252bn ($68.6bn) during Q1 2026, rising 31 per cent in value. Real estate investment reached AED173bn ($47.1bn) across 57,744 investments during the quarter.

Investment value increased 22 per cent year on year, compared with a 7 per cent increase in the number of investments.

The faster increase in investment value indicates that the average amount of capital represented by each investment increased overall.

Dubai real estate analysis

Loai Al Fakir, CEO of Provident Estate, said Dubai’s current property cycle should no longer be viewed solely through the lens of recovery. “Recovery means returning to where a market was before. Dubai is now operating at a different scale. The more important story behind AED252bn in transactions is the composition of that growth: foreign capital is increasing, thousands of new investors are entering and investment values are rising faster than participation. Those are indicators of a market gaining depth, not simply volume.”

Dubai’s luxury property sector also recorded an increase in investment. Luxury real estate investment climbed 26 per cent to AED87.71bn ($23.9bn) during the quarter.

The growing international investor base is also changing how Dubai competes for global property capital.

According to the source, investment decisions are increasingly influenced by a combination of economic growth, long-term residency, taxation, infrastructure investment, rental demand and Dubai’s position as a regional business and wealth hub.

This is increasingly placing Dubai in competition with a wider range of international investment destinations rather than solely regional property markets.

Dubai property investors

Rising capital inflows do not guarantee equal performance across every property development.

As new supply increases and buyers have more choice, investors are becoming increasingly selective about where they allocate capital.

Mohammad Jaafari, Off-Plan and Operations Director at Provident Estate, said the change is increasingly evident in Dubai’s off-plan market. “A growing market does not make every project a strong investment. Buyers are becoming far more analytical. They are comparing price per square foot, future supply, developer delivery history, payment structures, rental demand and exit liquidity before committing. That level of scrutiny is a sign of a market becoming more sophisticated.”

The Q1 performance follows a period of record real estate activity in Dubai.

The supplied source states that the emirate recorded 226,000 real estate transactions worth AED761bn ($207.2bn) in 2024. Transaction volume increased 36 per cent while value rose 20 per cent year on year.

The latest Q1 figures show transaction value continuing to increase from a high base.

Dubai rental market

Dubai’s rental sector is also providing a wider demand base for the property market. A total of 1.38 million tenancy contracts worth AED126.4bn ($34.4bn) were registered in 2025.

Contract volumes increased 6 per cent, while their total value rose 17 per cent.

The source argues that expansion of the rental sector alongside property sales and investment activity is providing a broader demand base for ownership.

It characterises the wider market as moving from a recovery-led cycle towards structural expansion, supported by population growth, international wealth flows, business formation, infrastructure investment and a growing pool of long-term residents.

What comes next?

Future transaction records will provide one measure of the emirate’s property performance, but the source identifies several other indicators as important to the market’s longer-term development.

These include whether foreign capital continues to increase, whether new investors remain in the market, how effectively future property supply is absorbed and whether rental and resale demand can support values beyond the initial launch cycle.

Al Fakir said: “Records show momentum. Market depth determines longevity. Dubai’s next phase will be defined by whether the diversity and quality of capital continue to grow alongside transaction values.”

With AED148.35bn ($40.4bn) of foreign investment, 29,312 new investors and AED252bn ($68.6bn) in total transactions during the first three months of 2026, the data show an increasingly large and internationally driven property market.

title.rendered: UAE seizes 8.45m non-compliant products as tax inspections surge 21%

content.rendered:
UAE tax authorities seized 8.45m non-compliant excise products during the first half of 2026 as the number of field inspections across local markets increased by 21 per cent.

The Federal Tax Authority (FTA) carried out approximately 103,680 inspection visits during the six-month period, while the total value of tax dues and fines associated with goods seized during the inspections exceeded AED174m ($47.4m).

The authority said the inspections formed part of regulatory efforts carried out in cooperation with relevant entities to enhance tax compliance, protect consumers and combat tax evasion.

The FTA conducted approximately 103,680 field inspection visits across local markets during the first six months of 2026.

That represented a 21 per cent increase from approximately 86,000 inspections during the same period in 2025. The visits were conducted across all emirates.

UAE tax inspections

Abdulaziz Mohammed Al Mulla, Director-General of the FTA, said: “The authority is also fully committed to protecting consumers, combating commercial fraud, and preventing the trade of low-quality and counterfeit products that negatively affect quality of life.”

FTA teams seized and confiscated 8.45m non-compliant excise products during the first half of the year. That compares with 17.6 million products during the corresponding period of 2025.

Tobacco and tobacco products accounted for the majority of this year’s seizures. Authorities seized 6.58m non-compliant packages of tobacco and tobacco products, compared with 15.8m during H1 2025.

A further 1.87m non-compliant packages of other excise goods were seized. These included carbonated drinks, energy drinks and sweetened beverages. The comparable figure for these other excise goods was 1.7m packages during the first six months of 2025.

Tax dues and fines

Sarah AlHabshi, Executive Director of the Tax Compliance Sector at the FTA, said the indicators demonstrate that the authority’s inspection campaigns delivered strong regulatory outcomes.

The total value of tax dues and fines associated with the non-compliant goods seized during inspection visits in the first six months of 2026 exceeded AED174m ($47.4m).

The figure represents the combined value of tax dues and fines associated with the seized goods, rather than fines alone.

The FTA also issued 3,343 registration notices to people who were not registered for Value Added Tax. That compares with 2,845 notices issued during the corresponding period last year.

Inspections are designed to check compliance with tax legislation, including requirements surrounding the issuance of tax invoices for sales.

Officials also check that tax-inclusive prices are displayed and that tax due on products traded in UAE markets is paid. The inspections are additionally used to identify cases of tax evasion and other violations of applicable tax legislation.

UAE steps up tax compliance inspections

Al Mulla highlighted cooperation between the FTA and other federal and local entities involved in regulatory operations.

He said, “The close and ongoing cooperation between the authority and its strategic partners from the relevant federal and local entities is a key factor in enhancing the efficiency, speed, and effectiveness of regulatory operations across all areas of the UAE.

“This is achieved through the exchange of information and the utilisation of the advanced capabilities available to the relevant entities, including qualified personnel, logistical support services, and monitoring and tracking systems that comply with international best practices.”

The FTA said its regulatory efforts are intended to enhance tax compliance, protect consumer rights and combat tax evasion across the UAE.

excerpt.rendered: UAE tax inspectors conducted 103,680 visits in H1 2026, seizing 8.45m non-compliant products linked to more than $47m in tax dues and fines

title.rendered: How Saudi Arabia coordinates cloud seeding as new operations centre opens

content.rendered:
Saudi Arabia has opened a new operations facility bringing together the teams responsible for weather forecasting, aviation, ground services and cloud-seeding technology as the Kingdom develops the infrastructure supporting its Regional Cloud Seeding Program.

The advanced briefing room at the National Centre for Meteorology (NCM) headquarters can accommodate up to 60 people across five operational teams, with a unified platform used to review weather forecasts and operational plans and assess the readiness of aircraft, systems and personnel.

The new facility is designed to bring the different operational elements involved in Saudi Arabia’s cloud-seeding programme into a shared working environment.

Saudi cloud seeding

It integrates:

  • Meteorological operations
  • Aviation
  • Ground services
  • Cloud-seeding technologies
  • Technical teams
  • Relevant departments

The approach is intended to strengthen coordination between the teams and entities involved in cloud-seeding operations.

It also aims to accelerate decision-making, improve implementation efficiency and increase operational readiness.

How are weather forecasts used in cloud-seeding operations?

The new facility provides an integrated platform through which teams can review the information required to support daily operations.

This includes displaying data and performance indicators and reviewing weather forecasts and operational plans.

Teams can also use the platform to assess the readiness of aircraft, systems and personnel involved in operations.

Bringing the different functions together is intended to improve communication, speed up response times and support faster decision-making.

The shared environment is also designed to allow operational issues to be identified and resolved promptly.

Saudi cloud-seeding facility brings together five teams

The advanced briefing room comprises five operational teams and can accommodate up to 60 people. It also includes 16 office spaces.

The facility is intended to serve purposes beyond daily operations.

It provides an environment for workshops, training programmes and knowledge-sharing sessions through a unified platform covering operational, technical and training requirements.

National Centre for Meteorology (NCM) CEO and General Supervisor of the Regional Cloud Seeding Program Dr. Ayman bin Salem Ghulam inaugurated the advanced cloud seeding operations briefing room on Monday.

The inauguration took place at NCM headquarters in the presence of a number of the centre’s leaders and officials.

The facility forms part of efforts to develop the Regional Cloud Seeding Program’s working environment and strengthen integration and coordination between relevant teams and entities.

During the inauguration, Ghulam stressed the importance of continuing to develop the programme’s operations and making optimal use of modern capabilities and technologies to enhance operational readiness and efficiency.

He also underscored the importance of teamwork and strengthening coordination between all teams involved in cloud-seeding operations.

Saudi Arabia focuses on cloud-seeding technology and training

The new facility combines operational, technical and training functions within the same environment.

NCM said the approach is designed to unify efforts towards achieving the Regional Cloud Seeding Program’s operational objectives.

Ghulam praised the programme teams for their field, technical and operational efforts.

He also affirmed support for developing and empowering their capabilities, providing an appropriate environment in which they can perform their duties efficiently and continuously improving the tools and methods used to achieve the programme’s objectives and enhance the quality of its operations.

The new Saudi facility is intended to support that approach by allowing meteorological, aviation, ground-service and technical functions to operate within a shared environment, with access to operational data, forecasts, plans and readiness information.

excerpt.rendered: Saudi Arabia has opened a new cloud seeding operations centre bringing together weather forecasts, aircraft readiness and five specialist teams

title.rendered: MENA M&A deals hit $46.7bn as UAE and Saudi Arabia drive outbound investment

content.rendered:
The MENA region recorded 390 mergers and acquisitions worth $46.7bn in the first half of 2026, with domestic and outbound investment helping sustain dealmaking despite geopolitical developments.

The UAE and Saudi Arabia remained the region’s most active outbound investors, while sovereign wealth funds and government-related entities continued to deploy capital across strategic sectors, according to the latest EY MENA M&A Insights report.

M&A activity moderated compared with the first half of 2025, when the region recorded 434 deals worth $58.8bn.

However, deal momentum accelerated during the second quarter of 2026, supported by sustained domestic and outbound activity and continued sovereign investment.

The improvement was particularly pronounced towards the end of the quarter. May and June accounted for 61 per cent of Q2 deal volume and 79 per cent of deal value.

MENA M&A deals reach $46.7bn

Large transactions valued at more than $500m contributed nearly three-quarters of total deal value between March and June, indicating renewed confidence in strategic, high-value investments.

Brad Watson, MENA EY-Parthenon Leader, said: “The first half of 2026 has shown the strength and resilience of MENA’s M&A market, with strategic investors continuing to pursue long-term growth opportunities despite a more measured global investment environment.

“Strong domestic capital deployment, active sovereign investors and the region’s continued focus on economic diversification have helped sustain deal activity, while improving momentum towards the end of the second quarter reflects growing confidence in the region’s long-term investment outlook.”

Domestic and outbound transactions remained the primary drivers of M&A activity during the first six months of 2026.

Domestic deal value accelerated significantly between March and June, reaching $16bn — more than four times the value recorded during the same period last year.

Domestic investment accelerates

Several large transactions across real estate, power and utilities and technology helped drive the increase.

Government-related entities continued to play a leading role in domestic dealmaking, reinforcing ongoing investment in infrastructure and national transformation programmes.

Outbound investment remained resilient, with 119 deals worth $25.5bn completed during the first half of 2026.

Regional investors continued to pursue strategic opportunities across technology, transportation, financial services and energy-related sectors.

The UAE and Saudi Arabia were the MENA region’s most active outbound investors, according to the report.

UAE and Saudi Arabia lead outbound M&A

Among the landmark transactions was Dubai Aerospace Enterprise’s $7bn acquisition of Macquarie AirFinance.

Saudi Electronic Gaming Holding Company’s acquisition of Shanghai Moonton Technology for $6bn was another major transaction during the period.

Anil Menon, MENA EY-Parthenon Head of M&A and Equity Capital Markets Leader, said: “The first half of 2026 reflects a disciplined investment environment, with investors continuing to prioritize transactions that support long-term strategic objectives.

“While geopolitical developments have influenced the pace of inbound activity, domestic and outbound investment has remained resilient, supported by strong corporate balance sheets, sovereign capital and continued investment across priority sectors. As market conditions continue to stabilize, we expect strategic, high-quality assets to remain at the center of M&A activity across the region.”

Technology remains M&A priority

Inbound investment moderated amid geopolitical uncertainty, but technology remained a priority for investors.

The sector accounted for the largest share of inbound deal value between March and June.

Investor interest was concentrated on AI-driven solutions, enterprise digitalisation, software platforms and technology-enabled business services, highlighting the strategic importance of the technology sector across MENA.

The UAE remained the region’s preferred destination for inbound investment, supported by its diversified economy and business-friendly regulatory environment.

Sovereign wealth funds shape MENA deals

Sovereign wealth funds and government-related entities also remained central to regional dealmaking throughout the first half of 2026.

Capital continued to be deployed across strategic sectors in line with long-term economic diversification agendas.

The EY report identified institutions including ADIA, PIF and Mubadala as continuing to play a pivotal role in shaping M&A activity across the region.

excerpt.rendered: MENA recorded 390 M&A deals worth $46.7bn in H1 2026, as UAE and Saudi investors drove outbound activity and sovereign capital supported dealmaking

title.rendered: Saudi Arabia’s flynas signs first government travel agreement, services to start in Q4 2026

content.rendered:
Saudi Arabia’s flynas has signed a deal to provide government travel services, marking the first time in the airline’s history that it has entered into such an arrangement.

The agreement was signed with the Expenditure and Projects Efficiency Authority (EXPRO) on behalf of government entities, with flynas targeting the beginning of the fourth quarter of 2026 to commence services following the completion of technical integration.

The agreement will enable flynas to provide government travel services within the low-cost aviation sector to government entities.

EXPRO signed the agreement on behalf of government entities in its capacity as the competent authority for unified strategic procurement under Saudi Arabia’s Government Tenders and Procurement Law.

The agreement represents the first time in flynas’s history that the airline has entered into such an arrangement.

flynas signs Saudi government travel agreement

flynas said it is now working with the relevant government entities to complete the technical integration necessary to activate the agreement.

The integration is expected to be completed in time for government travel services to begin at the start of the fourth quarter of 2026.

The agreement is also expected to begin having a financial impact on flynas during the fourth quarter.

However, this is subject to the technical integration being completed according to the targeted timeline.

The Saudi carrier did not provide an estimate for the value of the agreement or its expected contribution to revenue or profit in the supplied announcement.

The airline said it will announce any material developments relating to the agreement in accordance with applicable laws and regulations.

2,000 flights a week

flynas is the first airline listed on the Saudi Exchange (Tadawul).

The airline operates 156 routes serving more than 80 domestic and international destinations across 38 countries.

Its network comprises more than 2,000 weekly flights and the airline has carried 110 million passengers since launching in 2007.

Under its growth and expansion plan, the carrier aims to reach 165 domestic and international destinations, in line with the objectives of Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030.

excerpt.rendered: Saudi airline flynas has signed its first government travel framework agreement with EXPRO, with services and the expected financial impact starting in Q4 2026

title.rendered: Jeddah Tower reaches halfway to Burj Khalifa as Saudi megaproject rises

content.rendered:
Saudi Arabia’s Jeddah Tower has reached 430 metres and 106 levels as construction advances towards a planned height above 1,000 metres.

Kingdom Holding confirmed the milestone in its second quarter 2026 results. More than 300,000 cubic metres of concrete have been poured. Around 6,400 workers are deployed at the Jeddah site.

Prince Alwaleed bin Talal, Chairman of Kingdom Holding, inspected construction teams as vertical works continued. He said crews would complete “the tallest tower in the world”.

Jeddah Tower’s 430 metre elevation exceeds half the height of Dubai’s Burj Khalifa. Dubai’s landmark retains the global record among completed skyscrapers at 828 metres.

Construction passes 100-floor threshold

Kingdom Holding reports that structural works have passed 100 floors and remain on schedule. Concrete placement has reached about 67 per cent of the project’s planned requirement.

Site activity also covers façade installation and mechanical, electrical and plumbing packages.

Contractors have installed more than 3,000 façade panels. Kingdom Holding puts façade completion at about 11 per cent. MEP first fix installation continues across completed sections of the structure.

Workforce deployment has expanded alongside the tower’s vertical rise. Nearly 6,400 personnel are working across the project.

Kingdom Holding records more than 16 million working hours without a lost time incident and zero fatalities. The safety performance covers the current construction programme reported with its second quarter results.

Concrete volumes above 300,000 cubic metres indicate the scale of structural work already completed. Remaining works include further vertical construction, façade packages, building services and internal fit-out.

Vertical transport system takes shape

Jeddah Tower will provide about 530,000 square metres of built area when completed. Planned uses span residential, hospitality, office and observation facilities within the supertall structure.

Vertical transport requirements reflect the tower’s planned height.

Design specifications include 59 elevators, comprising 54 single-deck units and five double-deck elevators. Another 12 escalators will serve circulation requirements across the building.

Observatory elevators are designed to travel at 10 metres per second in both directions. That system will handle passenger movement across a building planned to exceed one kilometre.

Adrian Smith and Gordon Gill Architecture designed Jeddah Tower. The US-based practice also designed Burj Khalifa in Dubai.

Engineering requirements intensify as construction moves higher. Concrete pumping, façade access, vertical logistics and workforce movement require longer operating cycles as floor elevation increases.

Kingdom Holding reports wider project progress

Kingdom Holding’s second quarter disclosure places Jeddah Tower within a wider land and real estate portfolio concentrated in Riyadh and Jeddah Economic City.

Company land holdings reached SAR15.1 billion during the reporting period. That equals about $4.03 billion (AED14.8 billion) at prevailing currency pegs.

Kingdom Holding retained Jeddah Economic City at its year-end 2025 valuation despite substantial construction progress during 2026. Management plans to reassess that valuation at the end of 2026.

First half revenue reached about $320 million (AED1.18 billion), based on reported revenue of SAR1.2 billion. Revenue declined 12 per cent from the corresponding 2025 period.

Net profit fell 27 per cent year on year during the first half. Second quarter revenue declined 1 per cent, while quarterly net profit decreased 16 per cent.

Dubai retains the completed height benchmark

Burj Khalifa remains the world’s tallest completed skyscraper at 828 metres. Jeddah Tower is designed to exceed 1,000 metres once construction reaches its planned final elevation.

Dubai continues to hold a substantial concentration of completed supertall buildings. Burj Khalifa anchors that vertical development record alongside multiple towers ranked among the world’s tallest completed structures.

Jeddah Tower’s latest construction figures place the Saudi project at 430 metres. Structural work, façade installation and MEP deployment are progressing simultaneously as contractors extend the building above its 106 reported levels.
